fewer grain boundaries per unit volume, which are typically regions of  higher resistance to ion or electron transport. Furthermore, higher  temperatures promote densification by reducing the number and size of  pores, improving the contact between grains and thus lowering the  interfacial impedance. However, excessively high sintering tempera­ tures can sometimes lead to secondary phase formation, elemental  volatilization, or abnormal grain growth, which may counter the bene­ ficial effects and potentially increase interfacial impedance. Therefore,  an optimal sintering temperature range exists for minimizing grain  boundary resistance [25–27]. Other material options are also being  researched. Wang et al. at MIT mixed ion-electronic conductor tubes  were filled with lithium (anode), such that the tubes are coated and thus  are protected from the electrolyte, preventing dendrite formation [28].  Furthermore, the tube’s 3D honeycomb architecture permits expan­ sion/contraction that occurs during the charge/discharge process to  avoid cracking. Such research on the optimization of anode and cathode  materials can also help improve the energy density of SSBs. Coating  techniques, such as those explored by Wang et al. can further improve  thermodynamic instabilities. Other ways to improve energy density are  being explored with thinner electrolyte layers, which are also reported  to improve the economic attractiveness of SSBs, Therefore, such im­ provements are multifaceted, and future work should continue to search  for optimized materials, manufacturing methods, and life-time proper­ ties of SSBs, as this will not only make them more efficient, but also more  cost effective in comparison to liquid electrolyte batteries. 2. Manufacturing steps for SSBs 2.1. Transition to SSBs The increased efficiency, capacity, and safety features have ramped  up the industry efforts to transition from lithium-ion batteries to solid-  state batteries [29]. The movement of ions is facilitated by a solid  electrolyte in solid-state batteries. The transition to solid-state batteries  could increase the safety of batteries and improve the driving range  needed to widely adopt the use of electric vehicles. Solid-state batteries  use inorganic solid-state conductors that are non-flammable or have  higher resistance to temperature in comparison to lithium-ion batteries  which use organic liquid electrolytes [30]. The reactions that take place  between the liquid electrolyte and the electrodes also contribute to the  degradation of the battery. The use of a thermodynamically stable  inorganic material can mitigate the decomposition of the battery elec­ trolyte. The lack of solid materials containing ionic conductivities  similar to liquid electrolytes at room temperature has partly limited the  development of solid-state batteries. Recently, several solid electrolytes  have been reported to have an ionic conductivity that is similar or higher  than liquid electrolytes. However, the high conductivity is often nulli­ fied by the high impedance present at the interface between the elec­ trode and the solid electrolyte. The addition of a buffer layer between  the solid electrolyte and electrode is one of the most common strategies  that has been developed to reduce the impact of the reactions that occur  at the interface. Solid-state batteries have emerged as one of the more realistic ad­ vancements to follow-up on the progress of lithium-ion batteries [3].  Bipolar stacking in solid-state batteries make high energy and power  densities possible. In addition, electrode cross-talk could be prevented  with the use of solid electrolytes. Electrode cross-talk causes instability  in lithium-ion batteries due to the chemical interactions between the  dissolved active materials. Solid-state batteries have faster charging  capabilities due to the high lithium-ion transference number of inor­ ganic solid electrolytes. Solid Power, Samsung, Toyota, and Quantum­ Scape have made significant progress in the development of solid-state  Fig. 2. Conventional Lithium-Ion battery and Solid-State battery diagrams [29]. (a) the basic composition of a conventional lithium-ion battery. (b) The composition  of a solid-state battery. The major differences are that conventional batteries contain a porous anode and cathode while the solid-state battery consists of a metal  anode, solid electrolyte, and solid composite cathode. (c) The conventional solid oxide fuel cell is similar to the conventional lithium battery with the exception of the  solid electrolyte. battery technology. The safe use of high voltage cathode materials is one  of the main advantages of solid-state batteries [31]. In contrast, the  limited electrochemical stability window of liquid electrolytes does not  allow for the use of these cathode materials. 2.2. The manufacturing process for SSBs A study conducted by Schnell et al. compares the production of  lithium-ion cells with the manufacturing processes for sulfide based  solid-state batteries [32]. The study shows that the processes for com­ posite electrode production could be modified to fit solid-state battery  applications. However, the inclusion of a lithium metal anode and the  production of the solid electrolyte separator layer will need to be  developed completely. Solid-state batteries use lithium metal as the  anode material, which is enabled by the compact solid electrolyte  capable of acting as a barrier for lithium dendrites. The lithium metal  creates a dense lithium anode as opposed to the porous anode used in the  conventional lithium-ion battery. In addition, a dense cathode com­ posite is used instead of a porous cathode. The layers are serially stacked  in a dense manner as shown in Fig. 3b. The serial stacking is capable of  increasing the voltage of a battery cell and optimizing the packaging  design. Solid-state batteries also do not require the use of flammable  organic components, so a cooling system is not needed. This makes  solid-state batteries a much safer alternative to the conventional  lithium-ion batteries. Further research has shown that one of the main limiting factors of  solid-state batteries is low ionic conductivity of the solid electrolyte  [33]. Another critical bottleneck is the need for solid-state battery  components with stable interfaces, which includes the solid electrolyte,  conductive additives, and active material [34]. These major limiting  factors along with the other associated limitations need to be resolved in  order to efficiently manufacture solid-state batteries. Recently, solid  electrolytes with adequate ionic conductivities have been achieved;  however, engineering solid/solid interfaces with low impedance con­ tinues to be a challenge. Reaching the ideal composition could theo­ retically require extensive trial and error studies, which are both costly  and time consuming. As a result, computational models have been used  in various systems to predict the stability of solid electrolytes. High-capacity anodes with low potentials could help achieve specific  energies comparable with those of lithium-ion batteries [3]. One of the  most important things when it comes to charging batteries is that the  capacity is not affected. Therefore, it is imperative that the anodes used  for solid-state batteries allow a reversible high-rate operation. Currently,  a silicon-based anode or lithium metal anode are the most probable to be  used for the application of solid-state batteries. Abundant silicon anodes  with ultrahigh theoretical capacity (4200 mAh/g) are one of the most  promising options due to their extensive commercial prospects [35]. One of the main goals of current battery development is to design  reversible lithium metal anodes that have high-rate capability [36].  Lithium metal anodes are capable of increasing the energy density of  batteries that use intercalation-type cathodes. Specifically, lithium  metal has a high theoretical capacity of 3860 mAh/g [37]. Solid-state  batteries that use lithium metal anodes in tandem with solid electro­ lyte separators are promising because they are capable of preventing  dendritic growth of lithium in the cell. The use of inorganic solid electrolytes for solid-state batteries is  beneficial because they are potentially safer than conventional batteries  [38]. The ionic conductivities and mechanical properties of solid elec­ trolytes are crucial for energy density and cycle performance improve­ ments. Solid electrolytes such as Li7P3S11, Li10GeP2S12, and Na3PS4 have  reportedly shown high ionic conductivities, and in some cases, similar to  those of liquid electrolytes. There are several key features that solid  electrolytes must include such as high ionic conductivity, minimal  electrical conductivity, and the compound must be compatible with the  anode and cathode materials [39]. The cathode is capable of oxidizing  the solid electrolyte if the highest occupied molecular orbital of the  electrolyte is above that of the cathode. Inclusively, it is important that  the electrolytes act solely as an ion-conducting solid and do not actively  take part in the insertion and extraction process of lithium. Hitachi Zosen Corporation has reportedly designed a solid-state  battery using machine technology via a proprietary fabrication process  [40]. The structure consists of laminated positive electrode, solid elec­ trolyte, and negative electrode layers. The solid electrolyte acts as a  separator that successfully prevents contact between the positive and  negative electrode interfaces while enabling the flow of lithium ions.  The proprietary battery uses a non-flammable solid electrolyte. The  company performed a nail penetration test on the battery and it did not  smoke, ignite or explode, whereas conventional batteries would have  ignited. In addition, the battery has a wide operating temperature range  because the electrolyte does not solidify at low temperatures or  Fig. 3. It also con­ tains a configuration that does not experience significant expansion even  while under vacuum. The technology operates stably at a wide range of  pressures, even in an environment of 1.0 × 10−2 Pa, and is currently  being used selectively in aerospace applications, infrastructure, indus­ trial applications and medical devices. 3. Performance analysis and observed challenges While SSBs offer high energy density and safety, their fast-charging  performance is currently limited by lower CCD and longer cycling  times compared to LIBs. However, advancements in materials and  interface design are promising for improving SSBs’ fast-charging capa­ bilities. LIBs, on the other hand, continue to lead in fast-charging per­ formance due to better ionic conductivity and optimized charging  protocols. Table 1 summarizes the comparative fast-charging perfor­ mance of SSBs and LIBs. 3.1. Ionic and electronic conductivity The ionic conductivity of the electrolyte directly impacts the bat­ tery’s capacity, power density, and cycling stability. High ionic con­ ductivity allows for fast transport of ions within the electrolyte, and  high-power output and rapid charging and discharging rates. It also  reduces the polarization and resistive losses at the electrode-electrolyte  interfaces, improving the efficiency. High ionic conductivity allows for a  larger active surface area of the electrode materials, leading to higher  capacity and energy density. Low ionic conductivity can lead to poor  battery performance, including low power output, slow charging and  discharging rates, and low energy density. This can also result in elec­ trolyte decomposition and the formation of unwanted interfacial layers,  leading to capacity fading and reduced cycle life. The differences in ionic  conductivity observed between halide electrolytes like Li3YCl6 and  Li3YBr6 primarily stem from the size and polarizability of the halide  ions, which influence the lithium ion transport pathways and energy  barriers within their crystal structures. Bromide ions (Br-) are larger and  more polarizable than chloride ions (Cl-) [50]. This larger size generally  leads to an expansion of the lattice parameters, creating wider pathways  for Li+ ion migration and potentially lowering the activation energy for  hopping between sites. The increased polarizability of Br- can also affect  the electrostatic interactions within the lattice, further influencing Li+ mobility. Consequently, Li3YBr6 often exhibits higher ionic conductivity  compared to Li3YCl6 at the same temperature [50]. However, this sub­ stitution can also impact other properties like electrochemical stability.  Besides, the densification technique significantly impacts both the me­ chanical strength and ionic conductivity of sulfide-based SSBs. Hot  pressing, which involves applying high pressure at elevated  temperatures, generally leads to higher density, enhanced grain con­ nectivity, and reduced porosity in the solid electrolyte. This improved  microstructure typically results in higher mechanical strength and  enhanced ionic conductivity due to a larger number of conducting  pathways and reduced grain boundary resistance. In contrast, cold sin­ tering, performed at lower temperatures (often room temperature) with  pressure, may result in lower density and potentially higher porosity  compared to hot pressing. While cold sintering can still yield acceptable  ionic conductivity, the mechanical strength might be lower due to  weaker inter-particle bonding. However, cold pressing is often  employed for sulfide electrolytes due to their inherent softness and  ability to achieve sufficient density without high temperatures, which  can be detrimental to the electrolyte’s stability or interface formation  with electrodes. The choice of densification technique must therefore  balance the need for high mechanical integrity and ionic conductivity  with the processing limitations and stability of the specific sulfide ma­ terial and overall battery design [51]. Electronic conductivity has a crucial role in the cathode and anode  materials of SSBs. The transport of electrons occurs at the electrode-  electrolyte interfaces, which determines how efficiently electrons can  be transported. High electronic conductivity of the electrode leads to  high interfacial resistance which means poor battery performance, and  causes issues such as low power output, voltage polarization, and ca­ pacity loss. Low electronic conductivity can limit the rate of electro­ chemical reactions and lead to slow charging and discharging rates.  Various strategies to improve the electronic conductivity of electrode  materials, such as the use of conductive additives or coatings, such as  carbon nanotubes, graphene, or metallic nanoparticles, can improve the  electronic conductivity of the electrode materials. Other strategies also  include doping the electrode materials with elements that can enhance  electronic conductivity, such as transition metals or rare earth elements.  To decouple and quantify interfacial phenomena in practical solid-state  battery architectures, several experimental techniques are proposed.  Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS) is a widely used tech­ nique to separate and quantify different resistive components within the  battery, including interfacial resistances arising from charge transfer  and ion migration at the electrode-electrolyte interfaces. By analyzing  the impedance response over a range of frequencies, individual inter­ facial contributions can be deconvoluted. In-situ and operando charac­ terization techniques such as X-ray Diffraction (XRD), Transmission  Electron Microscopy (TEM), Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), and  X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS) allow for the real-time moni­ toring of structural and chemical changes at the interfaces during bat­ tery operation. These methods can help identify the formation of  secondary phases, interfacial voids, or changes in chemical states that  contribute to interfacial impedance. Kelvin Probe Force Microscopy  (KPFM) can be employed to image the local potential variations at the  interfaces, providing insights into the potential barriers that impede ion  transport. Furthermore, thermal wave sensing using modified 3ω sensors  offers a non-invasive method to probe the morphology of the lithium  metal-solid electrolyte interface and relate the thermal interface resis­ tance to the physical structure [52,53]. Combining these techniques  provides a comprehensive approach to decouple and quantify the  complex interfacial phenomena in solid-state batteries. Tables 2–5. The ionic conductivity in solid electrolytes can be measured using  impedance spectroscopy (AC technique), where a sinusoidal potential at  various frequencies is applied to an electrochemical cell with blocking  electrodes and the response in recorded. The resulting impedance results  can be analyzed using a combination of three RC-circuits, which  represent the bulk conduction, grain boundary-conduction, and diffu­ sion due to concentration gradient in the electrode. The resistance from  each portion of the circuit can be extracted, which allows for the ionic  conductivity to be determined with a known thickness and area of the  sample [75]. The electrical conductivity is measured by employing the Hebb-  Wagner method, where one blocking and one non-blocking electrode  is applied to the material, and measuring the current at steady-state as a  function of applied potential. As one electrode is blocking, this leads to a  buildup or depletion of mobile ions at the blocking electrode that is able  to offset the applied electric potential [76]. Similar methods have been  used to measure the ionic and electronic conductivity of halides. Poly­ mer solid electrolytes utilize a different transport mechanism than  ceramic solid electrolytes. The  ion conduction mechanisms in solid electrolytes are still not fully un­ derstood, and doing so will be the key to developing better solid elec­ trolytes. A combination of density functional theory (DFT) and  molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with in-situ or experimental  methods are needed to fully understand the correlation between ionic  conductivity and composition, chemical structure, electronic structure,  and the microstructure of electrolytes. The final goal is to develop solid  electrolytes with ionic conductivity of 10−3 - 10−2 S cm−1, which is  comparable to that of liquid electrolytes [54]. 3.2. Diffusion coefficient of species In an electrolyte, diffusion occurs by the movement of ions through  the crystal lattice of the electrolyte material. The diffusion of ions in the  electrolyte is important for the ionic conductivity of the material. At the  interface between the electrode and the electrolyte, diffusion occurs as  ions move from the electrolyte into the electrode and vice versa. This is  important for the performance of the battery, as it affects the rate at  which charge can be transferred between the electrode and the elec­ trolyte. In the electrode, diffusion occurs by the movement of ions  through the electrode material. This is important for the capacity of the  battery, as it determines the amount of charge that can be stored in the  electrode. In polycrystalline materials, such as some solid electrolytes  and electrodes, diffusion can occur more quickly along grain boundaries  than through the bulk of the material. This is because grain boundaries  can have a higher concentration of defects, which can act as diffusion  pathways for ions. In SSBs, where the anode is composed of lithium metal, the bulk  atomic diffusivity of lithium is often the limiting factor in determining  the cycling behavior. Fast bulk diffusivity of lithium atoms is required to  maintain a stable interface between the lithium metal electrode and the  solid electrolyte under realistic cycling current densities. This is due to  the movement of lithium ions into the solid electrolyte during stripping,  which creates vacancies at the surface of the electrode, which causes  contact loss at the atomic scale if the diffusion of lithium atoms to the  interface is not fast enough to refill the vacancies. These vacancies can  then form voids which lead to macroscopic contact loss and an increase  in the electrode-solid electrolyte interface impedance, which can even­ tually lead to the cell failure during subsequent cycles [79]. Many  studies have reported that the internal short circuits can be caused by  the localized electrodeposition arising from the inhomogeneous inter­ facial nature of the electrode and electrolyte, which is influenced by the  intrinsically low lattice–lithium diffusivity in dynamic lithium stripping  and deposition processes [80]. It is also important to mention that  diffusion of elements and chemical reactions at the cathode/SSE inter­ face also hinder Li-ion transportation, and negatively influence battery  performance [81]. Diffusion coefficients of species in solid-state batteries are important  parameters that affect the battery’s performance. In solid-state batteries,  the movement of ions or electrons through the solid-state electrolyte or  electrode material is primarily determined by the diffusion coefficient of  the species. The diffusion coefficient is a measure of how quickly the  species can move through the material [82]. D1 = D0e −EA RT (6)  Where D0 is the exponential prefactor, EA is the activation energy of  diffusion, T is the temperature in Kelvin, and kB is the Boltzmann con­ stant. The equation fundamentally assumes a well-defined activation  energy for the hopping of atoms or ions between specific lattice sites in a  crystalline material. While amorphous phases like glassy Li3PS4 lack  long-range order and distinct lattice sites, this model can still provide a  reasonable approximation of the temperature dependence of ionic  conductivity (which is directly related to the diffusion coefficient via the  Nernst-Einstein relation) [84]. In amorphous solids, diffusion occurs  through a distribution of energy barriers and jump distances within the  disordered network structure. The experimentally observed diffusion  behavior in glassy Li3PS4 often exhibits Arrhenius-like behavior over  certain temperature ranges, suggesting that a dominant average acti­ vation energy governs the transport process [85]. However, deviations  from ideal Arrhenius behavior, such as curvature in the Arrhenius plot,  can arise due to the distribution of energy barriers and potential changes  in the diffusion mechanism with temperature in the disordered struc­ ture. Therefore, while the Arrhenius equation offers a useful simplified  description, a more complete understanding of diffusion in amorphous  materials requires considering the inherent structural disorder and the  resulting distribution of energy landscapes. To determine the diffusion  coefficient of charge-carrying ions in a solid electrolyte, a structure is  fabricated and then studied using impedance spectroscopy [86]. Anal­ ysis of the impedance of the assembled structure leads to determining  the Warburg coefficient and amplitude. The Warburg amplitude value is  related to the diffusion coefficient of the charge-carriers by the following  equation:  Aw1 = U0 ̅̅̅̅̅̅̅̅ 2D1 √ Sqc0 (7)  Where U0 is the voltage amplitude across the electrodes, D is the  diffusivity coefficient, S is surface area, q is ion charge, and c0 is the  amplitude of oscillation of the non-equilibrium concentration of charge-  carrying ions near the electrode. Solving for the diffusion coefficient in  this equation, and replacing c0, results in the following equation:  D1 = 1 2( dδ AW12Sε0εr )2 (8)  Where d is the thickness of the electrolyte layer and εr is its relative  dielectric permeability, and δ is the distance to the electrode. There are  multiple methods that can be used to determine the diffusion coefficient  of charge-carrying ions in electrode materials. The galvanostatic inter­ mittent titration technique (GITT) is the most widely used method.  However, GITT can be time-consuming and may require sophisticated  interpretation models. GITT consists of two repeating steps: (1) a con­ stant current is applied for a duration where the assumption of semi-  infinite diffusion holds, (2) the current is switched off until the  voltage becomes invariant. carrying ions. The intermittent current interruption (IC) method is  another method that can be used. For IC, repeating transient current  interruptions are applied to the cell while it is under constant-current  cycling. Then, through linear regressions of the potential change  against the square root of step time during the current pauses, the time-  independent and time-dependent parts of the resistance are calculated,  which are also called internal resistance and diffusion resistance coef­ ficient. This can also characterize the diffusion processes. Both methods  calculate the diffusion coefficient, D, using the following equation:  D = 4 π (V A ΔEOC ΔtI dE d ̅t √)2 (9)  Where V is the molar volume of the electrode materials, A is the surface  area of the electrode, EOC is the open circuit potential, ΔtI is the period  when a constant current is applied between consecutive open circuit  potential measurements, E is the electrode potential, and t is the step  time [87]. Molecular dynamics simulation is also a tool that can be used  to study transport phenomena at the molecular level. There are possible methods being used and currently being devel­ oped to increase the diffusion of species through SSBs. Reducing particle  size of the solid-state electrode and the electrolyte can increase surface  area and decrease the diffusion distance. Increasing the porosity of the  electrode can increase surface area available for ion transport. Adding  conductive additives to improve electrode conductivity which can  decrease polarization and improve the diffusion coefficients. Intro­ ducing defects (vacancies or interstitials) can create additional diffusion  pathways for ions. However, too many defects can decrease stability and  durability of the electrolyte. Controlling the diffusion of species heavily  affects the ionic conductivity of an SSE. Being about to design materials  with specific diffusion rates could be the answer to developing materials  with higher ionic conductivity. Increasing diffusion rates of lithium ions  will have a big impact on decreasing dendrite formation [89]. Fully  understanding diffusion mechanisms and being able to control diffusion  rates will ultimately lead to better performing SSBs. 3.3. Thermal issues in SSBs Thermal issues are a key concern when considering the practical  performance and overall safety of batteries and battery-integrated sys­ tems. Though not limited to solid state batteries alone, thermal issues at  the material, interface, and battery level present complex interactions of  electro-chemical factors that contribute to decision making regarding  battery manufacturing approaches and impact device functionality.  Solid state batteries are, overall, understood to improve upon the ther­ mal stability of traditional liquid electrolyte systems regarding vola­ tility, flammability, and flowability, however the testing of solid-state  thermal interactions remains within its early stages, and development  must continue to allow for a full understanding of their general thermal  behavior. A primary concern for the thermal performance of solid-state bat­ teries is the risk of thermal runaway: a chain reaction of thermal in­ teractions that results in an uncontrolled temperature increase. Thermal  runaway can occur when the battery temperature exceeds the appro­ priate working temperature, causing the release of reactive byproducts  and, at best, leading to detriment of battery performance via damage or  melting, or, at worst, causing full device combustion or explosion that  could lead to user injury and even loss of life. In 2019, in a thermal  runaway event, caused by the failure of a single lithium-ion battery cell  due to “abnormal lithium deposits”, resulted in a large fire, explosion,  and the injury of four firefighters [90]. This incident helped bring  attention to the need for improved battery storage considerations for  thermal runaway prevention measures such as barriers to propagation  and a standardized response procedure. In the design of solid-state  batteries thermo-chemical interactions must be analyzed carefully and  comprehensively to allow a complete understanding of how the battery  system behaves under a range of thermal conditions at all levels. In addition to thermal runaway, researchers, developers, and man­ ufacturers of solid-state batteries must also consider the possibility, and  subsequent consequences, of morphological changes at the electrolyte  level caused by thermal exposure. Melting, shrinkage, and cracking of  solid electrolyte components under heating conditions can hinder  Fig. 4. electrochemical performance and ionic conductivity by altering the  interfacial interactions between the solid electrolyte and electrodes  within the battery. Additionally, the application of thermal variability to  solid-state batteries can cause material level decomposition behaviors  that could result in the emission of hazardous byproducts, leading back  to the possibility of thermal runaway and potential user harm [91].  Careful consideration of thermal safety at all levels for solid state battery  design, from material selection to interface and battery level in­ teractions, allows for the design and manufacture of solid-state systems  that permit for the maximization of energetic performance and user  safety. 3.3.1. Materials level analysis of thermal stability Within the field of solid-state battery development there exist several  key categories that are defined by their primary solid electrolyte mate­ rial selection: polymer, oxide, sulfide, hydride, and sulfide. Each  possible material selection provides a unique set of thermal character­ istics and interactions that define their feasibility and performance  within overall battery function. Primary temperature testing must pro­ vide definition for the key transition temperatures of the electrolyte  material alone. These values include crystallization temperature (TC),  glass transition temperature (TG), melting point (TM), and decomposi­ tion temperature (Tdec), which can be calculated using Differential  Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) or Differential Thermal Analysis (DTA).  These analysis methods utilize comparison of thermal behavior of a  sample with a known reference material to determine the temperatures  at which exothermic and endothermic events occur, indicating occur­ rence of reaction or transition events. As indicated in Fig. 6b the overall  decomposition temperatures of solid-state electrolytes are, for the most  part, higher than those of liquid batteries, with oxide and sulfide elec­ trolytes offering the highest overall decomposition temperatures.  Thermal stability characteristics are mostly determined by structural  properties of the material such as crystallinity, elemental combination,  and even degree of polymerization in the case of polymers. Material  level thermal stability can become a concern when thermal exposure  results in the morphological alteration of the electrolyte material, or the  release of hazardous or reactive byproducts. Polymer materials such as polyethylene oxide (PEO) and polymethyl  methacrylate (PMMA) are common choices in solid state polymer elec­ trolyte design for their high interfacial contact capabilities and chemical  stability, however, polymer materials suffer from relatively low tem­ perature thermal decomposition, typically below 400◦C [96]. Specific  polymer electrolyte decomposition and melting patterns are largely  influenced by the material composition, polymer chain length, and  polymer chemical structure. In some cases, composite polymer electro­ lytes are designed to integrate coordination between different polymer  types, or between polymers and inorganic materials, to improve elec­ trochemical performance or thermal stability. Magnesium aluminate  nanoparticle fillers, for example, have been shown to raise the decom­ position  temperature  of  polyethylene  oxide  lithium  hexa­ fluorophosphate (PEO-LiPF6) from about 200◦C to above 300◦C. In  addition to selective design of composite polymer electrolytes, thermal  stability at the material level can be further improved through careful  selection of fabrication methods as a means of controlling the polymer  crystallinity as it is intimately related to thermal decomposition tem­ perature. Construction of multilayer solid electrolytes can inhibit  interfacial reactivity while improving thermal stability, and heat treat­ ment processing can stabilize thermal reactivity by decreasing  Fig. 5. Composite solid electrolytes offer many improvements over other types of solid electrolytes [77]. R. Shang et al.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Nano Energy 142 (2025) 111232  11

crystalline impedance [96]. Among the material categorizations of solid electrolytes, oxides  provide the highest level of thermal stability with decomposition tem­ peratures ranging from 800 to 1600◦C due to their valent electron dis­ tributions and whether energetically stable configurations can be  formed [97]. The decomposition temperature for LATP(Li1.5A10.5­ Ti1.5(PO4)3), for example, is as high as 1394 K or about 1120◦C. Despite  their high thermal stability, oxide material electrolytes suffer from  morphological deformation with increasing temperature exposure.  These electrolytes undergo transitions in response to heat treatment that  cause structural defects such as shrinking and cracking that can interfere  with interfacial stability and efficiency of ionic conductivity. In the case  of ATP(Li1.5A10.5Ti1.5(PO4)3) morphological deformation is primarily  the result of the AlPO4 transitional production, and researchers have had  success in minimizing this production using Nb (niobium pentachloride)  doping [33]. Overall, although oxide solid electrolytes can provide a  high standard for thermal stability, formation of reactive byproducts  and risk of morphological deformation must be accounted for while  electrochemical and thermal properties are optimized. Similar to oxide solid electrolytes, sulfide solid electrolytes provide  high degradation temperatures, however, their thermal decomposition  may result in the formation of unfavorable byproducts, the most con­ cerning being highly toxic H2S gas [98]. When heated, sulfide electro­ lytes typically experience phase transitions that can alter ionic  conductivity. Li3PS4, for example, has three structural phases: α, β, and γ  with the β phase converting to α at about 500◦C, and no longer being  Fig. 6. capable of reverting to β, but instead forming the γ structure during the  cooling process, with an ionic conductivity of only 3 × 10−7 S cm−1  [99]. Structural alteration upon heating has also been observed, such as  in the case of Li7P3S11, which loses its structure after heating to 550◦C to  be replaced by phases that offer higher thermal stability [100]. Doping  of sulfide solid electrolytes, such as using Sn or lithium salts, has been  proposed as a method to increase glass stability temperature, however,  doping must be done selectively as improper material selection can also  shift the temperature and crystallinity behaviors unfavorably. Addi­ tionally, electrolyte manufacturing must be considered as the prepara­ tion method used can impact the glass stability without significantly  altering the ratio between the glass stability and crystallization value  [91]. Finally, halide and hydride solid electrolytes provide a unique set of  material characteristics. Although these electrolytes offer promising  ability to retain structure and increase ionic conductivity upon thermal  heating (up to nearly 400◦C), most heating beyond 300◦C results in  disorganization of crystallinity [55]. Some halide solid electrolytes also  exhibit unfavorable structural transformations at relatively low tem­ peratures at which they are susceptible to decomposition and fail to  recrystallize with sound structure [101]. Hydride solid electrolytes can  also behave unfavorably, such as LiBH4 which suffers from poor thermal  stability, causing detriment to ionic conductivity at only 115◦C [102].  Although some halide and hydride solid electrolytes have promise for  solid state battery development, they are, at present, unfavorable due to  relatively low temperature instability, risk of dehydrogenation, and risk  for production of flammable gas byproducts. Stabilization of thermal  degradation byproducts from halide/hydride solid electrolytes is  required to develop solid-state batteries that are safe and effective with  electrolyte selection [103]. 3.3.2. Interface level analysis of thermal stability Beyond solid electrolyte material selection, interfacial interactions  between the electrolyte and its electrode components (anode and cath­ ode) introduce an additional subset of thermal interactions with impli­ cations for performance capabilities and overall safety. As previously  described, thermal treatment of electrolyte materials can cause alter­ ations in material morphology, stability, and crystallinity, all of which  can impact interfacial interactions. Fig. 6c visualizes several prominent  interfacial interactions and alterations that occur under variable thermal  conditions, alongside the possible consequences such as thermal con­ duction interference and thermal runaway. Similar to material level  thermal interactions, interface level interactions can be analyzed using  differential thermal analyses to observe transition events among elec­ trolytes with different electrode component selections applied. Testing of polymer solid electrolytes with lithium metal anodes and a  variety of appropriate cathodes indicated that no strong interactions  between the polymer and anode occurred to cause material deformation,  however, contact with the cathode acceleration of material decompo­ sition attributed to the open-circuit voltage of the system [110]. Fig. 6d  gives the temperature dependence of ionic conductivities of various  solid polymer electrolytes with different compositions [94]. In addition  to detriment to ionic conductivity, thermal influence on interfacial in­ teractions can also introduce thermal runaway behavior such as in the  case of Li6PS5Cl in LiNi0.8Co0.1Mn0.1O2 SPE battery systems. This  detrimental reactivity occurs due to chemical reactivity between deli­ thiated Li1–xNi0.8Co0.1Mn0.1O2 and the solid electrolyte. This violent  reaction is, however, absent in systems using LiFePO4 as the electrolyte  is stable with delithiated Li1–xFePO4 showing that issues with thermal  runaway can be circumvented through careful design and selection of  electrolytes alongside electrode components [111]. Generally, oxide solid electrolytes suffer from insufficient interfacial  contact as well as high impedance levels and interface-level thermal  stability in this material classification is largely dependent on the con­ stituent elements and structures of the solid electrolytes being used.  Layered cathode structures have been observed to decompose into  transition metal oxides that can form byproducts with increasing ther­ mal conditions and some oxide solid electrolytes were even reported to  react violently with phosphate electrodes under high temperature con­ ditions [112]. Specific interphase compositions like Li2CO3 and Li3PO4  at the cathode/SSE interface are identified using a combination of  surface-sensitive analytical techniques. X-ray Photoelectron Spectros­ copy (XPS) is a crucial method, as it can determine the elemental  composition and chemical states of the interfacial layers by analyzing  the core-level electron binding energies. The presence of Li2CO3 is  typically indicated by characteristic C 1 s and O 1 s peaks corresponding  to carbonate species, while Li3PO4 is identified through P 2p and O 1 s  peaks associated with phosphate [113,114]. Complementary techniques  such as Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometry (SIMS) provide information  on the elemental distribution and depth profiling across the interface.  Furthermore, in-situ and operando techniques, like Electrochemical  Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS) coupled with mass spectrometry (DEMS),  can correlate electrochemical changes with the evolution of gaseous  products (e.g., CO2 from carbonate decomposition) and interfacial  resistance changes, indirectly confirming the presence and degradation  of these phases during battery cycling [115]. Thermal runaway among  oxide electrolyte materials was first observed in LAGP-Li whereas  melting of LAGP in argon gas resulted in “violent combustion” from the  release of O2. Thermal runaway risks have also been observed in LLTO  and the thermal runaway pattern may be the result of O2 production  causing exothermic reactivity and melting of lithium materials [116].  Interfacial thermal stability of oxide solid electrolytes could possibly be  improved by elemental doping treatments; however, such a possibility  requires further testing for confirmation. Little work has been done to examine the interfacial thermal stability  patterns of sulfide solid electrolytes, likely due to the risk of toxic gas  production (mainly H2S). Based on the available thermal studies on  sulfide solid electrolytes, interfacial thermal stability is understood to be  influenced by cathode state of charge, atmospheric pressure conditions,  and charge/discharge cycle number. Some researchers propose that  suppressing the exchange of sulfur and oxygen and selecting oxygen  stable sulfide solid electrolytes, could increase interfacial thermal sta­ bility [100]. To understand more about the thermal interactions of  sulfide solid electrolytes a relatively recent research effort proposed a  new method to examine the thermal stability pathways of sulfide  solid-state electrolytes using high temperature sulfur precipitation  [117]. The study proposes a new conceptual parameter ‘Th’, a term to  account for the different chemical bond characteristics contained in  sulfide solid electrolytes. Although this analytical strategy for the  analysis of sulfide electrolyte stability has not yet been widely adopted,  it presents an opportunity to better understand thermal patterns to  better guide sulfide SE production and verification strategies [117]. Although halide solid electrolytes, as previously described, have high  thermal stability, their interfacial thermal stability is complicated by  cathode and anode material selections with complex metal ion in­ teractions. Halide interactions without metal ion interactions, however,  such as a Li/Li2OHCl/Li cell, have shown promise for providing good  stability at high working temperatures [118]. Thermal runaway risk  trends require further analysis in the case of halide/hydride solid elec­ trolytes as the majority of test results are circumstantial, encompassing  only a select few specific materials rather than the material class as a  whole. For instance, a 2020 study of Li (CB9H10) – Li (CB11H12) complex  hydride solid electrolytes indicated both endothermic and exothermic  peaks during heating-cooling cycles, however no largely detrimental  runaway patterns were reported [119]. Further work must be performed  to examine the possible risks of thermal runaway in halide and hydride  solid electrolytes prior to commercial development in solid-state battery  systems. Composite electrolytes are designed to enhance mechanical proper­ ties, but the mismatch in thermal expansion coefficients (CTEs) between  polymer and ceramic phases in composite materials significantly im­ pacts interfacial stability under thermal cycling, especially at elevated  R. Shang et al.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Nano Energy 142 (2025) 111232  13  
--- FILE: A comprehensive review of solid-state lithium batteries.pdf | PAGE: 14 ---
temperatures [120]. Polymers typically exhibit much higher CTEs  compared to ceramics due to their weaker intermolecular bonds. During  heating, the polymer phase will expand to a greater extent than the  ceramic phase, leading to the development of stresses at the interface.  Upon cooling, this difference in contraction rates induces further stress.  Repeated thermal cycling exacerbates these stresses, potentially causing  interfacial debonding, cracking, and ultimately, the failure of the com­ posite. At elevated temperatures, the mechanical properties of the  polymer matrix often degrade, reducing its ability to withstand these  stresses and further compromising the interfacial integrity. The magni­ tude of the stress is directly proportional to the difference in CTEs and  the temperature change, highlighting the critical role of CTE matching  for long-term stability [120]. 3.3.3. Battery level analysis of thermal stability Among all levels of thermal analysis for solid state batteries, whole  battery performance testing remains the least developed, despite being  heavily important. Battery level testing for liquid electrolyte systems has  typically consisted of whole battery thermal runaway analysis using  differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and/or accelerating rate calo­ rimetry (ARC) to characterize heat release behaviors among all battery  components (electrolyte, cathode, anode, and separator). In a study about battery-level thermal performance capabilities, re­ searchers performed comparative analysis on Li/LiFePO4I whole-battery  systems to compare thermal performance of a polymer solid electrolyte  with a traditional liquid electrolyte [91]. This experiment showed that  the liquid electrolyte battery generated twice the amount of heat than  that of the polymer LIB, and the polymer LIB was also indicated to  provide overall higher thermal stability. Other studies have corrobo­ rated that, solid electrolytes can provide lower self-heating rates than  liquid electrolyte batteries while others report mixed results. For  example, a study of Li6.75La3Zr1.75Nb0.25O12 using an all-inclusive  microcell testing method demonstrated that, for electrolyte-electrode  behavior alone, high thermal stability was observed (except at approx­ imately 185◦C when lithium fusion in LLZNO occurred) [95]. Despite  the initially promising thermal stability, testing of the whole battery  system indicated unexpected exothermic peaking due to oxygen release.  Based on the battery-level observations collected thus far, further work  must be done to examine overall thermal performance of solid-state  batteries and to ensure that whole battery testing adequately encapsu­ lates overall safety performance. 3.4. Mechano-chemical analysis Solid state electrolytes for battery development provide a promising  alternative to conventional liquid electrolyte batteries by providing  improved energy storage capabilities. The interfacial relationships  within solid electrolyte systems, however, introduce a unique set of  mechano-chemical interactions that must be thoroughly analyzed and  understood for the design of battery systems that maximize efficiency of  ionic conductivity while minimizing the risks of dendrite formation,  morphological alteration, and undesirable coupling effects. Dendrites are branch-like projections of lithium metal that form on  the surface of the solid-state battery anode and can infiltrate the elec­ trolyte material. Dendrite formation is dependent on mechano-chemical  interactions of the anode and electrolyte, and can be influenced by  temperature, interfacial elements, and bulk microstructural features  [130]. Dendrite growth can lead to short circuiting of solid-state bat­ teries under high current density, despite the fact that solid-state bat­ teries are often praised for their high energy density, and interfacial  resistance continues to increase due to solid-solid contact interface when  compared to liquid lithium battery systems [41]. Understanding of  dendrite growth mechanics via mechano-chemical analyses can allow  for control of dendrite growth events in solid-state electrolytes. In addition to dendrite formation, other types of morphological  alteration can occur as the result of mechano-chemical interactions in  solid-state electrolytes. Morphological stability is best maintained when  there is a balance between the electrochemical and mechanical prop­ erties of the solid electrolyte. More specifically, these results were shown  in a study that looked at the interaction between a metal electrode and  binary solid polymer electrolyte through mechano-chemical analysis at  steady state [126]. The researchers found that there are many potential  factors that can influence the morphological stability of a system and  that simply increasing the mechanical stiffness of a material does not  mean better results. This is because an increase in mechanical stiffness  alone may inevitably lead to a decrease in transport properties, which is  extremely undesirable as it can then lead to unwanted morphological  alterations, such as protrusion branching (which takes place at the  perimeter of a protrusion during an extremely elevated current density  value). Some other factors that have the potential to influence  morphological stability include the coupling effects of “the normal stress  dependency of the equilibrium potential, the mechanical influence onto  the electrochemical potential in the electrolyte bulk as well as the value  of the exchange current density” [126]. Overall, the study showed that  both the charging rates and local modifications of the interface con­ ductivities play a role in altering the morphological stability plots be­ tween the lithium and polymer interfaces. 3.4.1. How mechano-chemical analysis is performed Mechano-chemical properties and interactions can be complex to  define, therefore, a variety of technical and mathematical methods are  utilized to characterize the nature and effects of chemical interactions  on the mechanical properties of solid electrolytes. The elastic modulus  mismatch between SSEs and electrode materials is a critical factor  influencing the mechanical stability and performance of all-solid-state  batteries. This mismatch can lead to interfacial stresses, delamination,  and capacity fade during battery cycling due to volume changes in the  electrode materials. Researchers have employed various experimental  and computational techniques to check or quantify this mismatch [131].  Experimentally, techniques like nanoindentation, ultrasonic sound ve­ locity measurements, and uniaxial testing are used to determine the  elastic moduli of individual components. Furthermore, in-situ and  operando methods such as X-ray diffraction (XRD) and electrochemical  strain microscopy (ESM) can provide insights into the stress and strain  evolution at the interfaces during battery operation. Computationally,  Density Functional Theory (DFT) and Finite Element Method (FEM)  simulations are utilized to model the mechanical behavior of the in­ terfaces and quantify the stress distribution arising from the elastic  modulus mismatch [132]. These simulations often incorporate experi­ mentally determined elastic moduli and thermal expansion coefficients  to provide a more accurate representation of the system. Based on  known interactions between lithium dendrite formation and grain  boundaries, analytical modeling methods can be used to understand the  specific nature of dendrite growth to allow guidance for methods to  reduce dendrite formation. This approach, described in a 2017 study by  R. Raj and J. Wolfenstine [127] uses Gibbs free energy calculations to  produce limit diagrams with “safe” and “fail” regimes to analyze  dendrite nucleation patterns. More specifically, Rishi Raj and Jefferey  Wolfenstine both introduce the use of current limit diagrams in deter­ mining the dendrite formation [127]. Solid-state electrolytes offer  appealing quality factors over organic liquid electrolytes such as  non-flammability and ability to remain stable with Li-metal. However,  solid electrolytes must have high ionic, low electronic conductivity, and  a high shear modulus as desirable features to oppose dendrite formation  [127]. The purpose of the current limit diagrams is to analyze the  dendrite nucleation of the solid-state electrolyte - Li interface [127].  These charts will provide insight into the nucleation of lithium dendrites  at the lithium anode-solid state electrolyte interface. The diagram will  indicate a “safe” and “fail” regime for battery function. The safe regime  suggests the chances of dendrite formation are unlikely whereas the  “fail” regime says otherwise. The governing equation used for the limit  diagrams is initially derived from the difference in the Gibbs Free Energy  R. Shang et al.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Nano Energy 142 (2025) 111232  14  
--- FILE: A comprehensive review of solid-state lithium batteries.pdf | PAGE: 15 ---
of two states: the supersaturated state and the state where the super­ saturation is relieved by the growth of a precipitate, both shown in the  Fig. 7c [127]. The governing equation for the limit diagram is the  calculated result of the critical current density result (j*) [127]:  j∗ = (2γΩLi/rc) + σFΩLi f d(1 −α)|e| ⋅1 ρ (10)  Where j* is critical current density, |e| is positive charge on Li-ion, Ɣ is  specific energy of the metal-electrolyte interface, ΩLi is the number of Li  atoms per unit volume has a relation with the volume per lithium atom  in the electrolyte, σF is mechanical resistance to fracture, 1/ρ is ionic  conductivity of electrolyte, f is the measure of the contribution of grain  matrix resistivity to total resistivity, and α is proximity factor measuring  how close a grain boundary is to the Li metal interface, as a fraction of  grain size. This governing equation defines the transition from a “safe”  to a “fail” regime. In Fig. 7d, the following were considered: (1) The  ranging factors were ionic conductivity of electrolyte (1/ρ) and me­ chanical resistance to fracture (σF), (2) The proximity factor (α) was  taken to be 0 and 0.5, (3) The contribution of grain matrix resistivity to  total resistivity parameter (f) was taken to be 1.0 and 0.5. As mentioned  previously, the Fig. 7d suggests how the critical values for current  density (j*) vary with the solid-state electrolyte’s ionic conductivity (1/  ρ). From observation, the current limit diagrams provide the following  information: (1) Lower fracture stress increases the probability of  dendrite formation [127], (2) The safe region also contracts if the grain  boundary is closer to the Li-metal interface (smaller α value) [127], (3)  Higher grain boundary resistance increases the chance of formation  (higher f value) [127]. (4) High ionic conductivity of the electrolyte is  expected to reduce the chance of dendrite formation [127]. The dia­ grams are consistent with the initial analysis that higher ionic conduc­ tivity and lower grain boundary resistance reduce the chance of dendrite  formation [127], which is essential information for the operation of  solid-state batteries. Other analyses have also been performed to capture the trigger  mechanisms resulting in the coupling effects of morphological alteration  and protrusion growth. More specifically, the same group of researchers  further expanded their experiment by using mechano-chemical analysis  to now look at the relationship between a solid electrolyte and metal  electrode interface during charging and discharging [126]. This is all  done with hopes of better understanding the possible reasons for the  unwanted development of inhomogeneous material deposition and  interface conductivity directly contributes to the damages/ alterations  of the solid electrolyte’s morphology. There were four hypotheses out­ lined for the potential trigger mechanisms that may contribute/ lead to  the development of inhomogeneous deposition and shown below. Hypothesis 1 suggests that a harmful protrusion growth in the  separator is caused by an initial movement/ protrusion due to surface  roughness and directly affects the transport paths. Hypothesis 2 assumes  that the cathode consists of an inhomogeneous current supply and  therefore lacks active storage particles. This then leads to the mirroring  of the morphology of the positive electrode on the negative electrode  and therefore increases the amount of applied current density by two  Fig. 7. Hypothesis 3  suggests that morphological alterations are caused by inhomogeneities  in the bulk while hypothesis 4 suggests it is caused by inhomogeneities  at the interface between the two materials. Out of these 4 hypotheses,  the most significant amount of deposition/ morphological instability  was seen to be caused by unwanted alterations to the interface con­ ductivity (hypothesis 4) and resulted in a proportional relationship be­ tween the tip velocity and rate of protrusion growth. To further  investigate Hypothesis 4, the group of researchers moved forward by  altering the Young’s modulus of the materials and observing the  resulting responses produced by the interface amplitude. Finally, critical  current density testing has been performed to analyze the effects of  interfacial mechano-chemical problems on the transport properties of  solid electrolytes. Depending on the salt-concentration gradient along  the separator and presence of external deformations, the current density  patterns of the electrode-electrolyte interface will vary [126]. 3.4.2. Current status of mechano-chemical characteristics for solid-state  electrolytes As previously indicated, the specific mechanisms and characteristics  of mechano-chemical variability in solid state systems can be difficult to  define, however, mathematical modeling can provide meaningful ap­ proximations to guide battery design and development. In addition to  simulation-based modeling, physical observation of dendrite growth  and morphological changes in response to mechano-chemical coupling  interactions have been observed in polymer electrolyte and sulfide  electrolyte systems particularly. While these interactions are relevant in  oxide, halide, and hydride systems as well, their specific characteristics  have been studied less extensively, likely due to risks associated with the  production of hazardous byproducts. Table 6 below summarizes a  number of common solid electrolytes alongside their conductivity, sta­ ble voltage windows, capacity and number of cycles until loss of  performance. Polymer class solid electrolyte materials, such as polyethylene (PE)  and polypropylene (PP), are not capable of inhibiting the growth of  lithium dendrites, creating risk for dendrite formation, especially under  conditions of high current density [133]. Based on the material  composition, degree of crystallinity, and selection of anode and cathode  materials electro-chemo-mechanical stability can vary greatly, however,  individual case studies have been performed to provide insight on some  of the most common polymer solid electrolytes. An early study by Brissot  et al. [134] used microscopy coupled with a CCD camera to observe  dendritic lithium deposition over time with respect to selected current  density. This baseline study provides a simplistic method for observation  of dendrite formation, as well as a preliminary understanding of  dendrite growth mechanisms that has been referred to in future studies  to further understand mechano-chemical coupling mechanisms in solid  electrolyte battery systems. Sulfide type solid electrolytes introduce risks for the production of  decomposition products, such as S, during mechano-chemical degrada­ tion, as well as lithium-indium dendrite formation. Sulfide electrode  decomposition products can interfere with coulombic efficiency and  increase polarization required for initial cycling while dendrite propa­ gation can reduce capacity and lead to eventual cell failure [133]. A  2021 study of the coupling interactions between a Li6PS5Cl solid elec­ trolyte and a Li(Ni0.6Co0.2Mn0.2)O2 electrode additionally confirmed the  impacts of current and loading on performance of sulfide electrolytes  with high current and high loading resulting in thermodynamic and  kinetic instability [129]. Overall, the coupling of in situ analyses and  mathematical modeling of mechano-chemical interactions can provide  significant insight into the performance, stability, and safety of  solid-state battery systems to guide further development and  improvements. 3.4.3. Potential improvements Although mechano-chemical interactions provide a significant  challenge to solid electrolyte battery development, there are several key  methods that have been proposed to minimize the ongoing formation  and consequences of dendrites as well as other morphological imper­ fections. The first possible method is to alter the bulk microscopic  properties of the materials using grain size control [135]. Since the grain  boundaries of various materials are often prone to dendrite growth,  altering the material sizes themselves would be a valid approach to try  and combat the issue directly. The second potential method is to mini­ mize interfacial defects as best as possible [135]. reaction/ materials are capable of directly influencing both the rate of  ongoing dendrite growth as well as morphological alterations. As a  result, attempting to minimize the interfacial defects while maintaining  its morphological integrity through methods such as crystal SCE [136] would be extremely beneficial when examining mechano-chemical in­ teractions. The third and final method is to optimize the selections of  materials with various processing approaches to try and minimize the  amount of stress caused by thermal expansions [137]. 4. Fast charging of SSBs and related challenges Solid-state batteries are becoming increasingly considered for its  applications in electric vehicles, pacemakers, and wearable electronics/  devices. However, one of the greatest requirements, yet drawbacks for  the current industry is the desire for solid-state batteries to be fast  charging and have a high rate of performance [44,46]. This is especially  applicable to electric vehicle owners who may find it extremely incon­ venient and undesirable to have to wait for an extensive period of  charging time [138,139]. Yet, it is difficult to ensure the fast-charging  capabilities with using solid-state batteries because fast-charging is  commonly known to quickly deteriorate and deplete the battery life  [140]. In fact, ongoing capacity degradation of the high-energy-density  SSB systems is one of the main factors preventing it from mass pro­ duction. Some factors that currently contribute to inhibiting  fast-charging capabilities of solid-state batteries include low Critical  Current Density (CCD), high internal resistance, low/slow ion conduc­ tion, ongoing dendrite growth/ high electrical conductivity, poor con­ tact area, increasing thickness of solid electrolytes, low interfacial  stability, and low lithium-ion transference number of composite solid  electrolytes and a low electrochemical window [41]. While there are  ongoing attempts to try and address these factors, some have been more  successful than others, there is still a long road ahead to an entirely  fast-charging solid-state battery. 4.1. Low critical current density (CCD) Low charging-discharging current density, specifically low CCD, is  one of the main factors preventing solid-state batteries from satisfying  commercial needs and applications. More specifically, the power density  of solid-state batteries remains at an all time low, when compared to  lithium-ion batteries and this means there is not very much capacity  available for the entire size of the cell. However, too high of a current  density also has its own drawbacks as it has been proven to contribute to  decaying a battery’s overall capacity. This is directly due to the differ­ ences in movement rates between ionic motion and the wire’s charge  distribution. The wire’s charge destructions move at a much faster rate  than the ionic motion which takes place within the electrodes/ across  the interface and is determined by the diffusion coefficient of the spe­ cies. Ideally, the diffusion coefficient should be a high number as it  directly correlates to how quickly the species can move through a  material. The CCD for lithium plating/stripping in different SSE systems is  determined through electrochemical testing, primarily using symmetric  Li|SSE|Li cells. The most common method involves cycling the cell at  progressively increasing current densities while monitoring the voltage  response. The CCD is typically identified as the current density at which  a sharp voltage drop occurs, indicating the onset of lithium dendrite  formation and cell short-circuiting. However, variations in testing pro­ tocols, such as the current step size, duration of each step, total lithium  plated/stripped (areal capacity), applied pressure, and temperature, can  significantly influence the reported CCD values [141]. Some advanced  techniques involve unidirectional plating to avoid complications from  stripping-induced void formation, and others focus on minimizing the  amount of lithium transferred per cycle to mitigate the impact of void  formation on CCD measurements [142]. Standardizing these measure­ ment protocols is crucial for obtaining comparable and reliable CCD  values across different SSE systems, facilitating the development of  high-power and long-cycle-life solid-state batteries. Additionally, attempting to increase the levels of CCD is not a simple  task. CCD performance is affected by a number of factors including:  mechanical strength, dendrite formation, relative density, poor interface  resistance between solid electrolytes and electrodes, ionic and electronic  conductivity, as well as electrochemical stability [41]. Since these fac­ tors are interconnected and some can be seen to directly affect the  fast-charging capabilities of solid-state batteries, it poses as a direct  obstacle for the field as changing one thing could negatively affect the  other and vice versa. However, this has not stopped researchers and  scientists from attempting to move forward and get more answers. For  example, Thangadurai and Sarkar [143] suggested a handful of potential  improvements that could be carried out to improve the critical current  densities of all-solid-state lithium-metal batteries. These strategies [143] include, but are not limited to (1) improving/ modifying the grain  boundaries with Li2CO3/LiOH, (2) creating more uniform interfaces  between the Li-metal and SE surfaces to better densify the solid elec­ trolytes and prevent dendrite formation in inorganic solid electrolytes,  (3) improving the wettability of solid electrolytes interfaces which can  directly reduce interface resistance, (4) lowering the electrical conduc­ tion of the bulk electrolyte to ensure the appropriate contact area is  maintained, and (5) properly maintaining temperature (which directly  affects Lithium wettability on solid electrolytes) and pressure (which  can alter the level of resistance at the interface between the Li-metal and  solid electrolytes). Overall, Thangadurai and Sarkar [143] suggest that  there is no definite solution/ method to improving the CCD of  all-solid-state lithium-metal batteries due to its complexity. However,  attempting to address the interfacial issues between the cathode and SE  is a good starting point as this will ensure better performance of the  battery as well as ensure a greater value of CCD for the solid-state bat­ tery [143]. Figs. 8 and 9 4.2. Dendrite growth Ongoing growth of lithium dendrites in solid-state batteries directly  correlates to low levels of CCD and therefore further prevents fast-  charging capabilities overall. Throughout the years, many factors have  been discovered to play a role in contributing to lithium dendrite  growth. These factors include low relative density [144], high porosity  [144], surface cracks/ bulk defects [145,146], as well as direct forma­ tion of the dendrites inside the solid electrolytes [145], rather than  simply impaling it from the surface. Additionally, it was confirmed in  2019 by Han et al. that increasing the amount of electronic conductivity  in solid-state batteries may be the primary reason for ongoing dendrite  growth within solid electrolytes [145]. In their experiment, Han et al. used a time-resolved neutron depth  profiling operando technique to look at real-time changes of lithium  concentration profiles within three different types of solid electrolytes,  lithium phosphorus oxy-nitride (LiPON), Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO), and  amorphous Li3PS4 (LPS) during the process of lithium plating. Their  results insist that lowering the electric conductivity is crucial for the  success of solid-state batteries in the long run. However, this poses a  direct issue to fast-charging concerns as an increase in electronic con­ ductivity in solid-state batteries is necessary for proper fast-charging  capabilities. Although dendrite growth mechanics/ mechano-chemical  analysis is an entire topic of its own and has been touched upon in the  previous section, its effects are extremely crucial to fast-charging per­ formances of solid-state batteries and is worth mentioning again. Despite the promise of solid electrolytes in mitigating dendrite for­ mation in SSBs, it remains a predictable challenge due to inherent ma­ terial properties and electrochemical processes. Quantitative techniques  like Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS) track interfacial  resistance changes indicative of dendrite growth, while Cyclic Voltam­ metry (CV) and Chronopotentiometry reveal anomalous voltage/current  responses signaling short circuits. In-situ microscopy directly visualizes  R. Shang et al.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    Nano Energy 142 (2025) 111232  17

dendrite nucleation and propagation, allowing for quantitative analysis  of their growth kinetics. Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) and  Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) non-destructively quantify dendrite  formation. Finally, Finite Element Method (FEM) simulations predict  dendrite growth morphology based on electrochemical principles  [149–151]. These methods consistently demonstrate predictable pat­ terns of dendrite formation under specific operating conditions. 4.3. High electronic conductivity Another factor that directly affects the fast-charging capabilities of  solid-state batteries and the potential for CCD to go from low to high is  the high electrical conductivity rates of the batteries. In fact, high  electrical conductivity also leads to the ongoing growth of dendrites and  therefore is considered to be a promising issue to address as it can  potentially lead to resolving two issues at once. A common technique  used to combat the issue of high electrical conductivity is to adjust the  thickness of the solid-state electrolytes by reduction. The thickness of  the electrolyte is believed to influence both the internal resistance of the  battery as well as its concentration polarization [41]. As a result, a  smaller thickness is believed to result in both a faster ion conduction and  lower internal resistance, especially when comparing the same materials  to one another, and is considered ideal for fast-charging applications. When developing a novel approach to creating thin and easily  reproducible electrolyte layers by nanoscopic polymer binding from  polysulfide solutions consisting of lithium polysulfide, phosphorus sul­ fide, and ethylene sulfide, Ping Liu et al. found the room temperature  (RT) ionic conductivity to be 2 × 10−5 S cm−1 [147]. Since the ionic  conductivity of solid polymer electrolytes is typically 1 × 10−4 S cm−1  [41], this is considered a major drawback to reducing the thickness of  the electrolytes because it seems to also reduces RT ionic conductivity in  an attempt to reduce electrical conductivity and dendrite formation. In  fact, reducing the value of RT ionic conductivity results in a decrease in  stability and therefore makes the solid-state battery undesirable for  applications. In another experiment, researchers attempted to adjust the  solid electrolyte thickness by creating Ta-LLZO powders through  solid-state reaction. In general, Ta-LLZO is more often favored over  other powders such as Al-LLZO and Nb-LLZO because it has better sta­ bilization potentials and can increase ionic conductivity levels with Li  metals better than others [152]. More specifically, once the Ta-LLZO  powders in the experiment were developed, it was then followed by a  high-temperature sintering process and were finally pressed into green  pellets under gradual and static pressure. This resulted in the formation  of thinner LLZO solid-state electrolytes ranging from 800 to 1000 µm  and 10–20 mm in diameter [41]. This is a significant amount of reduc­ tion considering the typical thickness for an inorganic SSE is around  several hundreds of micrometers [41]. However, this reduction in  thickness also led to a decrease in the amount of production by  manufacturing overall. This was due to the ceramic material being  inherently more brittle than others [153] and as a result, became a major  drawback for the technique. Furthermore, it puts scientists and re­ searchers in a position where they are required to either prioritize large  scale manufacturing or fast-charging capabilities of solid-state batteries,  but not necessarily both simultaneously. 4.4. Low interfacial stability, high internal resistance, and low ionic  conductivity Low interfacial stability is another factor that contributes to low CCD  levels, thus further preventing fast-charging capabilities of solid-state  batteries in the long run. Interface-level thermal stability refers to the  contact/ interaction between the solid-state electrolytes and electrodes  (cathode and anode). This means that the interface relationship is  capable of directly interfering with the ionic conductivity of the system  Fig. 8. Shang et al. as well. As a matter of fact, low, poor, and unstable interfacial contact  between the solid electrolytes and electrodes means that there is an  undesirably large interfacial resistance, thus resulting in low CCD and  directly hindering fast-charging capabilities of solid-state batteries.  Since the ionic conductivity of solid-state electrolytes (ion transport in  electrolytes) and the interface resistance (ion transport between elec­ trodes and electrolytes) are two chemical processes that play a signifi­ cant role in affecting a battery’s charging behavior, it would be it would  be ideal to consider increasing the ionic conductivity while simulta­ neously lowering the levels of internal resistance to achieve fast-  charging capabilities, since these two factors can lead to morpholog­ ical changes and decomposition of a battery. One technique often used  to improve interfacial deficits is known as high temperature co-  sintering. However, a common drawback to this technique is that it  triggers unwanted material decomposition, increasing the production of  high-impedance impurities, and overall weakening of the electro­ chemical capabilities. Thermal gradients play a crucial role in triggering  localized decomposition by creating non-uniform temperature distri­ butions within a material or system. Since the rate of thermal decom­ position reactions is highly temperature-dependent (often following the  Arrhenius equation), regions experiencing higher temperatures will  undergo decomposition at a significantly faster rate than cooler areas  [154]. This disparity in reaction rates leads to a localized breakdown of  the material, concentrating the decomposition process in the hotter  zones while leaving the colder regions relatively intact. This phenome­ non is particularly important in systems where heat transfer is inefficient  or where localized heat sources exist, leading to the development of  steep temperature gradients that can exacerbate material degradation in  specific areas [155]. This technique also results in high interfacial  resistance due to the chemical instability of cathode materials and solid  electrolytes, thus directly resulting in low CCD and therefore takes us  back to the original issue [148]. Finally, in an attempt to address this  issue, Han et al. [145] carried out a reaction that formed an intermediate  phase to remove the potential impurities produced by high temperature  sintering of LCO and LLZO. More specifically, the experiment relied on a  welding agent (Li2.3C0.7B0.3O3) that welded the LCO and LLZO together  and took place at 700 ◦C, which is way lower than conventional sin­ tering taking place at 1100 ◦C [148]. Doping strategies using elements like aluminum and gallium signif­ icantly influence the Li-ion conductivity and phase stability of garnet  electrolytes (e.g., Li7La3Zr2O12) under fast charging conditions. Doping  with Al3+ or Ga3+ on the Li+ site generally stabilizes the high Li-ion  conductive cubic phase of the garnet structure at room temperature,  preventing the formation of the low conductive tetragonal phase [156].  This stabilization is achieved by creating Li vacancies to maintain charge  neutrality, which in turn enhances Li-ion mobility and thus, the overall  ionic conductivity crucial for fast charging. Furthermore, doping can  improve the grain boundary conductivity by reducing impedance and  enhancing the density of the electrolyte, facilitating faster Li-ion trans­ port. The specific concentration of the dopant is critical, as excessive  doping can lead to the formation of secondary phases that impede  conductivity and potentially affect the long-term phase stability, espe­ cially under the stress induced by rapid Li intercalation and dein­ tercalation during fast charging [157]. 4.5. Low electrochemical window The electrochemical stability window of solid electrolytes is typically  low and is not ideal for fast-charging capabilities. More specifically, a  typical voltage window often compensates for the fast-charging efforts  by exerting overpotential on the entire solid-state battery. This then  leads to an increase in voltage, thus going above the stable voltage  window and is considered to be a major drawback of the fast-charging  feature. In fact, when the electrochemical window is incapable of  Fig. 9.
