the cell-to-cell process variations during the battery manufacturing processes. Liu et al. (Liu et al., 2021a) proposed a feature quantiﬁcation and electrode classiﬁcation framework based on the random forest method by analyzing four manufacturing features and parameters from the mixing and coating processes. The novel method effectively reduced model dimension and improved the sensitivity analysis of battery manufacturing. Guan et al. (Guan et al., 2021) proposed a reﬁned dehumidiﬁcation system as the substitu- tion of the conventional desiccant wheel deep-dehumidiﬁcation system to obtain a coefﬁcient of perfor- mance increase from 0.66 to 0.78 based on the on-site performance measurements, effectively reducing the cost of dehumidiﬁcation. The continuous cost reductions and technology improvements are the main reasons that EVs are becoming more and more competitive over ICE vehicles. Other than manufacturing improvement, Neubauer et al. (Neubauer et al., 2012) stated that driving patterns and charging strategies could all inﬂuence the overall lifetime cost of on-board battery packages. Finally, a good EOL recycling mechanism could also increase the cost efﬁciency of the battery products (Zeng et al., 2015). LIB recycling is considered as the ultimate approach to handle the EOL EV batteries to leverage ﬂuctuating battery costs, uneven production, and logistic transportation costs (Chen et al., 2019c). Sort and separation technologies, pyrometallurgical and hydrometallurgical processes, as well as direct recycling methods, are all the future research directions and challenges for the commercial EV bat- tery recycling industry. As a mature technology in the mining industry, bioleaching is potentially practical for the metal reclamation in the EOL batteries complementary to the pyrometallurgical and hydrometallur- gical processes, especially for the separation of cobalt and nickel which usually require extra solvent- extraction steps to separate (Harper et al., 2019). The microorganisms could digest metal oxides from the collected EOL cathodes and produce metal nanoparticles by reducing cathode oxides. Lander et al. (Lander et al., 2021) comprehensively proposed a techno-economic cost model for EV battery recycling. They found that the transportation, disassembly, scale, and raw material cost are the critical factors for re- cycling proﬁts. The deep collaborations between academia and industry are strongly recommended to know the real demands of recycling technologies and material testing standards (Ma et al., 2021). The scaling up is beneﬁcial to the economic success of the recycling business in terms of bringing more proﬁts and closing the huge gap between manufacturing and recycling. DISCUSSION The battery industry is a comprehensive ﬁeld of material science, chemistry, electrochemistry, physics, and thermodynamics. Multi-disciplinary skills and efforts are required for its future development. Studies and experiments about battery chemical compositions, morphology structures, and chemical/electrochemi- cal/thermal performances are the methodologies to explore better electrode, electrolyte, and separator materials to make better onboard power batteries. On the other hand, as the EV industry keeps growing, Figure 6. Predicted demands of Lithium-ion batteries for EVs ll OPEN ACCESS 26 iScience 25, 103744, February 18, 2022 iScience Review 
--- FILE: Connecting battery technologies for electric.pdf | PAGE: 27 ---
battery technology will continue to thrive to keep the pace of this promising transportation electriﬁcation revolution. McKinsey & Co. anticipated that about 70% of automobile sales in Europe in 2040 would be electric vehicles, indicating an astronomical annual demand, 1,200 GW-hours, which requires an approxi- mately $150 billion investment. The potential proﬁts of the business are so large that neither incumbents nor new entrants would ignore this lucrative niche market. However, another world-renowned consulting company, Boston Consulting Group, dampened the enthusiasm by saying ‘‘the stakes are very high’’, insin- uating the potential ﬁerce competition in the future EV power battery market. As a traditional high cost-performance and commercially viable anode material, graphite delivers reliable capac- ity and excellent cycling stability (Moradi and Botte, 2016), but its theoretical speciﬁc energy is lower than those of other novel anodes such as lithium-metal anodes and Si-based anodes (Zou et al., 2021). Si-based anodes exhibit excellent speciﬁc capacity and cycling performances with low costs, but their salient breathing effect and capacity degradation problems limit their commercial applications (Li et al., 2017c). LFP is generally re- garded as an excellent cathode material due to its durability, long cycle life, high thermal stability and safety, and low manufacturing cost, but it is still not favored by some OEMs who are seeking higher speciﬁc energy and lower self-discharge rate products. High energy density does not necessarily mean high risks. Any negli- gence or overlook of the existing safety standards during the R&D and manufacturing processes could lead to the production of the unqualiﬁed battery cells. The defective rate might be extremely low, but the risk of disas- trous results will be exponentially ampliﬁed by the large-scale productions. Owing to the most critical safety con- cerns, the battery cells with solid electrolytes and inﬂammable materials will be more popular in the future high energy commercial battery packages for the OEMs. Undoubtedly, the outstanding qualities of high energy density, low self-discharge rate, almost no memory effect, high OCV, as well as long cycle life will continuously help Li-ion batteries dominate the EV energy storage device market over most of the contenders (Kim et al., 2019b). Their reliability and feasibility for the deployment in EVs had drawn and would still be drawing exclusive attention from the global OEMs to replace their conventional ICE products inthe nextdecade (Cano etal.,2018; Li et al., 2014). power and energy, it is foreseeable that the LFP cell will be more favorable for commercial EV applications due to its supreme safety in a short term. Yang et al. (Yang et al., 2021c) developed a thermally modulated LFP cell which was capable of delivering a sufﬁcient cruise range by just a 10 min fast charging in all climates, effectively allevi- ating drivers’ range anxiety. Ni-MH battery is another but less commonly used onboard power battery due to its relatively high speciﬁc power, long cycle life, superb reliability, and outstanding cost performance (Young et al., 2013; Qiao etal., 2019).Fuelcellsuchashydrogen-oxygen fuel cellisbecoming an efﬁcientandcleanenergy stor- age device at some level, but their overall cost is still much higher than the Li-ion battery (Stambouli, 2011). Some state-of-the-art rechargeable batteries, such as Si-based anode battery, ASSB, Li-S battery, and metal-air battery are still not thermally stable, technically reliable, and commercially rewardable, but they all have the potentials to be commercially successful inventions and symbolize the revolutionary future of the next-generation recharge- able battery technologies. From a long-term perspective, the ASSB cell will be a competitive candidate for the onboard EV energy storage systems as a perfect combination of high speciﬁc energy and safety if its technical bottlenecks such as low ionic conductivity and poor interface compatibility are successfully overcome. Figure 7 comprehensively collated and evaluated the potentiality and feasibility of most reigning and po- tential battery technologies with six technical and economic aspects to be the next-generation EV power battery. The reasonable trade-off between performance, safety, and the cost is always the priority in battery research and development. In terms of the costs, except for the spot prices of the transition metals, battery second life use is also considered as a solution to reduce the EV overall costs (Martinez-Laserna et al., 2018). For ordinary consumers, the battery cost performance will probably be considered as a key factor for choosing an EV product from numerous models from the shelf. The Li-ion based batteries tower above the other batteries in most aspects at the current stage. Except for the Li-ion batteries (3.9 points) and lithium polymer batteries (3.3 points), the ASSB (3.55 points) and Si-based (3.3 points) batteries show the highest potentials to be the next-generation EV power battery with high speciﬁc capacity and safety per- formance. If their technical maturity could be improved to the level of commercial mass production vol- umes in the next few years, they will be leading the revolutions of the future EV battery market. Uncertainty is one of the enchantments of science and technology. The battery evolution is not a Schro- dinger’s Cat but just a matter of ‘‘when and how’’. There will probably be not one monopoly player but many participants in the future EV energy storage device market. But one thing is for sure, no matter what the next-generation technological breakthroughs will be, the unprecedented cooperation between industrial giants and academic communities will unswervingly create safer, stronger, and cheaper rechargeable onboard energy storage systems to let people embrace a brilliant new world of zero emission and green revolution with higher energy utilization efﬁciencies, less fossil fuel consumption, and less CO2 emissions. CONCLUSIONS In this research, both the conventional and future battery technologies for EVs were comprehensively re- viewed, covering most key aspects such as major component materials, operating characteristics, theoret- ical models, manufacturing processes, cost analysis, etc. Moreover, this article specially focused on some critical issues in the battery commercial applications and lifecycle management. Topics like accurate health diagnosis, RUL prediction techniques, advanced BTMS designs, and thermal runaway preventions could all further extend battery cycle life and reduce the EV lifecycle costs. Two novel hexagon radar charts were created to make a concise yet all-round evaluation of most reigning and potential EV battery technologies. Some speciﬁc conclusions were drawn: 1) In a short-term, Li-ion batteries, such as NCM, LMO, LFP etc., would be continuously dominating the onboard power battery market due to their superb properties including high speciﬁc power, no memory effect, low self-discharge, as well as long cycle life. 2) In a foreseeable future, some cutting-edge battery technologies such as ASSB, Si-based anode bat- tery, and Li-S battery are ready to be the next-generation commercial EV batteries once they are more thermally stable, technically reliable, and economically rewardable. 3) Battery aging detection and health prediction technologies could effectively enhance the safety and reliability of EV battery systems. The RUL prediction will be more accurate and efﬁcient with the help of advanced numerical models and monitoring methods. 4) The battery thermal energy management system plays an important role in securing battery perfor- mance, ensuring service life, and preventing thermal runaway. 5) The manufacturing costs of the batteries could be further reduced by advanced processes control methods and various numerical auxiliary improvement approaches including artiﬁcial intelligence analysis and data-driven optimization. But there will be a ceiling for the battery cost reduction due to limited yields and ﬂuctuating spot prices of some critical materials including lithium, cobalt, nickel, etc. 6) Other than the endless pursuit of the higher battery speciﬁc power and energy, the Zn-ion and Na- ion batteries might be the promising cheaper and safer substitutions of Li-ion batteries with a reasonable trade-off between capacity and cost due to their ample crust storage while the spot price of lithium has been rocketing with the increasing demand of the Li-ion batteries. Abstract: Electric and hybrid vehicles have become widespread in large cities due to the desire for environmentally friendly technologies, reduction of greenhouse gas emissions and fuel, and economic advantages over gasoline and diesel vehicles. In electric vehicles, overheating, vibration, or mechanical damage due to collision with an object or another vehicle can lead to the failure of lithium- ion batteries up to thermal runaway and fire. Therefore, the development of battery safety control systems is one of the most important factors contributing to the large-scale electrification of public and private transport. This review examines the design features of the location and management of the battery pack to achieve maximum safety and operational efficiency when using an electric vehicle. The power characteristics and life-cycles of various types of lithium-ion batteries depending on the chemical nature of their electrodes are considered, using the example of commercial vehicles’—Tesla, Nissan Leaf, Porsche Taycan, Zeekr, and Chevrolet Volt—strategic technologies for the placement and packaging of batteries, and battery cooling and monitoring systems (State of Health and State of Charge) are also discussed. In conclusion, the current challenges in the field are summarized and promising research directions are proposed. Keywords: electric vehicle; Li-ion battery; thermal runaway; battery pack placement; battery thermal management systems 1. Introduction Electric vehicles (EVs) are becoming increasingly in demand as personal and public transport options, due to both their environmental friendliness (emission reduction) and higher efficiency compared to internal combustion engine vehicles [1–3]. One of the most important and complex components of an EV is its battery, which determines the power reserve of the car, its dynamic characteristics, as well as passenger comfort and operation period. As a rechargeable battery, it is lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) that have become widespread, thanks to their high specific energy, high energy density, low self- discharge rate, and suitable shelf life [4–7]. However, the LIB power source is also a source of increased danger, since mechanical damage, including vibrations and collisions, non-compliance with the conditions of the recommended battery charge mode, and also temperature overheating can lead to the so-called thermal runaway of the battery [8–11] followed by the release of smoke or toxic gas and full-scale fire [12–14]. To ensure the ubiquity of electric vehicles, safety aspects should be considered including the location of the battery in transport; methods of cooling it; and battery management systems, i.e., monitoring its charge and temperature conditions. J. 2024, 15, 568 2 of 36 In addition to safety aspects, a major challenge is to improve LIB performance at extremely low or high temperatures in order to expand the geographical coverage of the distribution of electric vehicles. In addition to safety aspects, a major challenge is to improve LIB performance at extremely low or high temperatures, because modern electric vehicles are not able to operate at temperatures below −20 ◦C [15], while existing cooling systems are not effective when using an electric vehicle with an ambient temperature above 50 ◦C and leads to a high risk of thermal runaway [12,16]. Due to the incomplete knowledge of chemistry and engineering of the operating features of an LIB for EV, there have been cases of product recalls from the market due to the ignition of batteries, for example, GM Chevrolet Volt [17]. This led to the establishment of strict rules governing the safety of lithium-ion batteries [18]; however, incidents of fire of LIB-based EVs still occur [19–21]. There are many types of standards including the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC), the International Organization for Standardization (ISO), the Society of Automotive Engineers International (SAE) at the international level, as well as the European Committee for Standardization (CEN) and others. While standards are not within the main scope of this review, the interested reader can learn more about the standards in recent works [22,23]. Therefore, it is extremely important to develop effective thermal control systems for EVs with an integrated approach, including the features of the chemical structure of LIBs, cooling systems, battery packaging systems, and monitoring systems. Recent reviews have a narrow focus on describing only thermal control systems or engineering solutions of architecture [6]; the consequences and features of thermal acceleration for various devices [1–3]; or the chemistry of lithium-ion batteries for a wide range of equipment including smartphones, laptops, and other small devices [4]. The summary of several aspects of utilization of LIBs in EVs will allow us to evaluate and compare the latest trends in the development of the field. This review examines the progress over the past 5 years on existing methods and ap- proaches used by researchers in the development of BTMSs for electric vehicles. Section 2.1 describes the various features of the types of LIB depending on the cathode material. Section 2.2 describes the classification of batteries and design options for their location in the EV. In the Section 2.3.1, the methods of battery management systems (BMSs) are consid- ered. Section 2.3.2 is devoted to cooling methods, including air, liquid, phase-transition materials, etc. In conclusion, the article outlines future trends and challenges in the field of BTMSs for lithium-ion electric vehicles. 2. Electric Vehicle Battery Technologies 2.1. Chemical Aspects of Li-Ion Batteries A lithium-ion battery (LIB) consists of a cathode and anode separated by a porous separator impregnated with electrolytes. Since it is the cathode that plays a crucial role in the capacity of batteries, the nominal cell voltage, the number of charge–discharge cycles to reduce the capacity to 80%, and the load current relative to the capacity C, below is a description of the power and discharge characteristics depending on the chemical nature of the cathodes, including lithium ferrophosphate (LFP), lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide (NMC), and lithium nickel cobalt aluminum oxide (NCA). Lithium cobalt oxide (LCO) and lithium manganese oxide (LMO) were excluded because, although they are widespread, they are used in laptops and not in electric vehicles. 2.1.1. Cathode Materials LFP Lithium ferrophosphate (LiFePO4, LFP) is one of the most commonly used active positive electrode materials in modern lithium-ion batteries. An article published in 1997 by A. K. Padhi, K. Nanjundaswamy, and J. B. Goodenough (Center for Materials Science and Engineering at the University of Texas, Austin (USA)) discusses the principle of operation of LFP-based batteries [24]. The authors describe the electrochemical reaction occurring 
--- FILE: Electric Vehicle Battery Technologies.pdf | PAGE: 3 ---
World Electr. Veh. J. 2024, 15, 568 3 of 36 during cycling and characterize LFP as a promising candidate for use as a cathode of rechargeable lithium batteries (Figure 1a). Figure 1. Crystallographic structure and electrochemical reaction for three main types of cathode materials for EVs: (a) LFP; (b) NMC; (c) NCA. (1) The process of lithium extraction in the cathode; (2) the process of lithium insertion into graphite planes at the anode; (3) the general intercala- tion/deintercalation reaction occurring in the battery cell (image produced using VESTA [25]). In the chemistry of LFP-based cathodes, the use of iron (Fe2+/Fe3+) as a transition metal solves the problem of oxygen release, which often occurs due to the overlap of the 3d level of the transition metal and the 2p oxygen level in the electron shell of atoms. In the LFP structure, oxygen atoms form a dense package in which lithium is located in octahedral voids, and phosphorus forms covalent bonds with oxygen, which helps to stabilize the structure and improve battery performance [4]. At the moment, batteries using LFP are recognized as one of the most effective com- mercial solutions in terms of power, due to the high diffusion rate of lithium ions, stable cyclability due to the two-phase intercalation–deintercalation mechanism of lithium ions into the LiFePO4 structure, without significant changes in specific characteristics, as well as high temperature resistance and environmental friendliness [26]. However, the main disadvantages of batteries with LFP are low electronic and ionic conductivity, low specific characteristics compared to NMC/NCA (the specific energy intensity of LFP is about 115 Wh/kg versus 233 Wh/kg in systems with NMC or NCA). Modern solutions in an LIB with an LFP cathode are to achieve its theoretical capacity of 170 mAh/g (in practice, up to 160 mAh/g) at a nominal discharge voltage of about 3.3 V and increase electronic conductivity. Key parameters of LFP-based batteries and their comparisons with other materials are summarized in Table 1.

J. 2024, 15, 568 5 of 36 Current trends in improving the specific characteristics of LFP are aimed at the use of commercial organic binders [27], doping with materials such as nickel [28,29] and manganese [30–32], and improving stability during fast charging [33,34] and at extreme temperatures [35]. NMC The transition from LFP to lithium–nickel–manganese–cobalt oxides (LiNixCoyMn1−x−yO2, NMC) in LIB cathodes was due to the desire to increase energy density, which made it possible to create batteries with a larger capacity and a longer service life on a single charge. The NMC provides the best energy-to-weight ratio, which is especially important for electric vehicles and other devices where high capacity and compactness are critical. Although LIBs with an LNO-, LMO-, or LCO-based cathode have a number of disadvantages, the combination of nickel, manganese, and cobalt provides high specific performance, high stability, and low internal resistance, respectively [36]. The electrochemical reaction of a full charge and discharge for lithium-ion batteries with an NMC cathode (LiNixCoyMn1−x−yO2) is represented in Figure 1b. Modern approaches to improving lithium-ion batteries with NMC cathodes are aimed at increasing their efficiency and stability. One of these methods is to reduce the cobalt content. NMC111 cathodes (LiNi0.33Co0.33Mn0.33O2) have been widely studied until re- cently, and their modifications with a reduced cobalt content are of increasing interest since they reduce dependence on expensive and scarce cobalt [37]. Thus, the development of low-cobalt NMC cathodes has led to the emergence of various formulations, includ- ing NMC442, NMC523, NMC622, NMC811, and even NMC955 (LiNi0.90Mn0.05Co0.05O2), which significantly reduces the cost of raw materials [38]. In addition to the benefits as- sociated with a decrease in cobalt concentration, the increased nickel content increases the capacity, while NMC811 demonstrates an improved specific capacity of 200 mAh/g compared to NMC111 with a specific capacity of 160 mAh/g [39]. However, an increase in nickel content, although it contributes to an increase in energy density, leads to a decrease in the durability (cyclability) of the LIB. The use of special coatings like Al2O3, Li3PO4, and TiO2 on the surface of the cathode particles helps to extend the battery life by acting as protective layers to minimize degradation and improve cycling stability by preventing direct contact between the electrolyte and the cathode surface [40]. In the future, a tran- sition to solid-state electrolytes is also being considered, which will increase the safety of batteries, and nanostructured materials, which will improve the reaction surface and increase durability, which are especially important for multiple charging and discharging cycles [40–43]. NCA In commercial solutions, along with Ni-enriched NMC, lithium–nickel–cobalt–aluminum oxide is also widely used (LiNiCoAlO2, NCA) with increased specific energy and capac- ity [44]. The high nickel content (ratio—16Ni:3Co:1Al) allows for an increase in energy density, which is especially important for electric vehicles, where the priority is the range on a single charge. NCA and NMC have relatively similar electrochemical characteristics. The main difference between them is that the chemically inactive element Mn is replaced by Al. An LIB with a cathode based on LiNi0.8Co0.15Al0.05O2 has a theoretical capacity of 279 mAh/g (in practice, about 200 mAh/g) and provides an average operating voltage of 3.7 V. The electrochemical reaction during the charging and discharging cycle of an LIB with an NCA cathode is shown in Figure 1c. The presence of a relatively small amount of Al in the NCA structure increases the stability of cycling; however, when working with high currents, extreme charging voltage, and high temperatures, stability is disrupted [45]. When cycling under such conditions, NiO is formed on the cathode surface, which is a cationic defect, which provokes a rapid increase in resistance and worsens battery operation. In addition, secondary reactions can occur with the formation of compounds such as Li2CO3 and LiOH at the electrode– 
--- FILE: Electric Vehicle Battery Technologies.pdf | PAGE: 6 ---
World Electr. Veh. J. 2024, 15, 568 6 of 36 electrolyte interface, which reduces the capacity and negatively affects the cyclicity and speed of reactions [46]. The capacity of the NCA battery decreases to 93.3% of the original capacity at a discharge current of 0.5 ◦C, and when the discharge current increases to 3 ◦C, no additional capacity loss occurs. Obviously, both NCA and MNC batteries have high specific energy and can provide satisfactory operation at high current rates. 2.1.2. Anode Materials Natural and Artificial Graphite Graphite, the key anode material for lithium-ion batteries, exists in two main forms: natural and artificial. Natural graphite is extracted from deposits and processed to ensure an indispensable level of purity, which is due to its low cost. However, its properties can vary depending on the source, and its effectiveness is often limited by structural defects and impurities. Artificial graphite is produced synthetically by high-temperature treatment of carbon precursors, such as petroleum coke or coal pitch. This process allows for better control of the material structure, which leads to increased cycling stability, uniformity, and reduced resistance compared to natural graphite. Despite the fact that artificial graphite is more expensive due to its energy-intensive production, it has excellent performance characteristics in terms of speed and long service life, which makes it the preferred choice for use in batteries. The graphite structure consists of layers of carbon atoms, into which lithium ions are embedded (intercalated) during charging and deintercalated during discharge. The theoretical specific capacity of graphite is 372 mAh/g (in practice, about ~350 mAh/g), which corresponds to the stoichiometric limit of LiC6 content during intercalation. The key advantages of granite are its stable cycling, high Coulomb efficiency, and good compatibility with industrial electrolytes, which makes it a leader among anode materials in the production of LIBs for the electric vehicle industry. However, graphite anodes have limitations in terms of energy density and manufacturer news at high charge/discharge rates. Combining graphite with high-performance materials such as silicon can increase specific productivity while increasing graphite stability. Si/SiOx and Graphite Composite Materials Silicon (Si) and silicon oxide (SiOx) are promising candidates for next-generation LIB anodes due to their exceptionally high theoretical capacity—3579 mAh/g for silicon and 2194 mAh/g for SiOx, which are significantly higher than that of graphite [47]. The main problem of silicon-based anodes is a significant change in their volume (up to 300%) during charge–discharge cycles, which leads to mechanical failure and loss of electrical contact. To solve this problem, the researchers explored approaches such as nanostructuring silicon particles, introducing buffer layers (such as carbon coatings), and optimizing binder systems to increase mechanical flexibility [48–51]. LTO Lithium titanate (Li4Ti5O12, LTO) with a spinel structure is known as a “zero strain” material due to a slight change in its volume (<1%) during cycling. LTO operates at a relatively high potential (~1.55 V) compared to Li/Li+, which prevents the formation of lithium deposits (dendrites) and increases the safety level of the battery. Its low volume change during cycling also provides excellent durability, with a service life often exceeding 10,000 cycles [52]. However, LTO has a low specific capacity (~175 mAh/g) and a relatively low energy density. In addition, the electronic conductivity of the material is inherently low, which requires the use of conductive additives or coatings [52]. Recent advances in LTO research include alloying with elements such as magnesium and aluminum to improve conductivity and modifying particle morphology to improve lithium-ion transport [53]. These improvements are aimed at making LTO-based batteries 
--- FILE: Electric Vehicle Battery Technologies.pdf | PAGE: 7 ---
World Electr. Veh. J. 2024, 15, 568 7 of 36 more competitive in applications where safety and long service life are of paramount importance, for example, in electric buses and stationary energy storage systems [54]. 2.1.3. Post-Lithium-Ion Systems—Promising Materials Post-lithium-ion batteries represent a promising direction in the field of energy stor- age aimed at overcoming the limitations of traditional lithium-ion systems in terms of increasing cost, environmental friendliness, and energy density. Lithium–sulfur batteries (Li) are characterized by a high theoretical energy density (2600 Wh/kg, in practice up to 500 Wh/kg) due to their high theoretical capacity (1300 mAh/g) and low cost of sul- fur [55,56]. However, these systems have problems such as the polysulfide shuttle effect and low service life. Sodium-ion batteries (SIBs), using a more affordable chemical element—Na instead of Li—represent a sustainable and economical alternative, especially for large-scale energy storage [57–60], although they are inferior in energy density to lithium-ion. Solid-state batteries (SSBs), where liquid electrolytes are replaced by solid ones, pro- vide increased safety, energy density, and thermal stability, which makes them ideal for electric vehicles and high-performance systems. However, low ionic conductivity, diffi- culties in achieving a stable electrode–electrolyte interface, and mechanical degradation of materials during charging/discharging cycles due to volume changes prevent these materials from replacing LIBs with a liquid electrolyte [61,62]. Current research focuses on the development of advanced solid electrolytes such as sulfides, oxides, and polymers to improve ionic conductivity and interfacial stability. In addition, protective coatings and cell architecture optimization are being investigated to improve performance and durability [63–65]. 2.2. Requirements for EV Battery Architecture/Design The design of transport batteries includes the following factors [66]: specific energy consumption, performance under various external conditions, charging speed, service life, safety, and reliability. One of the most important characteristics is the specific energy consumption of the battery, since the power reserve of an electric vehicle depends on it. It is necessary to maintain a balance between the specific capacity of the EV battery pack as well as its weight and layout in an electric vehicle in order to achieve maximum power reserve with minimum weight and maximum free space in an electric vehicle. The efficiency of the EV battery packs is determined by its performance under various external conditions (temperature) and operations (charging modes and driving style)—for example, according to the considered model of LIB utilization, in 100 calendar days of use according to the IEC (International Electrotechnical Commission) at an ambient temperature of 45 ◦C and about 10% at 25 ◦C [67]. It is extremely important to maintain a uniform temperature of the battery; the difference between the batteries should not exceed 5 ◦C in the entire volume to maximize the prevention of accelerated aging of the battery. It was shown that for two similar batteries, with a difference in temperature change by volume of 13–15 ◦C and 1.4–1.6 ◦C, the difference in capacity after 600 cycles was 3.3 percentage points [68]. In many ways, uniformity is determined by the type of cooling system and the layout of the load cycle, and it loses about 15% capacity of the elements. Battery operation at high temperatures (over 40 ◦C) provides a relatively high charging speed but increases the rate of surface electrode interface (SEI) growth, which in turn shortens the battery life (insert values). For example, K. Amine et al. considered the aging of the LFP battery at room temperature (RT), 37 ◦C, and 55 ◦C [69]. It was found that the specific capacity at 55 ◦C is higher than at room temperature (158 mAh/g versus 140 mAh/g), but after 100 discharge cycles, samples at elevated temperatures showed a significant drop in the normalized capacity to 0.3 and 0.6 for 37 ◦C and 55 ◦C, respectively; at room temperature, the capacity almost did not change. On the other hand, the operation of batteries at low temperatures (less than 5–15 ◦C) slows down the growth of SEI and the processes of lithium ion transfer, leading to its precipitation and irreversible loss of 
--- FILE: Electric Vehicle Battery Technologies.pdf | PAGE: 8 ---
World Electr. Veh. J. 2024, 15, 568 8 of 36 capacity—for example, the dependence of capacity on the duration of battery heating at a temperature of −25 ◦C was shown, where at room temperature the battery capacity is close to 3 Ah and at a temperature of −25 ◦C it is close to 0 Ah, although preheated batteries show a capacity of about 2.2 Ah [15]. The charging speed of the battery plays an important role for the convenience of consumers. To fully charge most modern EVs, it takes about 6–12 h when charging from a home network and about 30–60 min when using charging stations (supercharging) [70]. The duration of the charge becomes a significant problem for long trips that require additional recharging along the way. Increasing the charge rate is one of the main challenges facing automakers. The main characteristics affecting the charge rate are the chemical composition of the elements, properties of their materials, SOH (state of health—degree of degradation), and temperature. With an increase in the charge rate, the cell temperature rises rapidly due to an increase in the released ohmic losses, which negatively affects the capacity, service life, and safety of the battery. This is how the short circuit of NMC and NCA batteries was considered in the work; with a short circuit, the cells were heated to a temperature of 80–100 ◦C in less than 100 s, which led to thermal acceleration of the batteries [70]. Usually, EV battery packs are not repairable, and the cost of replacing them is com- parable to the cost of the entire vehicle, e.g., replacing the Tesla Model 3 LIB costs about USD 12,000; therefore, it is assumed that their service life will be the same as that of an electric car. The claimed battery life is determined by the time during which its maximum useful capacity is reduced to 80% of the original, averaging 10–15 years. Common degra- dation mechanisms include an increase in the SEI, irreversible precipitation of lithium or its uneven distribution inside the electrodes, decomposition of the electrolyte, and gas formation as a result of adverse reactions. In each specific type of battery, the degree of degradation depends on the composition of the electrodes and electrolyte, as well as on the operating conditions. The design of the battery modules and the battery pack must take into account factors related to impact strength, vibration resistance, and heat resistance at each level, i.e., both at the module level and at the battery level. The main source of danger when using Li-ion batteries is thermal runaway. The causes of the onset of this phenomenon may be the following: mechanical damage to the battery, vibrations above 20 Hz, temperature rise above 70 ◦C, overcharging, and short circuit in the battery [71]. There are two main areas of research in the field of safety: (i) preventive strategy (optimization of the power struc- ture, cooling systems, and chemistry), which prevents thermal acceleration; (ii) reactive strategy (refractory gaskets and rupture membranes), mitigating the consequences of an emergency, i.e., protective mechanisms. The safety of lithium-ion batteries is determined by clear standards, both international and specific to each individual country or enter- prise. A recent review examines the existing battery safety standards but also shows the differences between the standards of different countries [72]. For example, the Chinese standard GB/T31485-2015 [73] (now replaced by GB 38031-2020 [74]) requires withstanding a short circuit ≤5 mΩfor 10 min, while the International Electrotechnical Commission in IEC62133 [75] requires only withstanding a short circuit of 80 ± 20 mΩ. 2.2.1. Classification of EV Batteries The complexity of the battery module design is largely influenced by the form factor of the batteries used and the design of the cooling system. For example, cylindrical elements have terminals at opposite ends of the element body, which significantly complicates the electrical switching of the elements and, thereby, the design of the entire module. Transport batteries consist of a large number of lithium-ion batteries that are switched into modules and batteries are assembled from modules (Figure 2). 
--- FILE: Electric Vehicle Battery Technologies.pdf | PAGE: 9 ---
World Electr. Veh. J. 2024, 15, 568 9 of 36 Figure 2. Components of EV batteries. According to the form factor, batteries are divided into three types used in the auto- motive industry: cylindrical, prismatic in a hard case, prismatic in a soft case (pouch cells), and coin cells used in small energy devices. The listed form factors and their applications are shown in Figure 3. Figure 3. The form factor of batteries, their features, and applications. Cylindrical batteries have good mechanical strength. However, such batteries are characterized by low values of volumetric energy consumption (less than 80% of the prismatic ones). Prismatic batteries have higher volumetric energy consumption but are more expensive to manufacture than cylindrical batteries [76]. A significant disadvantage of prismatic pouch batteries is low mechanical strength and a high probability of punctures and plastic deformations [77]. The batteries are switched into modules to ensure the required voltage level. The main purpose of the modules is the packaging of individual batteries and their fixation, mechanical protection, and temperature control. Many companies are striving to unify the modules used in their electric vehicles, making it easy to scale batteries for different tasks. In view of this, prismatic batteries have recently been used for modular tabs. The architecture of the EV battery packs is determined by the location of the modules in the electric vehicle. The safety and reliability of the battery depends on the architecture of the 
--- FILE: Electric Vehicle Battery Technologies.pdf | PAGE: 10 ---
World Electr. Veh. J. 2024, 15, 568 10 of 36 battery in emergency situations. The utilized EV architectures of batteries are shown in Figure 4. Figure 4. “Floor” and “T-Shape” arrangement of modules in an electric vehicle. Currently, the most common architecture used in electric vehicles such as the Tesla Cybertruck, Tesla Model S, Porsche Taycan, and Zeekr 001 is “floor-mounted” [78–81]. This architecture involves placing battery modules under the floor of the car to maximize the usable space inside the car. In addition, this arrangement improves the stability of the car due to the lower location of the center of mass. However, with this arrangement, the probability of mechanical impact on the battery increases when the bottom hits the ground or when hit by small stones and other road debris. The “T-Shape” architecture is used in EVs such as the Chevrolet Volt [82]. This architecture allows designers to place the battery modules in a safe area of the car from direct frontal and side impacts—that is, in the area under and between the rear passenger seats. This design reduces the internal useful space of the car but increases the protection of the battery due to the power structure of the car. 2.2.2. Trends in EV Batteries Architectures The most prominent new approach in the field of batteries is the “Blade Battery” cells manufactured by BYD. A distinctive feature of the “Blade Battery” is the large length of such cells—one can occupy the entire width of the battery module of an electric vehicle. Modules from such batteries outperform those assembled from batteries of other form factors by 9% in terms of volumetric energy density [83,84]. It is also an advantage to reduce the number of battery components by 70%, reducing the number of possible breakdowns [85]. In the early 2010s, during the active development of the electric vehicle industry, the battery architecture was mainly modular: battery cells are combined in series and in parallel into modules, and each module has its own protective housing with related systems; then, the battery pack is assembled from the modules, including a separate control unit for all modules and a temperature control system [86]. Currently, the vast majority of manufacturers still use modular architecture. In the early 2010s, the battery architecture developed in two clear ways—manufacturers used rechargeable batteries consisting of battery modules with cylindrical batteries or modules with prismatic batteries. Striking examples of that time are the first generations of Tesla cars using cylindrical batteries in their design and the first generations of BMW i3 cars using prismatic batteries, which are the most commercially sold cars as of 2016.

Thus, the most popular Zeekr electric vehicles in Russia, which occupy more than 30% of the entire market [88], are equipped with a battery made of prismatic cells [81]. It is also worth noting that since the already mentioned 2017, the share of electric vehicles for which the manufacturer does not specify the form factor of the cells used remains consistently high (about 30% of the total number), which is probably due to the reluctance to disclose trade secrets to other manufacturers [87]. However, innovations in the field of EVB design occur not only in terms of the transition to the use of more efficient battery cells in terms of energy density, safety, and manufacturability of form factors, but also in the use of a more efficient EVB architecture. So, now, the standard is the design by the Cell-To-Module (CTM) method, in which the battery cells are completed in identical modules, which are then connected to the battery. With this approach, it is easy to ensure the required structural strength, since the battery cells have two layers of protection—the module shell and the EVB deposition. It is also convenient from the point of view of manufacturing a battery of the required capacity, since it requires repeating the same assembly operations for the required number of identical modules. An example of this approach is the Volkswagen ID series of electric vehicles [89]. The presence of the module shell and its attachment elements to the EVB body and connecting electrical elements between the modules reduces the specific energy density of the EVB as a whole, which increases the mass of the electric vehicle and lowers its dynamic characteristics [90]. Currently, it is possible to identify the trend of transition from the modular architecture of lithium-ion transport batteries to the Cell-To-Pack (CTP) architecture (Figure 6, Architec- ture EVB) [91]. The CTP approach is to use fewer, larger battery cells, which reduces the number of connections and adapter parts of the battery, simplifies assembly, and potentially increases reliability. For example, the Tesla Model S battery pack has more than 7000 battery cells, each connection of which is a potential point of failure/malfunction. Switching to CTP, a large number of connections are made from the cell to the module and from the module to the battery, thereby minimizing the negative impact of transient connections. 
--- FILE: Electric Vehicle Battery Technologies.pdf | PAGE: 12 ---
World Electr. Veh. J. 2024, 15, 568 12 of 36   Figure 6. Various EVB architectures. Utilization of the CTP architecture allows the removal of the accompanying protective structure of the modules, including their side walls and covers. This allows manufacturers to free up more volume inside the battery case for the cells, increasing the volumetric energy density (kWh/L). Using fewer parts reduces costs and can also lead to shorter production steps and potentially lower overall design costs. Cell-To-Pack (CTP) technology leads to an increase in energy density of 15–20% and reduces the number of parts for the manufacture of a battery by 40% [91]. However, the absence of battery module housings reduces the protective mechanical properties and additional safety measures are required, which, for example, will reduce the spread of heat in the event of a cell fire and give mechanical strength to the battery cells. Developing new concepts for such architectures is an open task for manufacturers. Technology leaders are working on an alternative Cell-To-Chassis (CTC) technology, in which the elements will be integrated directly into the vehicle frame. Due to the abandonment of modules, more cells are placed in the same place for installation, which should increase the power reserve of the electric vehicle. In 2020, CTL announced a production schedule for CTC technology, with a plan to begin mass production as early as 2025 [85]. Table 2 shows a comparison of the described EVB architectures. Table 2. Comparison of the various EVB architectures. World Electr. Veh. J. 2024, 15, 568 13 of 36 With an increase in the energy consumption of electric vehicle batteries, there is a noticeable increase in the average values of battery voltages. For cars manufactured in 2014–2019, the average voltage of the LIB was 300–350 V, while for cars produced over the past five years, this value is 400–430 V; in some cases, the average voltage is 700–800 V. Another solution being developed is the use of replaceable batteries. This approach is good because instead of waiting for a long time at a charging station—on average, charging a medium-sized passenger car at a specialized charging station takes from 20 to 40 min [92], replacing the battery takes only about 3 min [93]. However, such a scheme has a serious design disadvantage—in modern electric vehicles, the EVB is often part of the supporting structure and needs liquid or other high-performance and economical types of cooling, which creates problems maintaining the integrity of the vehicle structure and the tightness of the cooling system when undocking and attaching the EVB. To improve the efficiency of battery replacement stations (Battery-Swapping Station—BSS), requirements for the unification of EVB and procedures for their replacement for various models of EVs are being developed [93]. 2.3. BMS (Battery Management System) Battery management systems (BMSs) are the diagnostic and control equipment of modern batteries that carry out temperature control and assessment of the state of charge and degree of degradation (state of health, SOH, and state of charge, SOC). The schematic diagram of the BMS is shown in Figure 7. The BMS board is all the blocks in this figure, except for the battery itself; the heater and cooler blocks; and the controller, which can be either part of the BMS or an external plug-in device. Figure 7. Scheme of BMS main components architecture. The BMS ensures the same level of charge for all battery cells, preventing overcharging or over-discharging of each element relative to the others. This optimizes performance and extends battery life. There are two techniques for balancing battery cells: passive [94] and active [95]. Passive balancing consists in releasing excess energy in the form of heat losses through resistors connected in parallel to the cells. The essence of active balancing is the redistribution of excess energy from recharged to less-charged packaging cells. Unlike passive balancing, instead of spending energy on heat losses, it is transported to other cells. The most important function of the BMS is related to temperature control and could be considered as a separate unit of battery thermal management systems, BTMSs. The features of BTMSs are discussed in the next section. BMS also monitors the charge/discharge and 
--- FILE: Electric Vehicle Battery Technologies.pdf | PAGE: 14 ---
World Electr. Veh. J. 2024, 15, 568 14 of 36 the state of the degree of degradation by evaluation of capacity (state of health, SOH, and state of charge, SOC), which is described in Section 3. 2.3.1. SOC and SOH Estimation and Prediction Methods SOC Methods for assessing the state of charge can be divided into several groups: lookup- table methods including OCV method and AC impedance method, hybrid method (adap- tive filtering), coulomb counting, model-based methods, and data-driven approaches (Figure 8). Model-based methods include electrochemical, equivalent circuit, and elec- trochemical impedance models. Data-driven approaches include neural network, deep learning, support vector machine, and fuzzy logic [96].   Figure 8. Classification of methods for assessing the state of charge, SOC. Coulomb Counting. This method is based on calculating the amount of current that has been flowing in the battery for a certain period of time [97]. SOC(t) = SOC(0) − Z τ 0 ηI Qmax dτ, (1) where SOC(0) is initial state of charge, SOC(t) is state of charge at the moment t, η is Coulomb efficiency, I is current, and Qmax is maximum capacity. The main disadvantages of this evaluation method are the need for high-precision measuring instruments, the accumulation of error, and the lack of correction [98]. Since it is necessary to know the value of the current strength for calculations, and this is the measured parameter, this implies the need for high-precision measuring devices. Due to the lack of auto-correction and the fact that the method is integral, there is a significant accumulation of error, which also requires certain methods of correction. With an error of 1–2% in determining the current and an abnormal deviation already on the 10th cycle, the error may amount to 20%. Open circuit voltage (OCV) estimation method. Due to the existence of a certain depen- dence between the open circuit voltage at rest (OCV) and the state of charge, SOC could be estimated using OCV [99]. Good accuracy for this method is ensured only when the battery is at rest and, if there was a pre-current load, the relaxation process is completed. Despite the simplicity of the method and good accuracy with the battery at rest, the dependence 
--- FILE: Electric Vehicle Battery Technologies.pdf | PAGE: 15 ---
World Electr. Veh. J. 2024, 15, 568 15 of 36 varies greatly from one type of battery to another and with differing conditions, which makes this method unsuitable in portable electronics and electric vehicles [100]. It has been shown that a CV measurement error of 1 mV leads to an error in the SOC indicator of about 5% for the SOC ranges of 40–60% and 80–90% for LP cells [101]. Thus, an inaccurate OCV definition leads to a high SOC error, which could not be used in practice. The OCV method can be combined with ML, which makes the results more accu- rate [102]. In a recent paper, it was shown that when comparing different results of fitting OCV–SOC dependencies at different temperatures and the results of neural network predic- tions in the case of the latter, the standard deviation and the coefficient of determination lie in the ranges 0.0015–0.0067 V and 0.9975–0.9999, respectively, while various approximations show results in the ranges 0.0071–0.0281 V and 0.9481–0.9967, respectively [103]. Despite the more accurate results, such improvements require a long and, therefore, resource- intensive data collection for neural network training and the huge computing power of the device used, which is difficult to implement in portable electronics and electric vehicles. Methods based on machine learning and big data. Certain machine learning tools such as neural network, deep learning, support vector machine, and fuzzy logic are also used to assess battery power. They can be used as an auxiliary tool or as an independent method [104]. The advantage of these methods lies in their high accuracy, the ability to take into account many factors and inaccuracies that are difficult to take into account when using other SOC assessment methods, and not requiring manual parameterization of the model or any special knowledge and understanding of the system to be studied [105]. For example, an XGBoost-based SOC estimation method was used in combination with an extended Kalman filter, which gave an SOC measurement error of less than 2%. Nevertheless, for high accuracy of the methods, a large array of experimental data is needed to train neural networks; in addition, the accuracy of the model strongly depends on the selected set for training and testing the model [106]. Adaptive filters. These mathematical algorithms work as iterative filters based on input measured parameters and predictions for the battery model [107]. Their equations differ but have the same basic principles, which will be described below for linear Kalman filter. Unknown states calculate a set of xk vector states from a set of measurements of yk process vector: xk = Ak−1xk−1 + Buk + wk−1, (2) yk = Ckxk + vk, (3) in which A is the state transition matrix; B is the model control matrix; uk is the vector of control actions; C is the observation model matrix; and w and v are defined as white noise with covariance Qk and Rk, respectively. Based on Equations (2) and (3), KF estimates xk state based on noisy measurement of yk. In Equation (3), xk is the estimation of the previous state. The main advantage of using these methods is the automatic correction of the error of the computer model of the battery and much lower requirements for computer computing power compared to data-driven methods. It was shown that the SOC estimation error reached 0.1% for a new battery and 1% for an old one [109]. However, for these types of methods to work well, a fairly accurate simulation of the measured battery data is required, which increases the requirements for the model used [110]. There are many modifications of the Kalman filter (KF) and other adaptive filters: the linear Kalman filter or simply the Kalman filter (LKF), extended Kalman filter (EKF), un- scented Kalman filter (UKF), cubature Kalman filter (CKF), robust Kalman filter (RKF), prob- abilistic Kalman filter (PKF), particle filter (PF), recursive least squares (RLS), etc. [111–114]. All of them differ in their accuracy and reliability in proportion to the increase in the com- plexity of the algorithms and the required computing power [113,115]. The complex steps of implementing the KF family algorithms in online model-based SOC assessment processes, such as battery model selection, initial SOC, and filter setup, are designed to effectively develop a battery management system, especially for use in electric vehicles. Current re- search is being promoted through KF-based online approaches to compatibility assessment, which are clearly highlighted by analyzing various studies to further advance research. SOH All experimental methods for estimating SOH can be divided into two large groups: methods based on direct measurement and methods based on indirect determination [116]. Methods using digital models of real systems, as well as experimental methods, can be divided into two subgroups: methods using adaptive algorithms and methods based on machine learning (Figure 10). 
--- FILE: Electric Vehicle Battery Technologies.pdf | PAGE: 17 ---
World Electr. Veh. J. 2024, 15, 568 17 of 36 Figure 10. Methods for assessing the degree of degradation of LIBs. Experimental methods based on direct measurements. These methods allow researchers to assess the battery condition relatively quickly and at no additional cost. The main methods are direct OCV measurement, coulometry, and impedance spectroscopy and destructive methods such as RAMAN spectroscopy, X-ray diffractometry, and scanning electron microscopy [114,117,118]. Their main disadvantage is the low accuracy of SOH estimation relative to other methods and the need for specific and/or high-precision equipment. For example, in [119], the SOH estimation error was 5%, while even one of the simplest adaptive solutions, EKF, had an error of 3%. Also, the problem with destructive methods is that they simply cannot be used in moving systems, including electric vehicles, since batteries must be opened during research in this way, violating their integrity and operability. Experimental methods based on indirect measurements. These methods are based on tracking and measuring parameters related to capacitance or internal resistance, and further calculating SOH through these parameters. These methods include the bit curve method, incremental capacity analysis (ICA) [120], and differential voltage analysis (DVA) [121]. These methods can be used to study the mechanisms of aging, but they are difficult to use for real-time tracking and special conditions are often needed, for example, low direct current, which is not achieved in real electric motors and portable devices. Also, among the disadvantages of these methods is compatibility with not all types of batteries. Data-driven methods. The advantage of data-driven methods over other methods is that there is no need to use a specific digital battery model or to know its device. In addition, they can be combined with other methods [122]. The disadvantages are similar to those when evaluating SOC and consists in high computing power and a large array of training data, which makes the process long and expensive. Adaptive filters. These methods show accurate and reliable results with relatively low labor intensity and computing power of the device, for example, in the SOH estimation, the error was no higher than 0.08% [123]. Nevertheless, a strong dependence on the accuracy and reliability of the model used, as well as in the assessment of SOC, remain weaknesses of these methods. Battery Thermal Management System Battery thermal management systems (BTMSs) are aimed at controlling the temper- ature of the battery to avoid thermal runaway, which may overheat due to fast charging or driving with high energy consumption (sudden acceleration, long-term maintenance of high speed, etc.). For example, it was shown that during tests at a controlled ambient temperature of 45 ◦C, the surface temperature of the battery increased by 5.2 ◦C at a dis- charge rate of C/2 and by 20.6 ◦C at a discharge rate of 3 C [124]. Also, during long-term operation at elevated temperatures, the aging and degradation processes of the battery are significantly accelerated [124–126]. In addition, the performance and life-cycle of the battery are affected by the uniformity of temperature distribution in order to avoid an imbalance in performance and accelerated degradation of individual batteries. Operation of batteries at subzero temperatures is also undesirable, since the internal resistance of batteries increases significantly, which, during active operation, leads to a significant irreversible loss of battery capacity. Thus, the BTMS should perform the following functions: (i) cooling and heat re- moval from batteries to maintain the operating temperature range; (ii) providing uniform temperature distribution in the battery pack. An overview of BTMSs depending on EV manufacturers is presented below, describing the main types of BTMSs currently used in the industry and new promising methods. Various BTMSs are used in electric vehicles and are divided into active, passive, and hybrid [127–129]. Active temperature control systems require an external power source, such as forced air cooling and liquid cooling. Passive BTMSs, such as cooling with phase transition materials (PCMs), and cooling based on thermoelectric elements and heat pipes, do not need external power sources. The combination of active and passive thermoregulation methods is called hybrid [130–132]. The classification of BTMSs with their division into types is shown in Figure 11. 
--- FILE: Electric Vehicle Battery Technologies.pdf | PAGE: 19 ---
World Electr. Veh. J. 2024, 15, 568 19 of 36 Figure 11. Classification of battery thermal management systems (adapted with permission from Ref. [127], Copyright 2018 Elsevier). Air Cooling The advantages of air cooling include a simple design, low weight of the system, and ease of maintenance compared to a liquid system, PCMs, thermoelectric converters, and heat pipes. It is also possible to highlight economic efficiency and reliability. Air cooling is divided into natural convection and forced convection. This cooling system requires the presence of air channels in the volume of the battery, which negatively affects the volume and specific characteristics of the battery. In addition, powerful, forced air-cooling systems consume relatively more energy than liquid and thermoelectric BTMSs [133]. Modern scientific and technical solutions in the field of air cooling are aimed at reducing the temperature gradient in the volume of the battery [134,135]. Examples of the use of air cooling in electric vehicles are the Renault ZOE, Toyota Prius, Hyundai IONIQ [136], Nissan Leaf [137], VW e-Golf, and Skoda CITIGO-e iV [138]. Many works are devoted to the study of the optimal shape and direction of cooling channels. Zhou et al. have developed new air ducts with distribution holes located longitudinally along them as auxiliary channels for air supply (Figure 12a) [139]. It has been proven that increasing the size (by 1.5 mm) and the number (five rows) of holes allows reducing the maximum temperature (from 52.7 ◦C to 32.6 ◦C) and ensuring a more uniform temperature distribution (maximum temperature difference ≤3 ◦C). Chen et al. developed a U-shaped parallel-cooled air-cooling system using a flow resistance network model [140]. The results of the study showed that the optimized U- type air-cooling system had 33% lower temperature differences at 5 C discharge currents compared to the standard Z-type air-cooling system without additional outlets (Figure 12b). In article [141], the BTMS “J-type” cooling channel was proposed by combining “U- type” and “Z-type” designs (Figure 12c). The new BTMS control system controls two exhaust valves in real time, switching channel configurations between “U-shaped” and “Z-shaped” in accordance to feedback on the thermal state of the battery. Using the “J-type” showed a 3 K reduction in maximum temperature compared to the “Z-type”.

(b) Three-dimensional view of the parallel air-cooled BTMS with U-type flow (adapted with permission from Ref. [140]). (c) J-type cooling channel (combined Z-type and U-type) (adapted with permission from Ref. [141] Copyright 2019 Elsevier). Liquid Cooling The most commonly used types of BTMSs in electric vehicles are air and liquid cooling, since their performance can be optimized depending on the thermal load of the battery, unlike other passive cooling methods such as the BTMS with PCMs and BTMS with heat pipes [133]. The Chevrolet Volt, Tesla Model S and Model X, Audi e-Tron, Toyota iQ, Mercedes-Benz EQS, Porsche Taycan Turbo, and BMW i3 are examples of BTMS liquid-cooled commercial vehicles [138,142]. The main advantage of liquid BTMSs is that such systems allow for higher heat transfer rates at lower energy costs than air-cooled systems [143]. Various types of liquids are used as heat carriers in BTMSs, including water, oils, ethylene glycol, dielectric heat-conducting liquids, and others. In order to achieve high heat transfer efficiency, the direct cooling coolant must have high thermal conductivity, low viscosity, and high heat capacity. Since a submerged battery is at risk of an external short circuit, the coolant must be dielectric. In addition, in accordance with the requirements of environmental protection and safety, its non-toxicity, chemical resistance, and low flammability should be taken into account. Key features of materials for liquid cooling are described in Table 4. Due to their high electrical conductivity of water-based heat carriers, BTMS sealing is crucial for system safety. The penetration of coolant into the space of the battery (the voltage of which can reach 800 V [138]), power/control electronics, or even into the interior of the car can lead to a short circuit, which in turn can lead to battery failure and fire. Therefore, when developing a liquid BTMS, great attention is paid to sealing and maintenance, which leads to a higher cost of liquid-cooling compared to air-cooling systems.

During direct liquid cooling, the battery cells are in direct contact with the liquid. With indirect liquid cooling, the battery cells transfer heat to the liquid through an intermediate cooling medium. Most often, indirect cooling methods include cooling plates or heat-conducting tubes to remove heat from a lithium-ion battery pack. The addition of a heat-conducting medium increases the total weight of the battery and the thermal resistance of the cooling system, which in turn reduces the cooling efficiency of indirect liquid BTMSs [146]. Direct liquid cooling maximizes the cooling surface area compared to indirect liquid cooling, and reduces the complexity of the system, which significantly increases the cooling efficiency of the battery. Immersion cooling is also possible in two versions: single-phase cooling and two- phase cooling. During single-phase cooling, the coolant remains in liquid form and is pumped through a heat exchanger, as shown in Figure 13a. Figure 13. Scheme of single-phase (a) and two-phase (b) immersion cooling for LIBs (adapted with permission from Ref. [134] Copyright 2024 Elsevier). Two-phase cooling involves the use of a coolant with a low boiling point and consists in the fact that during heat release, the coolant evaporates, converting the heat released by the battery into the heat of vaporization; then, the vapors of the coolant are cooled back to a liquid state using a condenser, as shown in Figure 13b. Due to the high values of the heat of evaporation of liquids (Table 4, 120 kJ/kg for 3M Novec 7000 (3M Company, St. Paul, 
--- FILE: Electric Vehicle Battery Technologies.pdf | PAGE: 22 ---
World Electr. Veh. J. 2024, 15, 568 22 of 36 MN, USA)) used in two-phase immersion cooling, the efficiency of a two-phase system is significantly higher than that of a single-phase system. The disadvantages of such systems include the risk of contamination by coolant vapors of other electronic components of an electric vehicle, gradual loss of coolant due to leaks from the condenser unit, complication of the system design, and increased maintenance costs compared with indirect methods. Despite the exceptional characteristics of immersion cooling, immersion cooling has several common disadvantages, which include the high viscosity of such liquids, increasing the required pump power; their high cost (the cost of 3M Novec 7000 is about $150 per 5 L; and additional liquid, which would increase the weight of the battery pack. Therefore, BTMSs with immersion cooling are better suited for batteries designed for fast charging and discharging. Xing Mobility [147] and Kreisel [148] are examples of companies producing bat- tery modules and rechargeable batteries for EVs with single-phase immersion cooling (Figure 14a,b).   Figure 14. (a) LIB by Xing. (b) LIB by Kreisel. The Kreisel solution features non-conductive cooling liquid in direct contact with each individual cell, therefore achieving the most energy-efficient cooling type. This system allows for achieving a low temperature difference in the volume of the battery (less than 1 ◦C) [147]. The Xing Mobility immersion-cooling battery system integrates the cooling system into the battery housing itself, without extensive coolant channels, cold plates, and coolant pipes. Pressure relief features are now part of the battery housing rather than only a cooling system feature. This system showed a maximum temperature 10 ◦C lower than the traditional indirect system and a gain in SOH of 10% after 2000 cycles [148]. Due to the simplicity of indirect cooling methods compared to direct ones, the most common type of liquid cooling of electric vehicles is currently indirect liquid cooling. In cooling systems of this type, the liquid is supplied through separate tubes, channels, or cold plates. A cold plate is a flat metal plate with internal channels through which a coolant is pumped. To increase the specific energy consumption of the entire battery, manufacturers use plates of the smallest possible thickness. The efficiency of cooling with a cold plate is significantly influenced by the geometry of the channels, and much attention is paid to this topic by researchers. The efficiency of cooling plates with different channel geometries was compared according to experiments conducted with an LFP battery (Figure 15) [149]. The experiments were carried out at different water supply rates from 0.1 to 1.1 L/min as a coolant with an inlet temperature from 15 to 35 ◦C. The results show that the use of a mini-channel cooling plate resulted in a decrease in the maximum average surface temperature of the battery of 5.7 ◦C compared to the serpentine geometry [149]. Two types of mini-channel cooling plates, namely, serpentine (1,2) and multi-channel (3,4), have been numerically and experimentally studied (Figure 15b) [150]. The optimal design obtained as a result of numerical simulation was manufactured and experimentally tested. The results showed that the use of grooved pin fins significantly improves heat transfer in both designs compared to using only fins. The average ratios of augmentation in exergy efficiency attributed to the use of pin fins and grooves reached 24% and 37% for serpentine and multi-channel, respectively.
