redox reactions. Since the energy storage process is not restricted by diffusion, it responds rapidly to potential changes, giving the opportunity for fast-charging at high currents. Moreover, Li-storage capacity tends to increase with the effective specific surface area of the electrode material.71−73 The thickness of the double electric layer relies on the concentration of electrolytes and the size of ions. Depending on the energy storage mechanism, pseudocapa- citors could be classified as adsorption, surface redox, and intercalation pseudocapacitors (see Figure 3c).74 Adsorption pseudocapacitance is also referred to as underpotential deposition (UPD), which describes the adsorption of one metal ion on the surface of another metal at a potential more positive than its thermodynamically reversible potential.75,76 Capacitance is seldom implicated in energy storage devices. Redox pseudocapacitance represents a procedure in which ions undergo electrosorption on or near the material surface, accompanying Faraday charge transfer and highly reversible.77 Intercalation pseudocapacitance involves the Faraday charge transfer accompanied by no crystalline phase change when ions are intercalated into the interlayer of materials.78−80 This pseudocapacitance not only undergoes a Faraday process similar to the charging and discharging of a Li-ion battery, but also demonstrates DELC-like properties. Based on the characteristics, a pseudocapacitor stands a chance to possess a high energy density equivalent to the battery material and a similar power density as the DELC material. Noticeably, the Li+ transport mechanism for both batteries and pseudocapa- citive devices is essentially a redox reaction. Pseudocapacitors store Li+ through redox reactions on the material surface or rapid insertion of ions into the material, unconstrained by the slow kinetics of solid-state ion diffusion and without inducing phase transitions.81 ION DIFFUSION IN CRYSTALS The crystal cell consists of the minimum geometrical unit selected from the lattice that exactly captures the lattice characteristics, which is the highest symmetry parallel hexahedron and represents the features of the atomic arrangement form. structures comprise straightforward cubic, body-centered cubic, face-centered cubic, and close-packed hexagonal crystals. According to Bravais lattice, seven crystallographic systems (cubic, tripartite, tetragonal, hexagonal, orthorhombic, mono- clinic, and triclinic) could be used to categorize lattices in the 3D plane. Based on the aforementioned theoretical, the diverse diffusion path of Li+ in the lattice is primarily summarized as interlayer diffusion, vacancy diffusion, and gap diffusion. Interlayer Diffusion. Most battery materials suffer from ion insertion into the crystal structure and accompanying phase transition, leading to inferior fast-charging performance. Nevertheless, intercalation-type pseudocapacitor materials exhibit a significantly different mechanism. Namely, Li+ does not react electrochemically with the electrode, and the electrode material typically stores Li+ via a fast transport pathway. For example, niobium base oxides exhibit a peculiar crystal structure and multiple redox couples of Nb3+/Nb4+/ Nb5+.82 Compared with the voltage of graphite (0.1 V vs Li+/ Li), the relatively high operating voltage (>1.5 V) could be useful in inhibiting the formation of Li dendrites and unstable SEI films on the solid electrolyte interface, resulting in an exceptionally prospective “fast-charging” anode materials.83−86 Hitherto, orthorhombic Nb2O5 (T-Nb2O5), TiNb2O7, and Nb18W16O93 have been demonstrated to be attractive “fast- charging” anode materials. Here, we concentrate on inves- tigating their crystal structures and Li+ diffusion paths. T-Nb2O5 primarily comprises heavily twisted octahedral and bipyramidal Nb ambiances (Figure 4a), where the unit cell exhibits twisted polyhedral sheets by sharing edges or corners parallel to the (001) plane, and each Nb ions is connected to pieces of 6 or 7 O2−, forming NbO6 and NbO7.87−90 The existence of empty octahedral sites among the (001) planes furnishes a reasonable channel for Li+ transport in the ab plane. The reaction mechanism can be expressed as91 Nb2O5 + xLi++xe−→LixNb2O5 (0 ≤x ≤2). Meanwhile, the crystal structure of the unlithiated T-Nb2O5 appears mainly in the form of alternating dense (4h)-loose (4g) arrangement. The loose 4g layer serves to store Li+, and the Li+ in the dense 4h layer could feasibly form a bridging site between oxygen and Li+ (Figure 4b). The exceptional bridging site creates a rapid Li+ diffusion channel along with low transport barriers.90 Additionally, in Figure 4c, the author marks the Li+ migration paths as path A and path B based on the bridged O4h being edge-shared or corner-shared by adjacent NbOx (x = 6 or 7) for carefully observing the Li+ storage process. The two diffusion paths both allow Li+ to be transported fast without requiring ions to move through a particularly narrow space. The large gap space (approximately 4 Å) in the 4h layer enables the ion transport at a rather weak energy barrier, and path B presents a lower energy barrier to overcome than path A. Therefore, path B serves as the optimal diffusion path for Li+. Such an unusual “room-and-pillar” structure ascribed to Figure 5. (a−c) Direct, vacancy, and gap-replaces exchange diffusion mechanism. NbO6/NbO7 delivers a stable structure for Li insertion with no phase transition.92 And the layer-like structure causes Nb2O5 to express excellent “fast-charging” performance unlike other classic intercalation-type materials, manifesting a superior intercalation pseudocapacitance.90,93−95 TiNb2O7 manifests a Wadsley−Roth phase and a crystallo- graphic shear structure in the C2/m space group (Figure 4d). The phase consists of a 3 × 3 × ∞ReO3-like block of corner- shared octahedra in each plane, and T1 and T2 represent two types of infinite tunnels.96−98 Typically, Li-ion is inserted in the (001) lattice accompanied by a change in the lattice constant.99 The intense anisotropy for ions and electron conductivity allows the Li+ to diffuse along the tunneling (b- axis) direction approximating the 1D direction.98 The octahedral ReO3-like block offers a weak potential barrier, enabling the Li-ion to diffuse rapidly. The crystal shear plane enables the framework to be in a state, which assists in accomplishing favorable structural stability. Besides, minor lithiation enhances the electronic conductivity of TiNb2O7, turning TiNb2O7 into a metallic phase.98,99 The mechanism of lithiation for TiNb2O7 is described as the gradual occupation of 4i(1) and 4i(2) sites by external Li+ during initial lithiation. Upon further lithiation, the Li+ at 4i(1) site migrate to 4i(3) and 4i(4) sites. Meanwhile, a large number of external Li+ continuously occupies 4i(3), 4i(4), and 4i(1) sites. Once the 4i(1) site is fully occupied again, Li+ at 4i(1) and 4i(2) sites is simultaneously transferred to the 4i(5) site. Subsequently, more Li+ ions are inserted into 4i(1) and 4i(2) sites. Meanwhile, the Li+ at 4i(3) site is migrated to 8j site, eventually forming Li4TiNb2O7.100 The findings reveal that TiNb2O7 develops noticeable intercalation pseudocapacitance and maintains a slight volume variation during the repeated charging and discharging, representing a promising “fast- charging” anode material of Li-ion batteries. Researchers are interested in V2O5 since it is a 2D structural material that resembles graphene. Obviously, path A (b-axis direction) is the fastest channel for Li+ diffusion in the lattice structure (Figure 4e), and it could be transformed into Li3V2O5 as a “fast-charging” anode material for Li-ion batteries.101−103 Additionally, a 1D channel exists in the Nb18W16O93 crystal structure, namely, pentagonal, square, and triangular channels (Figure 4f). The Li+ is preferentially inserted in the largest channel (pentagonal), then into the middle channel (square), and finally into the smallest channel (triangular) during lithiation, forming Li13Nb18W16O93, Li21Nb18W16O93, and Li35Nb18W16O93, respectively, subse- quently filling each type of channel.104 Thanks to rapid ion transport rates and lack of phase shift, the materials represent a promising “fast-charging” anode material. Vacancy Diffusion and Gap Diffusion. The ion diffusion in crystals mainly relies on Schottky vacancy diffusion and Frank interstitial diffusion mechanisms. For the operational system of Li-ion batteries, the diffusion mechanisms become further complicated, such as interstitial diffusion mechanism, collective diffusion mechanism, push-fill submechanism, interstitial site-lattice site exchange mechanism, vacancy mechanism, double vacancy mechanism, and so on. The interstitial diffusion mechanism mainly suits the diffusion of interstitial atoms in a solid solution. The interstitial atoms with tiny size diffuse from one interstitial site to another in the solid solution, which is termed direct diffusion (Figure 5a). The vacancy mechanism applies to the diffusion of replacement solid solutions, whereby atoms diffuse by leaping to adjacent vacancies (Figure 5b). In replacement solid solutions, the small difference in atomic sizes prevents the implementation of interstitial diffusion. Therefore, vacancy diffusion exerts an essential function in the solids. Currently, vacancies are routinely created by doping for increasing ionic conductivity, and a multivacancy mechanism could exist as well if vacancies are clustered. They could diffuse utilizing the exchange of interstitial-lattice sites if atoms simultaneously occupy interstitial and lattice sites (Figure 5c). The interstitial- substituent interaction mechanism may be used when the interstitial “solute” atom concentration is lower than that of the “substituent” atom concentration. The dissociation mechanism exists if the diffusion has been fulfilled through vacancies. Otherwise, a collective diffusion mechanism could be maintained, in which several atoms simultaneously move in a chain-like or track-like manner. The push-fill submechanism and the self-gap mechanism similarly belong to the collective diffusion mechanism. The theoretical information mentioned above offers a foundation for the creation of “fast-charging” batteries. In Li- ion battery systems, the transport of Li+ normally entails a phase change in electrode materials.105 For “fast-charging” batteries, electrode materials could contiguously accommodate Li through solid-solution transitions.106 For instance, Li4Ti5O12(LTO) anode with a spinel structure akin to that of LiMn2O4 displays exceptionally excellent rate capability, which could be regarded as a composite oxide of metal Li and transition metal Ti and belongs to the AB2 × 4 series with space group Fd3̅m.30 Figure 5d illustrates the crystal structure of LTO. The Li, Ti, and O elements exist in the valence states of +1, +4, and −2, respectively, of which the O atom occupies the 32e site, Ti atom occupies 5/6 times 16d site, and the remaining 1/6 times 16d site is occupied by the Li atom. Meanwhile, the Li atom also fills the 8a site of the tetrahedron, resulting in [Li]8a[Li1/3Ti5/3]16d[O4]32e framework structure.107 LTO stores Li using a two-phase conversion procedure During charging and discharging (Figure 5e). The initial disordered spinel phase (Li4Ti5O12) is directly transformed into the rock salt phase (Li7Ti5O12), which is referred to as a zero-strain material due to the almost constant lattice parameters.108,109 The rapid transport of Li+ in LTO is attributed to the presence of intermediate states (Li4 + xTi5O12, 0 ≤x ≤3), in which the Li migrates from the 8a site to the 16c site during the initial discharging state, leaving 8a vacant in the Li7Ti5O12. Further lithiation causes the reoccupation of the 8a site. Li+ occupies both 8a and 16c sites, existing as uniform-phase solid solutions or phase-separated nanomixes.110 Simultaneously, a distorted Li polyhedron and a redistribution of Li+ within the lattice lead to the rapid transport channel. The result could provide theoretical guidance for seeking “fast-charging” electrode materials. In addition, Liu et al. reported a disordered rock salt (Li3 + xV2O5) anode for “fast-charging” Li-ion batteries.102 The Li diffusion mechanism includes a direct tetrahedral to tetrahedral (t-t) jump and a jump through a noncooperative (t- o-t) mechanism, namely the Li+ jumps from one tetrahedral site to an empty octahedral site and then to another tetrahedral site (Figure 5f)).102 Due to a redistributed Li insertion process in DRS-Li3 + xV2O5, Li diffusion in the aforementioned material is an order of magnitude faster than in graphite, resulting in Li- ion battery anode materials with a “fast-charging” performance. In summary, the principle of “fast-charging” of Li-ion batteries involves several aspects such as electronic con- ductivity, ionic conductivity, and structural properties of ACS Nano www.acsnano.org Review https://doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.3c08712 ACS Nano 2024, 18, 2611−2648 2617

electrode materials. Here the principle of “fast-charging” from the perspective of material structure is explained. The fast migration of Li+ in the lattice could often be implemented in two ways. First, several materials with layered structures allow Li-ions to diffuse freely in the lattice, resulting in a faster charging rate. Second, the crystal structure of certain materials enables Li+ to be more easily inserted and deinsertion, such as the rearrangement of ions during the lithiation process activates more ion transport paths. Eventually, ions diffuse by the most superior transport paths, increasing the charging rate. CRYSTAL STRUCTURE AND “FAST-CHARGING” PER- FORMANCE AT MATERIALS LEVEL. Recently, the fast growth of portable electronic devices and electric vehicles has raised further expectations for Li-ion batteries, calling for high capacity, long life, inherent stability, and excellent “fast- charging” performance, among which the anode material turns out to be the critical bottleneck for achieving “fast- charging” capacity.13 Currently, the prevalent “fast-charging” anode materials for intercalated Li-ion batteries include mainly carbon-based, niobium-based, titanium-based, vanadium- based, and other anode materials. The following will mainly be investigated in detail their crystal structure and “fast- charging” performance. NIOBIUM-BASED MATERIALS The niobium-based material with a quasi-2D network structure possesses an open and stable Wadsley−Roth shear crystal structure, which makes it possible for Li+ to diffuse rapidly and have favorable cycling stability. Moreover, the multielectron redox reaction causes it to express high-theoretical specific capacity, providing the opportunity for the development of high energy density and high-power density batteries. Niobium-based materials mainly include Nb2O5, Ti−Nb oxides, and Nb−W oxides.111 It has appeared as an attractive candidate for “fast-charging” anode materials. Nb2O5. properties (Figure 6a). Nb2O5 subsists in multiple crystallo- graphic forms, among which the pseudohexagonal phase (TT- Nb2O5), orthorhombic phase (T-Nb2O5), and monoclinic phase (H-Nb2O5) are the most ubiquitous phases. The TT- Nb2O5 could be converted to the H-Nb2O5 by suitable heat treatment. Similarly, the amorphous niobate may be trans- formed to TT-Nb2O5 at lower temperatures. TT-Nb2O5 could be continuously transformed to T-Nb2O5 by successive heating at 600−800 °C. At 1,100 °C, any other form of Nb2O5 heated in the air could form H-Nb2O5.112 Among them, T-Nb2O5 represents an orthorhombic phase with a Pbam space group, which has been demonstrated to be the most promising “fast- charging” anode material. Second, a few studies have demonstrated that H-Nb2O5 is also a prevalent anode material for Li-ion batteries. However, the inferior electronic con- ductivity of Nb2O5 hinders the charge transfer rate and increases the ohmic resistance, limiting their application in high-rate devices. Hence, it is urgent to develop other strategies to ameliorate the electron transfer and Li+ diffusion rate. For example, the synthesis of H-Nb2O5 single crystals growing in the direction [001] by direct and efficient one-pot annealing in the air could not only more effectively cope with volume fluctuations and reduce side reactions with the electrolyte, but also exhibit a more efficient Li+ diffusion path. Single-crystal H-Nb2O5 displays ultrahigh-rate perform- ance and long life, with a capacity of 115.6 mAh g−1 at 25 C after 3000 cycles (Figure 6c).111 Besides, Nb2O5-δ/graphite composites are prepared through the ball milling method, and the presence of graphite in the mixture facilitates the formation of Nb12O29 during the ball milling process, which restricts the particle size of the active material and ameliorates the total conductivity of the composite electrode. Meanwhile, the energy barrier for Li+ migration in Nb12O29 with crystal shear structure is as low as in T-Nb2O5. The composite electrode demonstrates exceptional rate capability attributed to the enhanced electronic conductivity and ionic conductivity. The composite electrode provides a specific capacity of 120 mAh g−1 at 16 A g−1 in a half-cell and maintains over 150 mAh g−1 after 2000 cycles at 6 A g−1, indicating that it is a very promising anode for “fast-charging” Li-ion batteries materi- al.113 The diffusion of Li+ in Nb12O29 prefers to occupy the bridging oxygen sites in the structure (Figure 6d). The four most stable Li adsorption sites are located in the square cone sites of E1 and E2 and the square plane sites of H and C1 at the edge of the NbO6 block, the adsorption energy between these sites is rather close and stronger than the other sites. Li tends to distribute along the four locations as a result. Li+ diffuses effortlessly between the (001) planes in T-Nb2O5, and the main transport between the hexahedral and square pyramidal sites is path A and path B, with a small diffusion barrier (≤0.33 eV). The potential barrier of the inner block diffusion pathway is low (0.19−0.34 eV) when diffusing in Nb12O29. When the potential barrier is slightly higher (0.43− 0.50 eV), cross-block diffusion is much less likely. In Nb12O29 tunneling, the diffusion of Li in 3D occurs easily, and the diffusion barrier is as small as that of T-Nb2O5 (≤0.33 eV), allowing for fast Li-storage. Ti−Nb Oxides and Nb−W Oxides. Ti−Nb oxides (TiNbO) with insertion-type have been regarded as one of the finest promising alternatives to graphite and Li4Ti5O12 anode materials in recent years,114 which presents many merits. First, the high theoretical specific capacity (377−402 mAh g−1) compared with that of Li4Ti5O12 (1.5 V vs Li+/Li) correlates with multiple redox couples such as Ti4+/Ti3+ (about 2.0 V), Nb5+/Nb4+ (about 1.5−1.8 V), and Nb4+/Nb3+ (about 1.3−1.5 V).115 Second, the relatively high operating voltage (about 1.65 V) in comparison to the voltage of graphite (0.1 V vs Li+/Li) may effectively preclude the formation of Li dendrites and the unstable SEI films on the solid electrolyte interface, ensuring a favorable safety of Li-ion battery under fast-charging or even overcharging.116 Third, it is referred to as a low-strain anode material with high cycling stability owing to the slight cell volume change during repeated charging and discharging processes.117 Simultaneously, TiNbO also presents the Roth− Wadsley structure composed of corner-shared and/or edge- shared octahedra, and the sophisticated crystal structural coupled with its insertion characteristics render it to demonstrate a high cyclic stability.118 Fourthly, the discharging and charging curves of TiNbO in a certain voltage range exhibit a gradual drop/rise behavior at the end of Li-insertion/ deinsertion processes, which differs from that of Li4Ti5O12 with a sharp voltage change.119 The advantage assists in evaluating the state of charge (SOC) and boosting the design of battery management systems. Finally, TiNbO presents inherent pseudocapacitive behavior that favors Li-storage capacity and cycling stability.120 TiNbO possesses diverse compositions and structures, the general formula is TiNbxO2+2.5x, including TiNb2O7,121 Ti2Nb2O9, Ti2Nb10O29,122 TiNb24O62,123 TiNb38O97, and TiNb52O132, etc.94,124 The theoretical specific capacity of the TiNbxO2+2.5x materials can be obtained by adopting eq 7:125 C x 403 5441/(133 80) = + (7) According to eq 7 and the x value in the TiNbxO2+2.5x, the theoretical specific capacity of Ti2Nb2O9 (x = 1), TiNb2O7 (x = 2), Ti2Nb10O29 (x = 5), TiNb6O17 (x = 6), TiNb24O62 (x = 24), TiNb38O97 (x = 38), and TiNb52O132 (x = 52) are estimated to be 377, 387, 396, 397, 401, 402, and 402 mAh g−1, respectively. Each material exhibits a high Li+ diffusion coefficient owing to the Roth−Wadsley structure125 that differs only in the connectivity of each block formed by the presence of shear surfaces (Figure 6a).98 Of these, TiNb2O7, Ti2Nb10O29, and TiNb24O62 with the monoclinic ReO3-type crystal structures deliver the most widely investigated anode materials for Li-ion batteries, Ti2Nb10O29 offers a higher Li- insertion voltage (about 1.7 V) than TiNb2O7 (about 1.64 V).126,127 TiNb2O7, Ti2Nb10O29, and TiNb24O62 were discovered, and their crystal structures were elucidated by Roth and Wadsley in the 1950s and 1960s. TiNb2O7 is composed of a 3 × 3 × ∞ReO3-like block of corner-shared octahedra in each plane (C2/m space group), whereas Ti2Nb10O29 and TiNb24O62 are constructed of a 3 × 4 octahedral-block (A2/m space group) and a 3 × 4 octahedral blocks add 0.5 tetrahedra at the block corners (C2 space group), respectively (Figure 6a).129,130 In 1983, TiNb2O7 and Ti2Nb10O29 experienced a Li-insertion reaction at room temperature.131 In 2011, the team of Goodenough determined that TiNb2O7 could be utilized as a TiNbxO2 + 2.5x anode material for Li-ion batteries, and the group synthesized micron-sized TiNb2O7 particles employing the sol−gel method, a reversible specific capacity of 285 mAh g−1 could be remained at the current density of 38.7 mA g−1 and in the voltage range of 1.0−2.5 V.130 In 2012, Chen’s team identified Ti2Nb10O29 as another high-performance TiNbxO2+2.5x anode material, and the as-synthesized Ti2Nb10O29 μm-sized particles using a solid-phase reaction ACS Nano www.acsnano.org Review https://doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.3c08712 ACS Nano 2024, 18, 2611−2648 2619

technique presented an excellent Li-storage capacity of 247 mAh g−1 at the current density of 39.6 mA g−1 and in the voltage range of 1.0−2.5 V.132 Four years later, Lin’s team uncovered TiNb24O62 as the third TiNbxO2 + 2.5x anode material. The prepared TiNb24O62 porous microspheres by solvothermal technique possesses a favorable specific capacity of 296 mAh g−1 at the current density of 40.1 mA g−1 and favorable cycling stability.134 In addition to the above three anode materials, Ti2Nb2O9, TiNb38O97, and TiNb52O132 as anode materials of the TiNbxO2+2.5x family have also been identified. Furthermore, clarifying the detailed crystal struc- tures of TiNb38O97 and TiNb52O132 is extremely arduous on account of the fact that they are symbiotic phases of Nb2O5- TiNb24O62 at high temperatures.135 Consequently, TiNb38O97 and TiNb52O132 are not suitable to be used as anode material for Li-ion batteries. Ti2Nb2O9 with the pseudo-orthorhombic tunnel structure is also not considered a preferable anode material for Li-ion batteries owing to the relatively difficult preparation method as well as the fact that it is not a typical TiNbxO2+2.5x compound with monoclinic ReO3-type crystal structures.136 Accordingly, the Li-storage mechanism and electrochemical properties of TiNb2O7, Ti2Nb10O29, and TiNb24O62 are summarized in detail in this section. The Li-storage mechanism of TiNb2O7, Ti2Nb10O29, and TiNb24O62 represents the insertion and deinsertion of Li+ within the material for energy storage. For TiNb2O7, the mechanism of lithiation has been demonstrated by in situ XRD to be a complex three-stage inserting mechanism associated with the content of Li within LixTiNb2O7. The Li-storage process could be summarized as follows: (i) the external Li+ inserts into TiNb2O7, which gradually occupies 4i(1) and 4i(2) sites, and the Li+ at 4i(1) sites migrate to 4i(3) and 4i(4) sites to form Li0.88TiNb2O7 (the first solid solution); (ii) upon further lithiation, the large number of external Li+ continuously occupies 4i(3), 4i(4), and 4i(1) sites. Once the 4i(1) site is fully occupied again, Li+ at 4i(1) and 4i(2) sites are simultaneously migrating to the 4i(5) site, and Li+ at 4i(3) sites also transfers to the 8j site, Li0.88TiNb2O7 transformed into Li2.67TiNb2O7 during the discharging process (two phases coexistence); (iii) TiNb2O7 is completely lithiated to form Li4TiNb2O7 (final solid solution) (Figure 4d).100 Guo’s group investigated the structural changes of TiNb2O7 during Li- insertion/deinsertion processes using in situ XRD methods in Figure 7. 2014.137 In Figure 7a, the structural evolution could be categorized into two solid solution regions and one 2-phase coexistence region. The initial solid-solution reaction arises from the initial discharging stage to the S4 site, the second solid-solution reaction occurs in the last stage of discharging from S7 to S15, and the 2-phase coexistence region takes place in the S4 to S7 stage. The peaks are noticeably widened, and a minor voltage plateau at about 1.5 V is detected during Li- insertion process. Additionally, the changes in lattice parameters induced by the Li+ insertion appear to be extremely anisotropic. According to Figure 7b, the lattice parameter (b) and the cell volume (V) trade to increase linearly with the continuous insertion of Li+ during the discharging process, whereas the lattice parameters a and c present a trendless variation, the results are also substantiated by the XRD and neutron diffraction tests of LixTiNb2O7.138 The phenomena may manifest as a result of Li+ migrating via the tunnels of the material crystals. Crucially, the variation of lattice parameters and crystal cell volume during the repeated charging and discharging remain virtually reversible. The variation of crystal cell volume for TiNb2O7 is approximately 7.22−8.4%, and the relatively minor changes could be regarded as the primary reason for the long cycling life. The prepared nanoporous TiNb2O7 material delivers outstanding cycling performance thanks to the fact that the structure could significantly alleviate the volume expansion during repeated Li-insertion/deinsertion processes.137 The X-ray absorption near edge spectroscopy (XANES) and the numerical values of the edge energy positions (Figure 7c) demonstrate that the charge compensa- tion of Ti4+ and Nb5+ is considered to initiate simultaneously and equivalently as the insertion of more Li+ in LixTiNb2O7, the valence states of Nb and Ti present +3.6 and +3.2, respectively, at a discharge cutoff voltage of 1.0 V.139 Moreover, Griffith et al. analyzed the diffusion mechanisms of Li+ in TiNb2O7 based on experimental data and simulation calculations. In Figure 7d, the activation energy of 0.39 eV could be needed to jump between LiC and LiC along the b-axis in tunnel T1. Intriguingly, the minimum energy in tunnel T1 lies at the LiC site, yet the required activation energy for jumping betwixt LiC and LiC sites (conformation (ii) is not minimal. The energy discrepancy between the LiB and LiC sites (0.11 eV) is rather small, implying that the sites could be filled at room temperature. The energy of LiA sites presents 0.16 eV above that of LiB sites in tunneling T2 along the b-axis planar position. The activation energy from LiA to LiB (0.18 eV) is also lower, indicating that the b-axis conduction under the T2 channel could be readily achieved. The diffusion mechanism of ions in the ac-plane is illustrated in Figure 7e, the LiD, LiE, and LiF localize at the edges of the blocks in addition to the sites inside the tunnel (LiA-LiC). Apparently, the LiE and LiF sites exhibit the highest energies, the LiB and LiC sites inside the tunnel present the lowest energies. Nevertheless, the larger diffusion energy barrier (0.71−1.00 eV) in the ac-plane indicates that the diffusion along the b-axis is an optimal diffusion path. Albeit TiNb2O7 represents a prospective “fast-charging” anode material with a theoretical specific capacity of up to 387 mAh g−1, which is more than twice that of Li4T4O12. It tremendously elevated the energy density of the prepared Li- ion batteries.140 Additionally, the high working potential (>1 V) ensures inherent safety compared to graphite by avoiding the formation of Li dendrites and electrolyte reduction. Yet, the material exhibits insulator properties as a result of the highest oxidation state of Nb5+ ions and the absence of free electrons. Also, the inferior ion conductivity does not meet the requirements of fast-charging. In order to address the issues, the researchers polish up the ionic and electronic conductivity at the material level, including compounded or coated with the conductive substrates (carbon, carbon nanotubes, graphene), control of morphological, and doped TiNb2O7 with W6+, V5+, and La3+, etc.141−143 For instance, the introduction of oxygen vacancies and surface carbon coating at the atomic scale allows for superior ionic conductivity and electronic conductivity of titanium niobium oxide (TiNb2O7−x@C).84 The area specific capacity of TiNb2O7−x@C reaches 1.83 mAh cm−2. In a full battery, a specific capacity of 1.55 mAh cm−2 is available at a current density of 1.2 A g−1. Additionally, the C-coated porous TiNb2O7 synthesized on a large scale via a soft-template method is also a promising “fast-charging” anode material. In a full battery with LiNi0.6Mn0.2Co0.2O2 (NMC) as the cathode and TiNb2O7@C as the anode, a high energy density of 142.8 Wh kg−1 (357 Wh L−1) could be obtained, and the capacity retention of more than 80% could be maintained after 500 cycles in a 10 min fast-charging protocol (Figure 7f).83 The electronic conductivity of the material could be considerably enhanced by reducing TiNb2O7 at 900 °C in an atmosphere of H2.144 TiNb2O7 nanofibers with the 1D hollow structure are prepared using coelectrostatic spinning (Figure 7g),84 and the reversible capacity is maintained at 210.1 mAh g−1 after 150th at a current of 154.8 mA g−1, while the reversible capacity reaches 158.4 mAh g−1 after the 900th cycle at a current of 3.87 A g−1 with an excellent capacity retention of 80.6%.100 The Tb-doped TiNb2O7 is prepared by a one-step solid-phase reaction method, where Tb occupies the middle site of the Nb−O octahedron, and the doping of Tb could effectively ameliorate the transport process of the underlying ions accompanied by the reduced bandgap (from insulators to semiconductors) and the lowered ionic diffusion barriers, resulting in a considerable increase in the ionic and electronic conductivities of Tb-TiNb2O7.145 The reversible specific capacity reaches 192.8 mAh g−1 at a current density of 19.35 mA g−1, and the capacity retention is maintained at 98.9% after 1000 cycles. TiNb2O7 with a honeycomb structure is synthesized by employing polystyrene gel as a hard template, in which the structure facilitates the fast transfer of Li+ and electrons to realize favorable Li-storage performance.146 The excellent Li-storage performance could be maintained at 120 mAh g−1 at a current density of 19.35 A g−1, and the capacity retention reaches 82% after 1000 cycles at a current density of 3.87 A g−1, which evidence that TiNb2O7 manifests tremendous potential as a “fast-charging” anode material for Li-ion batteries. Ti2Nb10O29 with a layered structure presents a multitude of interstitial sites for the Li+ store. The interstitial compound could be created while Li+ accesses the interstitials from the electrolyte to materialize the Li-storage during the charging and discharging. The crystal structure of Ti2Nb10O29 parallels that of TiNb2O7, in which a few ordered cations are also noted in Ti2Nb10O29. The occupation of Ti amounts to 4.5% in the middle octahedral position compared to its occupation at the corner octahedral position (64.5%) using power neutron diffraction.147 The mechanism of lithiation for Ti2Nb10O29 has been demonstrated using in situ energy synchrotron XRD.148 In 2012, the two phases were distinctly identified in the biphasic region using in situ XRD tests of Ti2Nb10O29 by Chen’s team (Figure 8a).133 The Bragg peaks of Ti2Nb10O29 ACS Nano www.acsnano.org Review https://doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.3c08712 ACS Nano 2024, 18, 2611−2648 2621

undergo a noticeable shift during the initial charging and discharging, demonstrating the anisotropic of the lattice. Five monoclinic structures (M1-M5) are progressively uncovered, and four structure transitions occur consecutively as the degree of lithiation increases, intimating that the larger energetic barriers remain to be overcome (Figure 8b). The lattice parameter of Ti2Nb10O29 exhibits a nonmonotonic nature on account that the transition from M1 to M4 (3.0−1.5 V) is irreversible, which may be viewed as an activation process, namely the rearrangement of the crystal structure to allow the insertion of Li+. Concurrently, the increase of the lattice parameter (b) keeps being inhibited, while a/c grows slightly, illustrating that Li+ may diffuse along the b-axis.149 The effect of oxygen vacancies could be predicted by the first-principles calculations. The five oxygen vacancies could be established in the structure, among which the oxygen vacancies between Nb and Nb possess relatively lower energies, suggesting that oxygen atoms tend to be more susceptible to loss at the location. The electronic conductivity becomes significantly influenced by the oxygen vacancies as well, and the lack of oxygen may considerably improve the intrinsic electronic conductivity of Ti2Nb10O29 material. Furthermore, the Li+ diffusion paths as well as the required energy barriers of Ti2Nb10O29 and Ti2Nb10O29−x (O: Nb−Nb) could be investigated via the nudged elastic band (NEB) technique, Ti2Nb10O29−x (O: Nb−Nb) represents the Ti2Nb10O29 material with oxygen vacancies between Nb and Nb atoms.148 The energy barrier of Ti2Nb10O29 and Ti2Nb10O29−x (O: Nb−Nb) is depicted in Figure 8c, respectively. The initial position of Li+ lies at the oxygen vacancy site with the lowest energy barriers, and the ultimate position is located at the gap position at the lowest energy barrier. The high energy barrier (0.91 eV) for pure Ti2Nb10O29 compared with that of Ti2Nb10O29−x (O: Nb−Nb) (0.71 eV) is distinctly visualized, implying that Li+ tends to migrate more conveniently in Ti2Nb10O29−x (O: Nb−Nb) than in pure Ti2Nb10O29. According to the above-mentioned results, the materials with defects offer excellent electrical conductivity and ion transfer capability, and it is predicted to deliver significantly higher Li- ion storage performance. Although Ti2Nb10O29 enjoys the above advantages, the limited electronic conductivity restricts the “fast-charging” performance of the material. Accordingly, it is crucial to address the issue by controlling morphological, doping, and surface modification methods, etc.120,150−152 Ti2Nb10O29 hollow nanofibers (Figure 8d), with an average diameter of about 500 nm and a shell thickness of about 90 nm, are synthesized via a coelectrospinning method followed by high temperature calcination in the atmosphere air.153 The specific capacity could reach up to 278 mAh g−1 at a current density of 198 mA g−1, and the battery could still deliver a specific capacity of 136 mAh g−1 even at an extremely high current of 7.92 A g−1 (just about 3 min for complete discharging and charging). The Cr−Ti2Nb10O29@VGTC helical arrays consist- ing of Cr3+-doped Ti2Nb10O29 nanoparticles (Cr− Ti2Nb10O29) densely grown on vertical graphene@TiC-C (VGTC) are synthesized using a potent synergistic approach incorporating both ion doping and helical array structure to achieve the “fast-charging” performance of Ti2Nb10O29 (Figure 8e). The Cr3+ doping could open the crystal structure of Ti2Nb10O29 with fast ion transfer and superior structural stability.151 The excellent conductive network boosts the electronic conductivity of Cr−Ti2Nb10O29, therefore, the Li- storage capacity could reach a specific capacity of 308 mAh g−1 at an extremely high current of 15.84 A g−1. The work provides a solution for the preparation of fast Li-storage electrode materials. The porous Ti2Nb10O29 nanospheres are synthesized via a one-pot solvothermal technique with the assistance of F127 (the specific surface area of 19.43 m2 g−1 and the average pore size of about 10.5 nm),120 which exhibits a superior the reversible capacity of 172.1 mAh g−1 at a current of 39.6 A g−1, evidencing that Ti2Nb10O29 retains an enormous potential as a practical anode material for “fast-charging” Li-ion batteries (Figure 8f). The carbon nanofiber@ Ti2Nb10O29 arrays with binder-free are prepared on carbon cloth using a simple electrophoretic deposition-solvothermal technique.154 The entangled carbon nanofiber arrays serve as favorable bridges and powerful support structures, enabling the Ti2Nb10O29 to demonstrate high electrical conductivity and Li+ diffusion coefficient. The Li-storage mechanism of TiNb24O62 is based on the back-and-forth migration of Li+ between the cathode and the anode during the repeated charging and discharging, and the energy storage is subsequently accomplished by inserting Li+ into the vacancies of the TiNb24O62 lattice. The reaction mechanism could be expressed as:130 TiNb24O62 + xLi++xe− →LixTiNb24O62. The inserted Li+ refrains from occupying the 2c, 4f, and 8j sites when two Li are inserted in per TiNb24O62 because the Li−Li and Li−O repulsion becomes markedly increased, developing a conformation with substantially higher energies. The Li+ is expected to occupy the 4i site of the lattice during the discharge (Figure 9a). Yu et al. revealed that Li+ could diffuse along the a, b, and c axes through cubic-shaped cavities (Figure 9b). The energy of approximately 1.73 eV needs to be overcome as Li+ migrates along the a and c axis, demonstrating that the diffusion of Li+ becomes limited within each rectangle region. each rectangular region, Li+ probably gets trapped at the cavities of C3, C4, and C6 owing to the comparatively high- diffusion barrier (Figure 9c). Indeed, the diffusion of Li+ along the b-axis turns out to be extremely desirable because of suffering from a low diffusion barrier (0.110−0.385 eV), eventually occupying the 4i site of TiNb24O62 crystal lattice. Notwithstanding the fact that the optimal diffusion channel of Li+ is confined to a direction, TiNb24O62 still demonstrates exceptional diffusion kinetics (Figure 9d). Briefly, the Li- storage of TiNb24O62 is that Li+ diffuses along the b axis and gradually occupies the 4i site of the TiNb24O62 lattice to form Li11.4TiNb24O62 during the initial discharging. The material turns into Li28TiNb24O62 by complete lithiation as more Li+ inserts into the Li11.4TiNb24O62 crystal lattice. Once the battery undergoes charging, the Li28TiNb24O62 material is delithiated to form TiNb24O62, revealing that the TiNb24O62 electrode presents superior electrochemical reversibility during the charging and discharging. Even though TiNb24O62 demonstrates numerous advan- tages, the poor electronic conductivity restricts its practical application as a “fast-charging” anode material. Consequently, the issue could be tackled by controlling the morphology, surface modification, and doping, etc.123,130,134,155 The porous TiNb24O62 microspheres are fabricated by a facile solvothermal method to decrease the transfer distance of electrons/Li+ and increase the reaction area(Figure 9e).134 The 1D TiNb24O62 nanowires with oxygen vacancies are successfully prepared using a simple electrospinning and hydrogenation technique (Figure 9f).155 The nanoengineering narrows the Li+ diffusion path and increases the Li+ diffusion coefficient. A high charging capacity of 218 mAh g−1 at a current density of 200.5 mA g−1 is delivered, and the reversible specific capacity could reach 148.9 mAh g−1 even at a current density of 4.01 A g−1 after 900 cycles. Niobium−tungsten oxide (NbWO) has caught considerable attention as a “fast-charging” anode material in recent years due to its stable Li intercalation host structure. NbWO with crystalline shear structure offers desirable Li+ diffusion rates and electronic performance (Figure 6a).156 The idea Li+ diffusion coefficient is explained by the presence of 1D channels in the host crystal structure, indicating that the Li+ migration rate is significantly faster in NbWO than in TiO2.157 Furthermore, the tetragonal NbWO phases (Nb16W5O55,157 Nb14W3O44 158) and distorted tetragonal NbWO phases (Nb8W7O47,159 Nb18W16O93 157,160) exhibit excellent rate performance at 20 C after over hundreds of cycles. Thereby, NbWO is a promising material for a “fast-charging” anode as well. Meanwhile, it was recently noticed that W3Nb14O44 also exists in the Wadsley−Roth phase and the larger pentagonal tunneling, enabling it to act highly in terms of rate performance and Li-ion storage capacity.158 Hence, it has been also deemed a desirable “fast-charging” material by reason for the distinctive open crystal structure that furnishes abundant inserted Li sites. In addition, Nb18W16O93 powders with diverse crystal sizes are directly synthesized by the calcination method at different times, and the results manifest that the cycling performance and rate performance of Nb18W16O93 with the smaller crystal size are significantly enhanced. As a consequence, the crystal size is the essential parameter to diminish the lithiation kinetics of the Nb18W16O93 electrode.104 In conclusion, although all the above materials express “fast- charging” characteristics, the undesirable electronic conductiv- ity limits their wide application, therefore, further solving these issues is the key to realizing the “fast-charging” of Li-ion batteries. The Li-storage capacity of Niobium-based materials are summarized in Table 1. CARBON-BASED MATERIALS Carbon is one of the most abundant elements in nature and the basis of organic chemistry. Carbon with a variety of allotropes exhibits a significant difference in morphology, size, and local electron structure.183 The unique property has renewed the interest of researchers in “fast-charging” electrode materials. Carbon-based materials are widely used in the field of energy storage due to their superior chemical stability, intrinsic electrical conductivity, decent specific surface area, and unique porosity. Carbon-based materials mainly include ordered carbon and disordered carbon, such as graphite, graphene, fullerenes, carbon nanotubes, hard carbon, and soft carbon (Figure 10a and Figure 11a). Ordered Carbon. Graphite with a unique layered structure (layer spacing of 0.335 nm)184 is a transitional crystal between an atomic crystal, metal crystal, and molecular crystal, belonging to the hexagonal crystal system. In the graphite’s crystal, the carbon atoms in the same layer are hybridized with sp2 to form covalent bonds, each carbon atom is combined with the surrounding three carbon atoms, and the layers are combined through the weak van der Waals force. This means that the layers belong to the molecular crystal, and this spacing between them allows for reversible Li+ insertion and deinsertion.19 This lamellar structure consists of a series of six-membered rings made up of six carbon atoms. The spacing between the two carbon atoms is 0.142 nm. Meanwhile, each carbon atom has a p orbital, which overlaps with each other to form delocalized Π bonds. Graphite possesses conductivity ascribing to the free movement of electrons in the lattice. Graphite is one of the most common anode materials with a theoretical specific capacity of 372 mAh g−1, its ionic diffusivity parallel to the graphene plane and along the crystal boundary direction are ∼10−7−10−6 cm2 s−1 and ∼10−11 cm2 s−1, respectively.185 The typical Li-storage mechanism is that Li+ is adsorbed from the edge to inset graphite layers, forming LixC6 compounds for energy storage (Figure 10b).186,187 Specifically, the insertion of Li+ among the graphite layers proceeds from high order to low order. The graphite layer spacing gradually enlarges from 0.335 to 0.370 nm, and the capability of insertion gradually increases. During the discharging, Li+ is released from the graphite layers to restore the graphite crystal to its original state. The exposed carbon atoms at the edge end of the graphite sheet layer are in an amorphous state with high energy and are the active sites for Li+, which serves as the Li- storage. As the side ends, the carbon atoms on the graphite surface are bonded to Li+, which is the surface Li-storage. The above refers to the mechanism of Li-storage in graphite materials. The good layer structure of graphite materials facilitates the insertion and deinsertion of Li+ during the charging and discharging, thereby becoming the mainstream for the development and utilization of anode materials for Li- ion batteries. Nevertheless, as a “fast-charging” anode material, the sluggish dynamics of graphite could lead to over- potential,causing Li dendrites and battery explosion.47 At present, there are numerous schemes for accelerating the transfer of Li+ between graphite layers: 1) Designing a “fast- charging” electrolyte: low-voltage 1.8 M LiFSI in 1, 3- dioxolane,9 the electrolyte enables graphite electrodes to achieve 180 mAh g−1 at 18.6 A g−1, which is 10 times higher than conventional electrolytes (Figure 10c). 2) Opening holes on the surface to increase the insertion site, shorten the diffusion path, and ameliorate the transfer rate of Li+. For example, the simplest method is to corrode graphite with KOH to obtain graphite with nanoscale pores, which may be used as a “fast-charging” anode material.188 The results show that the capacity retention of the prepared multichannel graphite anode achieved 74% at the high current density of 2.23 A g−1, which excels significantly over pristine graphite (Figure 10d). Furthermore, multichannel graphite anodes are also obtained through a direct oxygenation process using natural graphite to increase the number and size of Li+ insertion and deinsertion sites.189 Compared to original graphite materials, the charging capacity of the multichannel graphite anode delivers high up to 83% and 73% of the total capacity at the current density of 2.23 and 3.72 A g−1, respectively (Figure 10e). The multichannel graphite anode has exceptional rate capability, cycling stability, and higher coulomb efficiency. 3) The expansion of graphite layer spacing and interface modification of graphite is a way as well to improve the “fast-charging” performance of Li-ion batteries. Kim et al. adopted a mild Hummers method to oxidize graphite, increasing the graphite spacing from 0.3359 to 0.3395 nm. And the established functional groups on the planes or edges of the graphite leave the conductivity at the conductor level without causing serious defects.190 The reversible specific capacity is up to 243 mAh g−1 compared with that of bare graphite (66 mAh g−1) at the high current density of 18.6 A g−1. Kim et al. fabricated a ACS Nano www.acsnano.org Review https://doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.3c08712 ACS Nano 2024, 18, 2611−2648 2627 
--- FILE: fast-charging-anode-materials-for-lithium-ion-batteries-from-perspective-of-ion-diffusion-in-crystal-structure.pdf | PAGE: 18 ---
composite anode by combining a strategy of implanting amorphous silicon nanolayers and activating graphite edge positions, and the structure effectively improves Li+ transport for achieving “fast-charging” characteristics (Figure 10f).191 The rate of charging could reach to 1.5 times faster than conventional graphite. Albeit the structural design and surface modification enable to advance the “fast-charging” capability and cycling stability of graphite, it remains arduous to significantly improve its rate performance to meet the fast- charging. Accordingly, the development of dissimilar alter- native materials becomes a current research hotspot. Graphene is one of the thinnest materials isolated from graphite. It has attracted extensive attention from experts in the field of energy storage thanks to the ideal electron conductivity (1 × 106 S cm−1), superior specific surface area (2630 m2 g−1)192 and rapid charge transfer rate (2 × 105 cm2 V−1 s−1). Nevertheless, graphene is the most active form of carbon attributed to the high reactivity of the transverse carbon atoms, and the strong van der Waals interactions between graphene nanosheets cause weak dispersibility.193 Consequently, it is usually used as an additive to ameliorate the conductivity of the material rather than as a direct application of the electrode material. Fullerenes represent hollow molecules composed of carbon, including six-membered rings, five-membered rings, and seven- membered rings. The most common fullerene is C60 with a molecular diameter of approximately 0.7 nm, which consists of 60 carbon atoms, including 20 six-membered rings and 12 five- membered rings.194−196 The material with precise structure, abundant unsaturated bonds, and good solubility may be well utilized in the field of energy storage. And superconductors may be formed between C60 and alkali metals. Fullerene, an allotrope of carbon, has a variety of unique properties that make it a potential anode material for Li-ion batteries.197 Nonetheless, the application of fullerene is limited in the field of energy storage on account of costly prices and inferior reversibility. Depending on the angle of wrapping, carbon nanotubes (CNTS) with a diameter of 1 to 2 nm might produce a metal or semiconductor.198 The electron conductivity and charge transfer rate of the material are 5000 S cm−1 and over 10 × 105 cm2 V−1 s−1, respectively. And it presents ideal thermal stability, satisfactory electron conductivity, superior theoretical specific surface area (SWNTs is 1315 m2 g−1), and desirable reversible capacity (350−680 mAh g−1). After chemical treatment, the capacity could reach 1000 mAh g−1. Therefore, the material exhibits the potential to be employed as the anode material for Li-ion batteries. However, the material is still not suitable to be used directly as the anode material owing to its larger specific surface area, which is prone to side reactions. Usually, the CNTS is employed as the anode material of Li-ion batteries by combining with other materials. Disordered Carbon. The aforementioned materials possess the distinctive traits of long-range order and high crystallinity. In addition, a class of disordered carbons with electrochemical activity could maintain a reversible specific capacity of approximately 500 mAh g−1,199 such as hard carbon and soft carbon. Hard carbon is obtained by sintering different organic precursors in an inert atmosphere (N2, Ar, or vacuum) at high temperatures. The properties of the precursor and synthetic parameters, such as heating rate, pyrolysis time, and protective gas, have a significant impact on the structure of hard carbon materials. Hard carbon features short-range ordered and long-range disordered properties,47 unlike ordered carbons such as graphite, graphene, and carbon nanotubes. Some defects and voids in the structure of parallel graphite are attributed to the fact that its planar domain is curved or turbo layered rather than planar. Li+ can be inserted into a disordered carbon layer or absorbed into the micropores of hard carbon during the lithiation (Figure 11a).200,201 Hard carbon is also known as “non-graphitized carbon” on account of the cross-linking of layers or the presence of C−O− C bonds, and it cannot be expanded or flattened to graphitize at 3000 °C. Figure 11b demonstrates the schematic illustrations and parameters of structures for hard carbon at 700 °C and 2000 °C. The Raman spectra of graphite, hard carbon, and soft carbon reveal that the complete disappearance of hard carbon in the 2D band at ≈2685 cm−1 arises from the decrease in the number of graphite crystals stacked. Furthermore, the intensity ratio of the D-band and G-band could serve to quantify the degree of disorder for hard carbon. The XRD pattern confirms that the structure becomes more disordered from graphite to soft and hard carbon, the (002) peak shifts to a lower degree, while d002 gets progressively enlarged. The wider the XRD peak, the smaller the average grain size.202,203 Hard carbon could be spherical, linear, or porous in shape. The different structures also endow different electrochemical properties. Hard carbons possess the following traits when used as anode material of Li-ion batteries: 1) It has a lower material density (1.6 g cm−3) than graphite (2.2 g cm−3). 2) The charging and discharging voltage distribution is slanted between 0 and 1.2 V. 3) The low initial Coulombic efficiency (ICE < 80%). 4) High-rate performance.47 5) The higher theoretical specific capacity (372 mAh g−1), Li insertion potential (0.2 V), and safety than graphite. 6) Stable structure, long cycle life.204 Besides, Li in hard carbon is easily trapped in microporous structures, resulting in low initial coulomb efficiency. And although hard carbon delivers a large attraction for high-power applications, the undesirable material density limits its application in high energy density batteries. Therefore, a trade-off between energy density and power density is a key step in solving fast-charging. For instance, the uniform ultramicropores hard carbon are obtained using an optimized pretreatment process as a “fast-charging” anode material.205 The HC-P6D7 electrode exhibits a well-retained rate of 82% at 3.72 A g−1 and excellent reversible capacity of 80% and 40% after 100 cycles at high rates of 0.74 A g−1 and 1.86 A g−1, respectively. (Figure 11c). Besides, hybrid anodes prepared by mixing graphite and hard carbon may achieve “fast-charging” Li-ion batteries with an energy density exceeding 180 Wh kg−1. The high energy density and power density are achieved simultaneously by adjusting the mixing ratio of graphite and hard carbon.47 The optimized hybrid anodes retain an initial specific energy of 87% and 82% after 500 cycles at 1.49 A g−1 and 2.23 A g−1, respectively, which is significantly higher than the 61% and 48% specific energy retention of graphite anodes under the same conditions (Figure 11d). Meanwhile, the different degrees of calendaring for graphite (Gr) and hard carbon (HC) could suppress the formation of Li dendrites, thus improving the “fast-charging” capability of the electrode. Soft carbon, bitumen, or asphalt derivatives, as a disordered carbon composed of several highly defective, curled, and twisted “graphene sheets”, which contain several nonsix- membered rings and impurity atoms to impel it more complex and disordered. Soft carbon, also known as graphitized carbon, ACS Nano www.acsnano.org Review https://doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.3c08712 ACS Nano 2024, 18, 2611−2648 2628

the crystallinity can be controlled by a heat treatment process and can be converted to graphite at above 2500 °C.206 For the mesophase nongraphitized carbon microspheres or micro- crystalline structures, it is beneficial to obtain higher Li-ion storage capacity, and the spherical structures can achieve tight filling to achieve higher volume ratio energy. Besides, soft carbon has the advantages of low cost, short-range, stable structure, long cycle life, high Li insertion potential (>0.2 V), and high safety compared to graphite. When soft carbon is used as the “fast-charging” anode material, improvements need to be made in the following aspects. 1) Strengthening the energy density and cycle performance of the anode material, reducing the irreversible capacity of the first cycle and the cost. 2) Ameliorating the compatibility and stability of carbon materials in organic electrolyte systems, such as heat treatment, surface modification, preparation of core−shell structure composite materials, and formation of nanopore structure in carbon materials. TITANIUM-BASED MATERIALS Titanium-based materials have been investigated for several years as “fast-charging” anode materials thanks to their excellent structural characteristics and Li-storage properties. Nevertheless, the unsatisfactory electron electrical conductivity limits the application of the material in “fast-charging” energy storage devices. Therefore, the search for a strategy to modify it is crucial to address the “fast-charging” of next-generation Li- ion batteries. Titanium-based materials mainly include TiO2 and Li4Ti5O12 (Figure 12). Li4Ti5O12. Li4Ti5O12 with a spinel structure was investigated extensively as a superconducting material by G.H. Jonker in 1956, it was not until the late 1980s that Li4Ti5O12 was again selected as the cathode material for Li-ion batteries for further study. Nevertheless, the low Li-insertion voltage (1.5 V) and inferior theoretical specific capacity (175 mAh g−1) of Li4Ti5O12 materials significantly restrict its development in the field of cathode materials in comparison to cathode materials like LiCoO2.214 In 1996, K. Zaghib initially proposed the research of Li4Ti5O12 as an anode material for Li-ion batteries. Eventually, the investigation of Li4Ti5O12 with spinel structure as an anode material for Li-ion batteries has been rapidly developed. Li4Ti5O12 possesses a virtually invariable skeleton structure and large crystalline channels during charging and discharging, and is known as a “zero-strain” material. The comparatively higher Li-insertion voltage compared to graphite could avoid the formation of Li dendrites.22 Li4Ti5O12 undergoes the following charge transfer reactions during the discharging: Li4Ti5O12+3Li++3e−→ Li7Ti5O5. Figure 12a represents the crystal structure of Li4Ti5O12 and Li7Ti5O12.215 Moreover, Li4Ti5O12 material belongs to an oxygen-containing anode, which provides a stronger binding capacity with Li+ and enables more rapid acceptance of Li+ compared to graphite. Consequently, Li dendrites are effectively averted during the fast-charging, while next-generation Li-ion batteries demonstrate extended life, “fast-charging”, and high safety. However, since Li4Ti5O12 materials is severely constrained by their poor electrical and ionic conductivity, improving its electrical conductivity is critical for realizing fast-charging. For instance, a synergistic combination composite of nitrogen-doped Li4Ti5O12 (N− Li4Ti5O12) nanoparticles and highly conductive vertical graphene (VG) backbone is gained by a facile hydrothermal nitriding method. The N−Li4Ti5O12/VG core layer array consists of interconnected N−Li4Ti5O12 shell layers and VG core layers express desirable specific surface area, satisfactory structural stability, and inherent conductivity. Compared with the undoped N−Li4Ti5O12/VG electrode, the synthesized N− Li4Ti5O12/VG electrode exhibits outstanding high-rate per- formance, reaching a high specific capacity of 142.5 mAh g−1 at 3.5 A g−1 and a capacity retention rate of 98.9% after 10 000 cycles at 0.88 A g−1 (Figure 12b).216 Besides, a mesoporous single crystal lithium titanate (MSC-Li4Ti5O12) microrod is prepared by a simple solution method. The microrods present a single crystal structure with interconnected pores inside the whole single crystal to shorten the Li+ diffusion distance and allow the electrolyte to penetrate inside the single crystal during battery cycling. As a result, MSC-Li4Ti5O12 exhibits excellent “fast-charging” performance and good long-term stability. More importantly, the porous single-crystal microbars greatly mitigate structural degradation during long-term cycling tests (Figure 12c).217 TiO2. Compared with Li4Ti5O12, TiO2 is regarded as one of the best choices of anode materials for high-power Li-ion batteries owing to its considerably higher theoretical specific capacity than that of Li4Ti5O12. Recently, various structures of TiO2, including anatase, rutile, bronze, and brookite have been extensively explored (Figure 12a).218 Anatase TiO2 belongs to the tetragonal crystal system, in which four TiO2 molecules form a cell, and each octahedron is connected to the surrounding eight octahedra (four coedges, four coapex angles), primarily used as a photocatalyst under UV irradiation. The high electron mobility, low dielectric constant, and low- density render anatase TiO2 attractive for solar battery applications, and the material represents potential applications as high-rate anodes in medium and large energy storage devices.219 Rutile TiO2 belongs to the tetragonal crystal system as well, where two TiO2 molecules form a crystal cell, the Ti atom is located in the center of the lattice, six oxygen atoms are located on the prongs of the octahedron, and each octahedron is connected to the surrounding 10 octahedra (of which there are eight cotop corners and two coedges). Rutile-phase TiO2 appears to be stable at most temperatures and pressures. As a catalyst, the rutile phase TiO2 is primarily utilized as a white pigment in coatings on account of the low activity. Bronze-type TiO2 ascribing to the monoclinic crystal system exhibits a unique open crystal structure. It is thought to facilitate pseudocapacitor charging because of its low-energy diffusion path from the surface to the ground.220 Plagioclase TiO2 refers to the rhombohedral crystal system consisting of six TiO2 molecules forming one crystal cell. The crystal structure of the platy titanite phase is relatively unstable, so it is rare to exist in nature. Among anatase, rutile, bronze, and brookite TiO2, anatase and bronze phase TiO2 are the most promising “fast- charging” anode materials for Li-ion batteries. For example, a mesoporous bronze TiO2(TiO2-B) microsphere is prepared by template-assisted ultrasonic spray pyrolysis, which consists of micron-sized particles with a diameter of about 1 μm, uniform mesopores of 12 nm, and nanoscale grains of about 6 nm. The mesoporous material features a fast pseudocapacitance response and sufficient electrode−electrolyte contact and exhibits a specific capacity of 165 mAh g−1 at 3.35 A g−1 and excellent multiplicative performance of 116 mAh g−1 at 20.1 A g−1 (Figure 12d).221 Besides, Fang et al. probed the thermodynamics of the structural evolution of C (graphite), Si (cubic), Sn (cubic), and TiO2 (anatase) et al. after lithiation and discover highly stable anode materials for “fast-charging” Li-ion batteries. Among them, all materials manifest noticeable volume expansion and undergo solid−solid phase transition when they exhibit high capacity. Nonetheless, TiO2 receives interest from authors on account of its minor volume expansion, favorable cycling performance, and fast kinetics (Figure 12e).222 Previous investigations223 have demonstrated that the highest theoretical capacity of about 335 mAh g−1 could be achieved for anatase TiO2, and relatively higher multiplicative performance is obtained for comparatively low capacity Lix (x ≤0.5)TiO2 (∼100 mAh g−1), which is attributed to the fact that Li+ diffusion enables the synthesis of some polycrystalline LixTiO2.224 Conclusively, a 3D tunneling ACS Nano www.acsnano.org Review https://doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.3c08712 ACS Nano 2024, 18, 2611−2648 2630 
--- FILE: fast-charging-anode-materials-for-lithium-ion-batteries-from-perspective-of-ion-diffusion-in-crystal-structure.pdf | PAGE: 21 ---
TiO2 (TiO2-S) phase is derived as a promising high- performance anode material. The TiO2-S phase possesses a spinel-like structure, attains only 5.5% volume expansion under a capacity of 335.5 mAh g−1 (Li + TiO2 →LiTiO2), and features a low Li diffusion barrier with fast-charging kinetics over a wide range of Li concentrations. Normally anode materials with stable structures demonstrate poor electro- chemical performance under fast-charging conditions, yet substable phases with 3D open structures may be the choice for the next generation of Li-ion battery anodes. This may be due to the delithium crystalline phases with open skeletons that remain stable enough to survive subsequent (discharging) charging cycles. Consequently, TiO2 with (spinel) tunneling crystal structure delivers comparatively outstanding Li-ion battery “fast-charging” performance. Although TiO2 and Li4Ti5O12 represent promising “fast- charging” anode materials, the inferior electronic conductivity limits their extensive application. Therefore, addressing the electronic conductivity of the materials is a current research hotspot in the field of energy storage. VANADIUM-BASED MATERIALS Vanadium-based materials have a prospective prospect for developing “fast-charging” Li-ion batteries due to the ideal capacity, unaffordable cost, abundant resources, unique crystal structure, and variable valence of vanadium ions. Next, the structure, “fast-charging” performance, and Li-ion storage mechanism of the representative Li3 V2O5 and Li3VO4 “fast- charging” anode materials are systematically summarized, looking forward to the most significant breakthrough points of the class of materials. Li3V2O5. Li3V2O5 is a disordered rock salt that was once considered as a Li-ion battery anode material, recently, the fast- charging feature was found among disordered rock salt materials, safely charging thousands of times within minutes.102 In the Li3V2O5 structure (Figure 13a), oxygen completely occupies the 4a site, while the 4b site of the octahedron is almost completely occupied by Li and V, occupying 52% and 40%, respectively. The remaining Li occupies the 8c site of the t e t r a h e d r a , e v e n t u a l l y f o r m i n g t h e [□9.6Li0.4]8c[□0.4Li2.6V2]4b[O5]4a framework structure, which possesses many tetrahedral vacancies to accommodate more Li+. The eccentricity of the four adjacent LiO6 octahedra is displaced when Li+ is inserted in DRS-Li3+xV2O5 at the 0-TM (T1) site. Li3V2O5 as a “fast-charging” anode material could reversibly cycle two Li+ ions at 0.6 V and possesses a specific capacity of 266 mAh g−1 at a current density of 0.1 A g−1. Compared with graphite (0.1 V), it exhibits a higher voltage and can effectively avoid Li dendrites during fast-charging. Compared to Li4Ti5O12 (1.5 V),30 it possesses a lower voltage, exceptional specific capacity, and ideal energy density for a full battery. The average operating voltage is between Li4Ti5O12 and graphite, which is ideal for applications in fast-charging and high-energy density batteries. More importantly, the capacity degradation is negligible after 1000 cycles using Li3V2O5 anode material. Also, it delivers excellent “fast- charging” performance, reaching 40% capacity in 20 s (Figure 13a). The “fast-charging” performance of the disordered rock salt Li3V2O5 is attributed to a redistributed Li intercalation mechanism by the following mechanism: at the start of discharge, Li migration in the Li3+xV2O5 (x ≈0) material occurs via a coordinated mechanism.102 Namely, Li migrates Figure 13. from a tetrahedral site to an adjacent face-shared LiO6 octahedral site. Simultaneously, Li migrates from the octahedral site to another face-shared tetrahedral site. The average potential barrier for the mechanism is about 247−330 meV. The average potential barrier for direct tetrahedral- tetrahedral migration is approximately 794 meV, which may be attributed to the fact that all octahedral positions in Li3V2O5 are occupied at the beginning of the discharge. The direct tetrahedral-tetrahedral migration features a transition state, and the migrating Li+ is very close to the Li+ at the octahedral positions, forming an electrostatic repulsion. The cooperative mechanism is favored as a result. At the end of the discharging, Li3+xV2O5 (x ≈2), most of the Li+ is located in the tetrahedral sites, and about half of the octahedral sites are vacant. Here, the average potential barrier from the direct tetrahedral to tetrahedral migration mechanism is about 241 meV, while the average potential barrier by the empty shared octahedral migration mechanism is about 932 meV. This may be assigned to the fact that only half of the octahedral positions are occupied at the end of the discharging. Therefore, the lower electrostatic repulsion in the transition state leads to a lower potential barrier. The “fast-charging” performance of Li3V2O5 is attributed to the fact that the disordered state could activate more Li+ migration paths that do not exist in the ordered state (Figure 13b).225 The process is as follows: in the ordered configuration, only one path is feasible, i.e., since vanadium atoms have the least spatial position resistance and the minimal coulomb repulsive force, a reverse path from tetrahedron to octahedron and then to tetrahedron is formed. the disordered configuration, the weak covalent bonding causes a sharp decrease in the activation energy, activating all migration paths, i.e., the direct tetrahedron to tetrahedron, tetrahedron to octahedron to the tetrahedron, and reverse tetrahedron to octahedron to tetrahedron paths could be spontaneously driven. Nevertheless, Li3V2O5 is almost an insulator with low electronic conductivity and poor electrical conductivity, which is prone to polarization during fast- charging. Besides, weak charging and discharging capacity restrict the range of the battery. Despite existing the aforementioned disadvantages, Li3V2O5 still has promising application possibilities as a high energy density and high- power density energy storage material taking into account the “fast-charging” and safety characteristics. It has been reported that Li3V2O5 anode materials could be synthesized from V2O5 by electrochemical in situ method.101 Specifically, during the initial lithiation, V2O5 is transformed into various LixV2O5 phases in the voltage range of 1.9−3.4 V. It is hypothesized that the amelioration of electronic and ionic conductivity of Li3V2O5 could be achieved indirectly by improving the electronic conductivity of V2O5. For example, the 3D hollow porous V2O5 microspheres assembled from nanoflakes were synthesized by a template-free hydrothermal method (Figure 13c),226 and the discharging specific capacity reached 527 mAh g−1 after 100 cycles at a rate of 0.1 A g−1 and up to 318 mAh g−1 at 3.0 A g−1. In addition, carbon-coated V2O5 nanocrystals were prepared by a thermal polymerization process using porous carbon as a hard template, and the discharging specific capacity achieved 255 mAh g−1 at a current density of 14 C (Figure 13d).227 V2O5 and V2O5/Au composites were synthesized by the one-step hydrothermal method and liquid-phase dispersion method. An Au-doped Li3V2O5 anode material with a disordered rock salt structure was synthesized by an electrochemical in situ method using the electrochemical activity of V2O5 in the low voltage region. The capacity decay is negligible after 4, 000 cycles by using Li3V2O5 anode material, and it also has an excellent rate performance, which can reach nearly 40% of capacity in 30 s. Li3VO4. Compared with commercial graphite and Li4Ti5O12 anode, Li3VO4 is a promising anode material due to the special crystal structure for “fast-charging” Li-ion batteries.228 The special configuration allows Li to be inserted in Li3VO4 crystals without disrupting the structure, the process is reversible. As can be seen from Figure 14a, Li3VO4 is a hollow lantern-like structure composed of VO4 and LiO4 with a common corner, which is similar to a hexahedral close-packed framework. Oxygen atoms occupy each vertex of the tetrahedron, forming ionic deintercalation structure.229 As the estimated energy density (both potential and capacity) of Li4Ti5O12 is no more than one-third of that of graphite, and the Li+ insertion potential of Li4Ti5O12 is up to 1.5 V, which exists at a lower energy density when forming a full battery with a typical 4 V cathode material (Figure 14b).230 In contrast, for Li3VO4, the Li+ insertion potential is between 0.5 and 1.0 V, which is lower than that of Li4Ti5O12. In addition, it exhibits a higher potential than graphite, avoiding the formation of Li dendrites. Therefore, the Li3VO4 with low voltage, safety, high specific capacity, and low cost is expected to be other insertion-type anode materials for Li-ion batteries. Nevertheless, Li3VO4 possesses a very undesirable inherent conductivity and rate capabilities. Therefore, mitigating the issue of inferior conductivity for these materials is essential for actualizing fast charging. For example, Li3VO4 was crushed into nanoscale by high-energy ball milling method to increase the active surface and shorten the Li+ diffusion distance, and then the nanolayer carbon was uniformly coated on the particle surface by chemical vapor deposition method to enhance the electronic conductivity (Figure 14c).231 Compared with untreated Li3VO4, the modified Li3VO4 shows 15 times increase in Coulomb efficiency from 68.8% to 79.5%, reversible capacity from 225 to 315 mAh g−1, and excellent rate performance due to the synergistic effect of nanocoating and carbon coating, demonstrating that particle size and electronic conductivity play an essential role in the electrochemical performance of Li3VO4. Besides, Li3VO4/N-doped C fibers (NN-LVO/NC-Fs) are synthesized using a size-constrained strategy of hybrid electrostatic spinning and diffusion- controlled solid-phase reaction (Figure 14d).232 The designed NN-LVO/NC-Fs exhibit the discharging capacities of up to 375 mAh g−1 after 1000 cycles at high currents of 10.0 A g−1, revealing the excellent rate performance Carbon-coated Li3VO4 spheres are synthesized using a morphogenetic method (Figure 14e).233 Compared with other inserted anode materials, the carbon-coated Li3VO4 spheres exhibit higher capacity, favorable sample stability, and excellent rate capability. Based on a Li3VO4 anode combined with LiNi0.5Mn1.5O4 cathode for a Li-ion full battery, the battery exhibits superior electrochemical performance than existing systems. Meanwhile, Huang et al. designed that Li3VO4 materials were embedded evenly onto MXene by a sol−gel method (Figure 14f).234 During fast-charging, the specific capacity of the Li3VO4/Ti3C2Tx MXenes composite is significantly higher than that of the prepared Li3VO4 Since the Ti3C2Tx MXenes with multilayered support framework served to provide a more abundant transmission path for rapid entry of Li+ and electrons, the modified electrode demon- strated an excellent specific capacity and “fast-charging” behavior. Unlike graphite anode materials, Li3VO4 has a relatively high voltage. In brief, these vanadium-based materials offer the potential for a safe and “fast-charging” Li-ion battery by the higher voltage platform than graphite. However, the issue of undesirable electronic conductivity is currently the most urgent one that needs to be resolved. OTHER MATERIALS Except for the aforesaid “fast-charging” anode materials, the conversion-typed transition metal oxide (MxOy) has garnered significant attention owing to the high theoretical specific capacity and excellent cycling stability. The lithiation mechanism can be expressed as235 MxOy+2yLi++2ye−↔xM +yLi2O (M = Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, and Mn), the redox reaction exhibits reversibility during the charging and discharging. Regrettably, MxOy typically undergoes significant volume variation during charging and discharging, contributing to severe capacity degradation. The poor conductivity also limits its “fast-charging” performance. Consequently, several adjust- ments are necessary for MxOy to be used as a “fast-charging” anode material for Li-ion batteries. The section illustrates the potential of several typical MxOy as “fast-charging” anode materials for Li-ion batteries, including Fe2O3, Fe3O4, CoO, Co3O4, WS2, VS2, SnS2, P, and so on. The iron oxides (Fe3O4 and Fe2O3) have received significant attention thanks to their low cost, nontoxicity, resource abundance, relatively high theoretical specific capacity (1000 mAh g−1), and the convenience of large-scale fabrication. Nevertheless, the volume expansion during charging and discharging causes inferior cycling stability, and the undesirable electrical conductivity results in an unsatisfactory fast-charging capacity. Numerous modification methods are carried out by researchers to enhance the “fast-charging” properties of the material. The synthesizing of nanoscale active materials serves as an effective method to abridge the diffusion path of ions inside the material, which could also lessen the stress induced by volume swell.236 For instance, carbon-coated Fe3O4 nanospheres featuring a hollow structure are successfully fabricated using a distinctive competitive coating technique, in which SiO2 nanospheres are utilized as a sacrificial template as well as ferrocene acts as a source of iron and carbon (Figure 15a). The specific capacity could reach up to 1200 mAh g−1 at a current density of 0.2 A g−1, and the battery still could deliver a specific capacity of 850 mAh g−1 even at an extremely high current of 10 A g−1, and a high specific capacity of roughly 500 mAh g−1 is maintained after 10 000 cycles at an ultrafast rate of 20 A g−1, which benefits from that the special hollow structure dampens the volume expansion and the carbon enhances the electrical conductivity of the material. The surface coating of conductive material could separate the active material from the electrolyte, minimizing the occurrence of side reactions. Moreover, the surface coating could also ameliorate the electrical conductivity and mitigate the volume expansion during the lithiation, effectively boosting the Li-storage capability of the material. The 3D N-doped carbon nanosheets encapsulated Fe2O3 nanoparticles with hollow structures are successfully prepared by chemical blowing and moderate oxidation in air methods (Figure 15b).237 The material Figure 15.
