           Characterization of Li-ion Battery Aging through HPPC  Experimental Tests and Equivalent Circuit Model  TESI MAGISTRALE IN ENERGY ENGINEERING  Mulè Cascio, Antonino, 101663  Advisor:  Prof. Claudio Rabissi  Co-advisors:  Ing.Martino    Fortunati  Academic year:  2023-24    Abstract: The study of aging in lithium-ion batteries by non-invasive  testing methods is a key area of research in automotive applications. In  particular, effective monitoring of battery aging and preventive  maintenance scheduling are essential to extend battery life and improve  its performance. This work presents an experimental methodology  applied to two important battery chemistries and geometries: Nickel  Manganese Cobalt (NMC) in prismatic cell and Lithium Iron Phosphate  (LFP) in cylindrical cell, in different aging conditions: calendar (for the first  sample) and aged in automotive applications (for the second sample). The  approach, following a detailed preliminary analysis of the electrochemical  characteristics of the tested samples, is based on an industrial and non- invasive test called Hybrid Pulse Power Characterization (HPPC), which  allows, through the imposition of controlled current pulses, to evaluate  the voltage response of the cell and therefore to extrapolate parameters  that reflect its operation in different conditions. Afterwards an equivalent  circuit model using the estimated parameters has been developed on the  commercial software Simulink.  Finally, an analysis of the results found and in particular their correlation  with the different aging phenomena has been carried out. The results  contribute to a deeper understanding of the aging dynamics and support  the development of optimized battery management strategies.    Key-words: lithium-ion batteries, HPPC, EIS, aging, degradation, experimental testing, Simulink  Model  1.   Introduction  The European Union (EU) is actively working to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions through  the implementation of both EU and national policies. These efforts have led to improvements in  energy efficiency and an increased reliance on renewable energy sources. GHG emissions have in  fact declined in recent years ,having reached levels 24 % below those recorded in 1990 [1].However  to reach the predetermined 2030 target of reducing greenhouse gas emission of at least 55% by 2030  [2] significant progress is still required. Two important sectors to focus on for GHG reduction are

  Antonino Mulè Cascio    3  1.State of Art  Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have become one of the primary energy sources for electronic devices,  including electric vehicles, due to their high energy density and long cycle life. [5] These are  electrochemical devices that operate based on redox (oxidation-reduction) reactions occurring  between lithium atoms and the active materials within the cells. These reactions enable the storage  of chemical energy, which can subsequently be converted into electrical energy. The fundamental  components of LIBs include two electrodes, the anode and the cathode, made from different  materials. [6] Their interaction is facilitated by an electrolyte, usually in a liquid state, and a separator  that permits the passage of lithium ions but blocks electrons, that, instead, flow through two current  collectors, which are typically connected to an external load linked to the battery [7].  1.1 Components and operating principle of lithium-ion battery  A lithium-ion battery consists of many components, as shown in Figure 1, these components can be  distinguished as: [8]        Figure 1: Schematization of lithium-ion cell [9]  •  Electrodes: These are porous layers that facilitate the storage of lithium, they are  characterized by an electric potential which is an indication of the lithium content inside. The  electrode characterized by a greater electrical potential is the positive electrode, commonly  referred to as the cathode, while the other is the negative electrode, known as the anode.  Redox reactions occur at the electrodes during the battery's operation. The anode is typically  made of graphite. Due to its structural stability as well as minimal electrochemical reactivity  with lithium ions, it conducts electrons and allows lithium ions to flow within its structure.  The cathode's active material instead varies based on cost and desired properties [10], [5].  •  Electrolyte: It is a solution containing dissociated salts which allows and facilitate the passage  of ions between the electrodes, which are immersed in it. It is an essential part of the battery  since it provides ionic conductivity and enables 𝐿𝑖+ ion to move between the electrodes while  not being electronically conductive. It can be in liquid or solid form [10].  •  Separator: The separator is a porous solid insulator membrane that allows the passage of  lithium-ions while preventing the flow of electrons that must instead pass through the  current collector. It separates the electrodes and acts as a safety device to prevent short circuit  [10].  •  Current Collectors: They are electrically conductive plates that enable the passage of  electrons, typically made of aluminum and copper, they connect the external terminals of the  
--- FILE: 2024_12_MulèCascio.pdf | PAGE: 4 ---
  Antonino Mulè Cascio    4  electrodes to the outside circuit, allowing the flow of electrons between the individual  components [7].Once the electrodes are connected externally the chemical reaction take place  [8].  The operation of a Li-ion battery (LIB) can be summarized in two main oxidation-reduction  reactions, which occur at the electrodes during charging and discharging process:  Negative Electrode     𝐿𝑖𝑥𝐶6 ↔𝑥𝐿𝑖+ + 𝐶6 + 𝑥𝑒−  Positive Electrode   𝑥𝐿𝑖+ + 𝐿𝑖1−𝑥𝑀𝑂+ 𝑥𝑒−↔𝐿𝑖𝑀𝑂  The main cell reactions occurring within the battery are reversible Li-ion intercalation and de-  intercalation cycles between two layered compounds with the source of lithium in these batteries  being the cathode material. The charging process is always the first step in the operation of the cell.  During this process graphite intercalates reversibly with lithium to form 𝐿𝑖𝐶6 as the final product ,  with the intercalation of lithium into graphite occurring in stages [11].During the discharge reaction,   Li-ions flow from the anode and intercalate into the spaces between the layers of cathode crystals.  Instead during charging the li-ion migrate from the positive side of the battery’s cathodes and insert  into the anode during charging. These reactions are reversible, which allows for the charging and  discharging of the battery. For the two reactions to take place we must have a potential difference  between the electrodes both characterized by an open circuit potential (OCP).  1.2 Nickel Manganese Cobalt (NMC) battery  The primary lithium-ion battery technologies are Nickel Manganese Cobalt (NMC) and Lithium Ion  Phosphate (LFP). In particular, NMC batteries currently hold a significant share of the market, and  this share is expected to grow in response to the rising demand for electric vehicles. [12]. NMC  cathodes combine nickel, manganese, and cobalt in a way that leverages each element’s strengths:  nickel contributes high specific energy, though it lacks stability, while manganese provides a stable  spinel structure that reduces internal resistance. Cobalt balances the structure, enhancing overall  stability and performance in high-energy applications. [10].  The main reactions happening in the cell are:   Negative Electrode   𝐿𝑖𝑥𝐶6 ↔𝐿𝑖𝑥−𝑧𝐶6 + 𝑧𝐿𝑖+ + 𝑧𝑒−  Positive Electrode    𝐿𝑖𝑥−𝑦𝑁𝑖𝑎𝑀𝑛𝑏𝐶𝑜𝑐𝑂2 + 𝑧𝐿𝑖+ + 𝑧𝑒−↔𝐿𝑖𝑦𝑁𝑖𝑎𝑀𝑛𝑏𝐶𝑜𝑐𝑂2  The high energy density and operating voltage make this technology interesting for automotive  applications. However, a significant ethical concern arises from the reliance on cobalt, which is  primarily mined in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, accounting for approximately 60% of the  global market share. Notably, about 20% of this cobalt is sourced from the artisanal mining sector,  where child labor and exploitation of vulnerable communities are prevalent, often leading to unsafe  working conditions and resulting casualties [10]. For this reason, at a technological level, there is a  strong push to reduce the use of cobalt and replace it with alternative new materials.  1.3   Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) battery  Lithium Iron Phosphate (𝐿𝑖𝐹𝑒𝑃𝑂4) technology has been a cornerstone in the lithium battery industry,  despite generally having lower energy density, LFP is preferred as a cathode material due to its  excellent chemical stability, safety, and cost-effectiveness [13].  The two main reactions happening on the cell are:  Negative electrode:               𝐿𝑖𝑥𝐶6 ↔𝐿𝑖𝑥−𝑧𝐶6 + 𝑧𝐿𝑖+ + 𝑧𝑒−  Positive electrode:             𝐿𝑖𝑥−𝑦𝐹𝑒𝑃𝑂4 + 𝑧𝐿𝑖+ + 𝑧𝑒−↔𝐿𝑖𝑦𝐹𝑒𝑃𝑂4  During discharge lithium ions (𝐿𝑖+) and electrons (𝑒−) are released from the graphite (𝐿𝑖𝐶6)  electrode. 𝐿𝑖+ ions flow through the electrolyte and separator while 𝑒− move towards the positive  electrode through the external circuit. Conversely, during charge instead, lithium iron phosphate is

  Antonino Mulè Cascio    5  then reconverted to iron phosphate (𝐹𝑒𝑃𝑂4). Due to its properties, LFP remains one of the most  widely used commercial cathode chemistries.  However, its performance is constrained by low  electronic  conductivity  and  slow  kinetics  of  lithium  ion  diffusion  across  the  LiFePO4/FePO4  interface, leading to substantial capacity loss at high current rates [14].  1.4 Degradation mechanism in Lithium-ion batteries  In lithium-ion batteries, the identification and differentiation of degradation mechanisms impacting  cell performance is challenging due to the simultaneous occurrence of multiple interdependent  physical and chemical processes. In literature, these mechanisms are commonly divided into two  main categories: cycle aging and calendar aging. Cycle aging includes all degradation processes  affected by the battery's operational conditions, such as voltage, current, depth of discharge, and  cycle rate. These conditions induce stress on the battery materials, accelerating wear during repeated  charge and discharge cycles. Calendar aging, on the other hand, refers to degradation linked  primarily to the cell’s state of charge (SOC) and storage temperature, independent of active cycling.  This form of aging is often dominant in situations where the battery spends extended periods at a  high SOC or elevated temperature, both of which contribute to electrolyte decomposition and  structural fatigue over time. However, other classification schemes also exist, reflecting the multi- faceted and complex nature of battery degradation.  As shown in Figure 2, battery degradation affects nearly all internal components—electrodes,  electrolyte, separator, and current collectors—and varies with operating voltage, temperature, and  current. Due to the complex interplay of these variables, accurately modeling degradation is a  considerable scientific challenge. Many physics-based models aim to focus on the most impactful  mechanisms.       Figure 2: Degradation mechanism in LIB [15]   In this framework, degradation mechanisms are often classified into three primary groups:  1.  Loss of Lithium Inventory (LLI): LLI is caused by the reduction of cyclable lithium within  the cell. This can occur due to lithium becoming trapped in non-reversible reactions or bound within  passive layers on electrodes, such as the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) and cathode electrolyte  interphase (CEI) layers. Capacity fade is a typical result of LLI, as the quantity of lithium ions able  to transfer between electrodes gradually decreases. Additionally, electrolyte decomposition and  lithium plating can contribute to LLI, particularly at high SOCs and during rapid charge rates. The  formation of lithium dendrites, metallic structures that can grow on the anode, may also pierce the  separator and cause short circuits with the cathode, leading to potentially hazardous failures.  
--- FILE: 2024_12_MulèCascio.pdf | PAGE: 6 ---
  Antonino Mulè Cascio    6  Lithium plating is especially problematic in cold temperatures or high current situations, where it  can form even at moderate SOCs, accelerating LLI and increasing safety risks [15].  2.  Loss of Active Material (LAM): LAM arises from the gradual depletion of reactive sites  within the battery’s electrodes. Common mechanisms leading to LAM include particle cracking,  binder degradation, graphite exfoliation, and the dissolution of transition metals from the cathode.  Electrode particle cracking, often due to mechanical stress from cycling and lithium-ion  insertion/extraction, increases internal resistance and reduces the reactive surface area. In the  cathode, transition metal dissolution (often from manganese or cobalt) results in the migration of  these metals to the anode, where they deposit on the SEI, further increasing resistance and  contributing to LLI. Over time, structural disordering, binder breakdown, and current collector  corrosion exacerbate the loss of active material, reducing the battery’s ability to sustain high currents  and limiting its lifespan[15].  3.  Resistance Increase (RI): RI is closely related to the formation of resistive layers, primarily on  the anode, that impede ion movement and increase internal resistance. The SEI, a passivation layer  formed on the anode from electrolyte decomposition during initial charging, plays a significant role  in this process. The SEI is crucial to the battery’s operation, as it prevents continuous electrolyte  decomposition and mitigates further side reactions. However, under high temperatures, voltages,  or currents, SEI can degrade, triggering the formation of additional SEI layers that further increase  internal resistance and reduce cyclable lithium. A similar layer, the CEI, can form on the cathode,  adding to the overall impedance within the cell. The cumulative effect of these resistive layers is an  overall reduction in battery efficiency, slowing charge/discharge rates and diminishing power  output over time.  Specifically capacity loss occurs when active material is transformed into inactive phases due to  parasitic chemical reactions. In contrast, power loss occurs when battery materials convert into  compounds that act as transport barriers, increasing internal impedance and reducing operating  voltage at various discharge rates [10].    1.4.1  Calendar Aging   Calendar aging encompasses all aging processes that lead to battery cell degradation independent  of charge-discharge cycling. In general batteries will experience extended periods of inactivity, the  calendar aging, will happen through internal degradation due to the chemical reactions happening  without an applied current. This factor is critical in many lithium-ion battery applications, especially  where active operation periods are significantly shorter than idle intervals, as in electric vehicles. In  contrast to cycle aging, where mechanical strain on the electrode active materials or lithium plating  can cause severe degradation, the primary mechanism of calendar aging is the formation of  passivation layers at the electrode-electrolyte interfaces.  The formation, growth, or reconstruction of these layers consumes cyclable lithium, resulting from  electrolyte decomposition reactions: reduction at the anode and oxidation at the cathode interface.  Moreover, the growth of the passivation layer at the anode, typically known as the Solid Electrolyte  Interphase (SEI), is further catalyzed by dissolved transition-metal ions from the cathode, which are  subsequently reduced back to metals at the anode.  Numerous studies on calendar aging identify the primary factors as high storage state of charge  (SOC) and elevated temperatures, which accelerate degradation in lithium-ion cells with graphite  anodes and layered transition-metal oxide cathodes. Specifically, temperature significantly affects  calendar life through overall parasitic reactions, leading to loss of active material (LAM), loss of  lithium inventory (LLI), and conductivity reduction due to electrolyte consumption, all of which  
--- FILE: 2024_12_MulèCascio.pdf | PAGE: 7 ---
  Antonino Mulè Cascio    7  increase as temperature rises. These losses further highlight the importance of understanding  storage conditions for lithium-ion batteries [16].  Nevertheless, the performance loss due to the calendar life and associated aging mechanism remains  poorly investigated since calendar life tests require extended time and are resource- intense  obligations. Cost and active reservation of equipment for years can limit the number of researchers  able to undertake these studies. However, the impact of calendar aging cannot be underestimated  as it is critical for the eventual deployment of advanced battery chemistries and design. Because  calendar and cycling aging are not additives, battery degradation under different aging conditions  needs to be carefully investigated.   1.5 Aim of the thesis   This thesis work was carried out at the MRT Fuel Cell & Battery Laboratory and at the EN:LAB  within the Department of Energy Engineering of the Politecnico di Milano. This work focused on  the study and implementation of a methodology widely used in the industrial field, the HPPC  (Hybrid Pulse Power Characterization), with the aim, through both an experimental campaign and  a modeling activity, to use it in an innovative way, as a diagnostic tool for aged batteries. In  particular, a characterization of different cell geometries, cylindrical and prismatic, was performed  in different conditions (temperature), and with different aging states: the cylindrical ones aged in a  real automotive application and the prismatic ones aged in the laboratory through calendar.   Subsequently, an experimental campaign was carried out (through HPPC profiles) dedicated to the  calculation of the parameters for the calibration of the model carried out on Simulink (MATLAB).  Finally, the methodology was validated, and the results analyzed to confirm and assess the aging  conditions of the batteries.

The smaller one, a climatic chamber, is primarily used for calendar aging (Binder KT 53) while the  larger climatic chamber, (Binder MKF 720, accuracy of ±1 [K]) is mainly used for tests. The majority  of tests were conducted on the latter, which was used to conduct charge and discharge test, EIS and  HPPC tests. The testing station is composed of two parallel circuits, each associated with four  independent channels and equipped with five Chroma 6340-80-80 electron loads for a total of ten  electronic loads [17]. The Power supply is provided with a NIRMX-4124 which can impose a current  of approximately 100 [A] with an accuracy for the current [ ± 0.5 % +0.1% F.S ] (full scale) and of  [0.025 % +0.01 % F.S] for the voltage. Temperature and voltage data are acquired using three  acquisition boards connected to the cells: two NI CDAQ 9211 w/K-TC boards for temperature  measurement [uncertainty of ± 3 [K] ] while one NIDAQ USB 6218 board for voltage[uncertainty of  2.69[µV] [18].To further increase the security of the system the testing station has been coupled to  an Arduino Uno microcontroller board to assess operating conditions, with the function of aborting  test if the conditions of the test were out of a range of parameters. The station is being administered  by a code developed in NI LabView ® software.  2.3  Diagnostic methods   The main tests conducted on these stations included charge and discharge at different C-rates,  electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and Hybrid Pulse Power Characterization (HPPC).  2.3.1   Charge and Discharge   Charging tests are conducted at various C-rates, as shown in Figure 4 the protocol begins primarily  in constant current (CC) mode until the cell reaches maximum voltage, after which the process  transitions to constant voltage (CV) mode, with current gradually reduced to a cutoff of 0.18 [A]  based on nominal capacity. During the charge and discharge processes, cell capacity and voltage are  recorded, with temperature and C-rate being the main parameters affecting variations in these  values. Temperature influences sample performance as it rises, impacting ion mobility and diffusion  within the solid-state structure. C-rate, defined as the ratio between the applied current and the  
--- FILE: 2024_12_MulèCascio.pdf | PAGE: 10 ---
  Antonino Mulè Cascio    10  nominal battery capacity at Beginning of Life (BOL) conditions, further influences these  characteristics, leading to fluctuations in charge and discharge curves and, consequently, battery  capacity. It is also possible through discharge tests to obtain a quasi-static curve, known as the Open  Circuit Voltage (OCV) that informs about the potential difference across the entire battery in  equilibrium conditions, to acquire it discharges tests are conducted at 0.04 C and 25°C.      Figure 4: CC-CV charging profile [19]  The NMC cell analyzed has been discharged at varying C-rates—specifically, 0.04 C, 1 C, 2 C, 3 C, 5  C, and 10 C—and at different temperatures: 0°C, 10°C, 25°C and 45°C. In contrast, charging tests  were conducted under nominal conditions.  2.3.2  Incremental capacity (IC) and differential voltage (DV)  Through the discharge process it is possible to derive the Incremental Capacity (IC) and differential  voltage (DC) that are, respectively, the derivative of exchanged charge divided by the voltage  (dQ/dV) and the derivative of voltage with respect to the exchanged capacity (dV/dQ). IC and DV  are typically used for studying lithium-ion battery aging mechanisms. An IC analysis involves  plotting dQ/dV revealing supposed changes in the battery capacity. On the other hand, a DV  analysis plots the dV/dQ providing a supposed insight into the internal changes in batteries over  their lifetime. As battery undergoes charge and discharge cycles specific voltage plateaus occur due  to the intercalation and de intercalation of lithium ions in the electrode material. Using an IC-DV  helps transform actual voltage data obtained from charging and discharging batteries in peaks and  valleys on IC and DV curves. By analyzing these peaks and valleys it is possible to gain access to  non-invasive yet comprehensive insight into the battery health and age . Studies indicate that peak  height in incremental capacity (IC) curves correlates with battery aging and capacity loss, with shifts  in peak positions indicating changes in electrochemical reactions and increased internal resistance.  A reduction in peak height and area reflects active material loss and decreased capacity, while total  IC area correlates with available capacity, diminishing as the battery degrades. IC analysis allows  estimation of State of Health (SOH) by comparing peak features to initial values and helps  distinguish between degradation types like loss of lithium inventory (LLI) and loss of active material  (LAM) [20].  2.3.3   Electrochemical Impedance spectroscopy (EIS)  Electrochemical Impedance spectroscopy (EIS) is a characterization technique widely adopted in  electrochemistry primarily used to study battery degradation. It is a non-invasive and non- destructive technique, that can be applied at various stages of a battery's life cycle as a diagnostic or  prognostic tool. It is a powerful technique for investigating electrochemical systems, with its main  
--- FILE: 2024_12_MulèCascio.pdf | PAGE: 11 ---
  Antonino Mulè Cascio    11  strength being the ability to deconvolute complex electrochemical processes into basic processes  based on different relaxation times. To perform EIS the battery has to be stationary; by applying a  current at different amplitudes, the voltage response of the system to the perturbation can be  measured, allowing for the calculation of the system’s impedance via the corresponding transfer  function [21].The measurement involves applying a sinusoidal current (I) over a specified frequency  range (f) in steady state conditions followed by the acquisition of the voltage output(V). The cell  impedance can be then computed as the ratio between the voltage and the current, then it is  processed through the Fast Fourier Transform to obtain complex values. This procedure is repeated  across a range of frequencies to gather as much information as possible and generate a detailed  impedance spectrum. Battery impedance is a critical characteristic that directly affects its operating  voltage, rate capability, and efficiency. It is also closely related to cell aging due to degradation of  electrode materials, electrolytes, and electrical contacts within the cell [22]. The test, repeated across  a frequency range typically from kHz to mHz, enables the examination of processes within the  battery that operate at different time constants. Features on the resulting Nyquist plot (where the  imaginary part of the impedance is plotted against the real part) and / or the Bode plot (where either  magnitude and phase or real and imaginary parts are plotted as a function of frequency) allow for  the parameterization of resistance, capacitance, and inductance of various cell components and  processes. As shown in Figure 5 at very high frequencies (f > 2 kHz) the inductive behavior observed  in the upper-frequency range of the spectrum may be an artifact of the measurement system (e.g.  connecting the cell to the measuring device). For lower frequencies (2 kHz < f < 1 kHz), the ohmic  effect, known as High-Frequency Resistance (HFR), can be isolated, providing an estimation of  purely resistive effects within the cell that exclude slower phenomena. The high frequency intercept  with the real axis where inductive effects are properly subtracted, corresponds to the sum of ohmic  resistances, including those of the electrolyte, active material, and current collectors. The arcs in the  mid-frequency range are mainly due to electrochemical processes occurring at the  electrode/electrolyte interfaces, combining resistive and capacitive effects. Typically, a cell’s  impedance spectrum and the contribution of different processes vary with temperature, State of  Charge (SOC), and SOH. EIS can also be used to determine parameters for equivalent circuit models  developed to describe and predict the behavior of LIBs [22].    Figure 5: example of Nyquist plot  
--- FILE: 2024_12_MulèCascio.pdf | PAGE: 12 ---
  Antonino Mulè Cascio    12  2.4 Hybrid Pulse Power Characterization (HPPC)   The Hybrid Pulse Power Characterization (HPPC) test is a well-established method used to evaluate  the dynamic performance of lithium-ion batteries across a range of charge levels. Typically  conducted once, by applying a series of charge and discharge pulses at different states of charge  (SoC), the HPPC test helps determine the cell’s power and energy capabilities, along with key  parameters such as internal resistance and efficiency. These parameters are essential for accurately  modeling battery performance and ensuring reliable operation in real-world applications.  2.4.1  HPPC Procedure  The HPPC procedure begins with laboratory testing, then through the analysis of the tests it is  possible to identify the model parameters by approximating the HPPC voltage response with single-  or multi-exponential functions, followed by creating and validating a simulation model[23].  The  HPPC model simulates the rapid power demands that batteries frequently experience in  applications like electric vehicles and grid storage systems. By analyzing a battery’s voltage response  to these pulses, we can gain insights into its internal resistance, assess power delivery capability,  and estimate efficiency under various load conditions. This information is fundamental for  designing Battery Management Systems (BMS) and predicting battery behavior over time.  To interpret HPPC test results, an equivalent circuit model (ECM) is typically built to represent the  battery’s behavior. This model often comprises two RC pairs to simulate the time constants of the  dynamic model. In this type of circuit it’s also present an ideal voltage source 𝑈𝑜𝑐 , an internal  resistance 𝑅0 and the two RC networks 𝑅𝑗,𝐶𝑗,𝑗= 1,2 [24]. The open-circuit voltage (OCV) source  represents the battery’s internal potential at a given SoC, as well as resistive and capacitive elements  that capture the internal resistance and transient characteristics of the cell.  In the ECM, the OCV is dependent on the battery’s SoC and provides a baseline voltage level.  Internal resistances (often represented by series resistance components) simulate the immediate  voltage drops when high currents are applied or withdrawn. Capacitive elements in the model  capture the transient behavior as the battery voltage stabilizes after current pulses, accounting for  the polarization effects seen in real battery responses. By tuning these components to match the  voltage response data from HPPC tests, the ECM can accurately replicate the dynamic performance  of the battery.  ECMs typically incorporate one to five RC pairs, each associated with a distinct time constant,  among ECMs, the second-order RC model is widely utilized for its simplicity and accuracy. As the  number of RC networks grows, the accuracy of the ECM model correspondingly increases.   2.4.2  Pulse Duration and Relaxation Time  The HPPC test, as previously described, involves applying a current pulse followed by a relaxation  period. To accurately determine time constants, the pulse duration should be several times longer  than the anticipated time constant, as extended transients improve measurement precision.  However, to minimize changes in the battery's state of charge (SoC), HPPC pulses should ideally be  as short as possible [23].  HPPC profiles may include varying numbers of pulses but always consist of an even number, as  pulses occur in pairs (one charge pulse followed by one discharge pulse) to minimize SoC variation  in the cell. The number of pulse pairs can vary: some protocols use only one pair, while others use  multiple pairs, each with potentially different current values. Higher current levels produce stronger  voltage responses, which improves data quality but also increases SoC fluctuation during each  pulse.   The sequence of pulses is also critical. At high SoC values, a discharge pulse should precede a charge  pulse; if a charge pulse is applied first, it may raise the cell voltage to a point that forces the  
--- FILE: 2024_12_MulèCascio.pdf | PAGE: 13 ---
  Antonino Mulè Cascio    13  measurement system to switch from constant current (CC) to constant voltage (CV) mode,  potentially cutting the pulse short. Conversely, at low SoC values, a charge pulse should be applied  first to avoid similar measurement disruptions.  Finally, the relaxation period between pulses should ideally be significantly longer than the cell’s  expected time constants. This interval allows the cell voltage to fully stabilize, reaching both  electrochemical and thermal equilibrium before the next pulse is applied. Ensuring complete  stabilization is essential for accurate subsequent pulse execution and consistency in measurement  results [23].  2.4.3  Impulse Evaluation  After executing the pulses, they must be carefully selected for time constant identification. However,  not all recorded impulses are suitable for analysis, as some may exhibit defects due to the  measurement method (such as the CC/CV mechanism) or the physical properties of the cell.      Figure 6: Healthy and Trimmed Impulse [23]  As depicted in Figure 6, pulse trimming can be readily identified by examining the sequence of  previously recorded edges and the time intervals that separate them. An accurately executed pulse  should present two edges: one that falls and one that rises, with their order determined by whether  the pulse is in charging or discharging mode. These edges should be spaced by the specified pulse  duration. Any departure from this expected pattern indicates that the pulse has been trimmed,  trimming happens when the cell voltage reaches its threshold during the pulse duration, leading the  measurement system to transition from constant current (CC) mode to constant voltage (CV) mode.  Trimming consistently coincides with a secondary issue: distortion resulting from the characteristics  of the open-circuit voltage (OCV). Pulse distortion manifests at both low SOC values, close to 0, and  high SOC values, close to 1, due to the steepness of the OCV curve in these regions, as illustrated in  Figure 6. Consequently, even a minor variation in SOC during the pulse duration can lead to a  considerable change in the cell's open-circuit voltage 𝑈𝑜𝑐 , hereby impacting the recorded waveform  U. This distortion modifies the shape of the waveform, making it no longer solely dependent on the  time constants 𝜏1 and 𝜏2, which is critical for the accurate identification of these constants [23].  2.4.4  Matrix of tests conducted   The HPPC protocol begins by bringing the cell to either a fully discharged (0% SoC) or fully charged  state (100% SoC), followed by adjusting the cell to the desired target SoC level. Once the target SoC  is reached, the cell undergoes a rest period of at least one hour to allow for electrochemical and  
--- FILE: 2024_12_MulèCascio.pdf | PAGE: 14 ---
  Antonino Mulè Cascio    14  thermal stabilization, ensuring accurate measurement conditions. After this relaxation phase, a brief  current pulse is applied to generate the HPPC curve, which is then used to estimate key parameters  such as resistance, power capability, and relevant time constants. This pulse is typically followed by  another relaxation period, and additional pulses may be applied as needed to refine parameter  estimation is often conducted under different thermal conditions to assess temperature-dependent  behavior [25]. In this study, tests were conducted at 10°C ,25°C and 45°C. For each temperature, the  HPPC protocol was performed at various SoC levels—specifically from 0% to 100% SoC at intervals  of 10% - to comprehensively profile the cell’s performance across its full operational range.  To further enhance accuracy, the relaxation time before and after each pulse should be sufficiently  long to allow the cell to reach equilibrium. The choice of pulse duration also requires careful  consideration: it must be long enough to capture the transient response necessary for parameter  estimation yet brief enough to minimize SoC fluctuations. This balance helps in accurately  determining the internal resistance and dynamic response characteristics without significantly  altering the SoC, which could impact subsequent measurements.  The protocol used is   1) Charge at SOC 100  2) Discharge to desired SOC  3) Relaxation time of 1 h   4) HPPC test (at higher SOC is advised to start the pulse with a negative current, at lower SOCs  to start with a positive current)  5) 1 h of relaxation   6) Discharge followed by another charge to desired SOC   7) Repeat the HPPC test     2.4.4.1  Parameters in the ECM: Fast Dynamics and Slow Dynamics     Figure 7: Example of an Equivalent Circuit Model [24]  The Thevenin ECM, shown in Figure 7, consists of an open-circuit voltage component OCV, an  internal resistance 𝑅0, polarization resistances 𝑅1 & 𝑅2, and effective capacitances 𝐶1 & 𝐶2. In the  ECM 𝑅1 and 𝐶1 are used to simulate the fast charge of terminal voltage induced by the charge  transfer process and their time constants 𝜏1 is generally about 10s. This configuration is generally  considered part of fast dynamics, reflecting surface effects on the electrodes and the kinetics of the  reactions. Specifically, 𝑅1 represents the charge transfer resistance while 𝐶1 represents the  electrochemical double layer capacitance. Furthermore, the product of 𝑅1 and 𝐶1 defines the time  constant for the RC pair.  Conversely, 𝑅2 and 𝐶2, instead, are employed to simulate the slow gradual change of terminal  voltage induced [26].They represent the slower dynamics of the cells in order of hours since they are  
--- FILE: 2024_12_MulèCascio.pdf | PAGE: 15 ---
  Antonino Mulè Cascio    15  more representative of the diffusion processes in the electrolyte and active material. The time  constant 𝜏2  is generally large, usually a few hundred seconds, so this RC network is usually  considered as a part of the slow dynamics. It should be noted that since 𝑈𝑜𝑐 changes slowly in the  actual use of Li-ion batteries, it is usually treated as part of SD as well.  In summary, components of this model can be sorted into two different time scales, Fast Dynamics  and Slow Dynamics, depending on their different dynamic processes. [23]  2.4.5  Meaning of 𝑅0 𝑅𝐶𝑇 𝑅𝑃      Figure 8: 𝑅0, 𝑅𝐶𝑇 and 𝑅𝑃 visualized on the impulse [24]  The initial purpose of the HPPC test is to determine the dynamic power capability of the battery  across a range of voltages. For this reason, before implementing the HPPC test to identify ECM  parameters it is necessary to study the correlation between each parameters and their physical  representation. [25] The HPPC test mainly consists in measuring the voltage drop ( ∆V ) resulting  from a square-wave current load ( ∆I ) applied to a cell. The resistance ( 𝑅𝑝𝑢𝑙𝑠𝑒  ) is then typically  defined as the ratio ( ∆V / ∆I) and involves contributions from:  •  Ohmic resistance, 𝑅0 , which comprises all electronic resistances of the cell and the bulk  electrolyte ionic resistance of the battery, it is typically responsible for the steep voltage drop  instantaneous of applying the current pulse.  •  Charge transfer resistance, 𝑅𝐶𝑇 , which is attributed to the charge transfer reaction at the  electrode/electrolyte interface (typically occurring from circa instantaneous up to 2- 5  seconds of applying the current pulse [24] ) is due to the battery’s double layer capacitance.  •  Polarization resistance, 𝑅𝑝 , which accounts for ionic diffusion in the solid phase and is  usually considered to be the rate determining step for Li-ion cells.    Although 𝑅0 𝑅𝐶𝑇 and 𝑅𝑝 are not completely distinguishable at their respective timescales, they are  expected to be the primary contributors to the total resistance of the battery system.  The individual contributions of these three components can be calculated separately to gain an  intuitive understanding of the complex electrochemical processes involved. Conversely, a bulk total  cell resistance can be derived from the overall voltage drop during the pulse, as commonly reported  in the literature. However, a drawback of using direct current to assess resistance is the inability to  fully isolate the different resistance components, since all contributions to resistance are imposed  simultaneously [24].  When the current load is removed, the system reaches equilibrium, allowing the non-intercalated  cations in the double layer to diffuse back into the bulk electrolyte. The difference in Li-ion  
--- FILE: 2024_12_MulèCascio.pdf | PAGE: 16 ---
  Antonino Mulè Cascio    16  concentration at the electrode/electrolyte interface between the rising and falling edge of a pulse,  results in a small voltage difference and consequently 𝑅0. [24]  The second order ECM also includes effective capacitance 𝐶𝑝𝑎 and 𝐶𝑝𝑐 which represent the transient  response of the battery’s charge and discharge process and the polarization characteristics  respectively [24], [27]. They also represent the double-layer capacity, formed between the electrode  surface and the electrolyte.  All resistances, capacitances, as well as the Open Circuit Voltage (OCV) depend on the cell's State of  Charge (SOC), which is estimated based on the cell current.  2.4.5.1  Variation of the Parameters in comparison to Temperature, SOH and Degradation  All these parameters are functions of the State-of-Charge (SOC) of the battery, temperature (T) and  current (I) [27]. According to the literature [28], it is evident that the ohmic resistance 𝑅0 experiences  a notable increase as the temperature decreases across all states of health (SOH). Additionally, the  influence of SOH on 𝑅0 is temperature-dependent, highlighting a significant interaction effect  between SOH and temperature. It has also been noted that it tends to rise with battery aging,  particularly at lower temperatures; however, this increase in resistance is not as pronounced at  higher temperatures across varying SOH levels. Lastly, 𝑅0 shows minimal variation with respect to  the state of charge (SOC).  Moreover, as detailed in [28] , the polarization resistance 𝑅1 is observed to increase with SOH. Unlike  the ohmic resistance 𝑅0, this effect is consistent at both elevated and reduced temperatures. 𝑅1 also  demonstrates an increase with decreasing temperature, exhibiting a relatively linear and inversely  proportional correlation. Importantly, the polarization resistance 𝑅1 shows significant variation with  SOC, with resistance values rising as the battery approaches both high and low SOC levels. This  parameter exhibits a greater degree of variability in the collected data.   It is also stated that the polarization capacitance 𝐶1 is notably influenced by SOH across all SOC and  temperature conditions, as indicated by the parallel nature of the three surfaces.   Overall, 𝐶1 decreases with decreasing SOH while increasing with rising temperatures. The effects of  temperature and SOC on the polarization capacitance remain unchanged with respect to SOH,  indicating that the interaction effects between temperature and SOH, as well as SOC and SOH, are  not significant.   Taking into account the relationship between parameters and degradation it can be observed that  an increase in battery degradation does not exhibit a clear trend in the behavior of R0. However,  during degradation 𝐶1 tends to decrease with increasing degradation, while 𝑅1 increases. This is due  to the fact that the RC pair represents the charge-transfer phenomenon, and degradation affects the  available charge within the battery, corresponding to its capacity. Changes in these parameters may  not be significant over short periods, such as during a few drive cycles, but can become pronounced  over the battery's lifetime [29].  All three ECM parameters 𝑅0, 𝑅1, and 𝐶1 are affected by SOH, as well as SOC and temperature.  Therefore, it is possible to represent each of these parameters as a function of SOH and SOC [28].  2.5 Thermal Sensors  During the HPPC and discharge tests, cell temperatures were monitored using thermocouples and  Fiber Bragg Gratings (FBGs).   Thermocouples utilize the Seebeck effect, generating an electromotive force (EMF) when there is a  temperature gradient between two junctions, allowing accurate temperature measurement without  interfering with the measurement medium [30].  For this study, Chromel-Alumel thermocouples were used, chosen for their stable EMF-temperature  relationship.  
--- FILE: 2024_12_MulèCascio.pdf | PAGE: 17 ---
  Antonino Mulè Cascio    17  FBGs instead are optical sensors sensitive to both strain and temperature, reflecting light at a specific  wavelength (Bragg wavelength) that shifts in response to temperature changes. Despite their high  sensitivity and quick response times, FBGs are more costly and require careful calibration [31]. For  this thesis measurement these sensors were put inside low bend loss (LBL) fibers, which allow a  maximum radius bend of 6 [mm], in order to maintain the surface strain level below 1%. All the  fibers had a coating of 70 [μm], made of a particular material called ORMOCER-T® while the  interrogator used to employ the fibers was the FAZT IX I4W.  Finally, the software used for controlling and monitoring interrogator and fibers was Femtosense®,  which allowed also to analyze and extract data in combination with NI Labview.  2.6 Analysis ex-situ    An ex-situ analysis refers to examining the cell outside its functional or operational environment,  typically under controlled lab conditions. Initially, an overview of the cell's external characteristics  is performed, taking into account the current collector, casing materials, and safety vents.  Subsequently, an examination of the cell's internal components can be conducted, including the  multilayer electrode roll and the current collector connected to the external circuit.  Before opening the cell, it is essential to fully discharge it through a resistor to eliminate any risk of  electric shock to the operators. Once discharged, the cell can be opened, and its internal components  can be examined. After carefully separating the internal structure, the main components can be  identified, extracted, and analyzed, typically using techniques such as Field Emission Scanning  Electron Microscopy.    3.   Experimental campaign  The experimental campaign was divided into two main phases. In the first phase, preliminary tests  were performed on the prismatic cells and LFP cells to assess their key characteristics. At first an ex- situ analysis on the NMC was carried out to evaluate the cells chemistry under controlled conditions,  following this, the cells underwent various tests, including discharges at different C-rates and  different temperatures. Additionally, Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS) measurements  were taken, and the cells were studied under compression to assess the impact of mechanical stress  on their performance.  In the second phase, the cells were subjected to Hybrid Pulse Power Characterization (HPPC) tests,  which provided voltage response data under applied current. This data was then used to develop a  Simulink model designed to estimate the aging conditions of the cells and simulate the changes in  cell performance over time as the aging process progresses.  The final outcome of the second phase was the successful validation of the HPPC Simulink model,  which accurately simulated the performance of both NMC (Nickel Manganese Cobalt) and LFP  (Lithium Iron Phosphate) cells. A comparative analysis was then conducted between the BOL and  aged cells parameters for both cell chemistries, providing insights into how aging affects cell  performance over time.  3.1 Nickel Manganese Cobalt (NMC) battery   3.1.1  Analysis ex-situ  An ex-situ analysis was conducted to investigate the main characteristics of the cell. This process  began by discharging the battery through a low-resistance load, effectively creating a controlled  short circuit to enhance safety and eliminate electrical risks. After the discharge was complete, the  cell casing was carefully opened to allow inspection of its internal structure. Inside, a tightly wound  multilayer roll connected to the current collectors was revealed. Upon unrolling the roll, it was  observed that the two electrodes were separated by a plastic separator and immersed in an  
--- FILE: 2024_12_MulèCascio.pdf | PAGE: 18 ---
  Antonino Mulè Cascio    18  electrolyte solution. The multilayer roll was then stored in a controlled environment to facilitate the  evaporation of the electrolyte. Once the drying process was complete, the positive and negative  electrodes were separated, and samples were collected for further analysis. These samples  underwent examinations using Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) at the Department of  Mechanics of Politecnico di Milano. The analysis was performed with a Field Emission Scanning  Electron Microscope (FE-SEM), known for its ability to produce high-resolution images of material  microstructures. This microscope operates under high-vacuum conditions to prevent interference  from gas molecules with the electron beam and the secondary or backscattered electrons generated  during imaging. The FE-SEM analysis provided detailed information on the surface morphology  and structural properties of the electrodes, enabling an estimation of the composition and overall  architecture of the battery materials [32].  After careful analysis, it was possible to estimate the composition and structure of the materials used  in the battery.   •  As it is shown in Figure 9 ,the negative electrode, or anode, is made of graphite and exhibits  spherical grains with an average diameter of 9.26 μm. Given that the anode has a thickness of 24.5  μm, it can be hypothesized that the structure consists of at least two layers of graphite.  Additionally, small traces of contamination from materials such as zirconium and silicon were  detected, which could suggest some impurity during the manufacturing process or from external  sources. These findings provide useful insights into the anode's microstructure and potential  sources of degradation.    Figure 9: Grains of the Negative Anode Mag. 10.00 K X  •  As it is shown in Figure 10 ,the positive electrode, or cathode, is composed primarily of Nickel  (Ni), Manganese (Mn), and Cobalt (Co) in a near 1:1:1 ratio, with respective percentages of 3.9%,  3.4%, and 3.0%. This confirms that the cathode is based on a Nickel Manganese Cobalt (NMC)  chemistry. In addition to these primary elements, graphite is present, which suggests its role in  enhancing conductivity and overall performance. The analysis also detected contaminations of  Aluminum and Fluorine, which could be indicative of impurities or additives from the  manufacturing process. The grain size of the cathode material was found to be 5.21 μm, providing  additional insight into its microstructure and potential performance characteristics.

  Antonino Mulè Cascio    19              a)                b)          Figure 10: Grains of the Positive Anode a) Mag. 1.00K X b) Mag. 20.00 K X  3.2 Preliminar tests  After identifying the battery's chemistry and primary characteristics, it was possible to carry out  preliminary testing, focusing initially on deriving the Open Circuit Voltage (OCV) profile. Then for  a deeper understanding of these degradation effects, Differential Voltage (DV) and Incremental  Capacity (IC) analysis methods have been applied. Further tests were conducted under various  conditions, including different temperatures, C-rates, and compression states (with and without  mechanical compression), to observe how these factors influence the battery's electrochemical  behavior and capacity over time. Finally, Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS) tests were  conducted to gain a deeper understanding of the cell’s resistance.  3.2.1  Discharges at different C-rate and Temperature  As illustrated in Figure 11, discharged profiles at lower C-rates, such as 0.04C (0.2 A) and 1C, show  higher capacity retention. Conversely, as the C-rate increases, the curves shift downward, indicating  a reduction in capacity. Both the C-rate and temperature play critical roles in influencing ion  mobility and diffusion within the solid-state structure of the battery, which significantly impacts its  overall performance.  A higher C-rate intrinsically results in accelerated capacity fading due to the increased heat  generation within the battery and the mechanically induced damage to the active materials. Further  analysis of effective current and capacity loss at various C-rates reveals that the rate of battery  degradation intensifies as effective current increases, this is largely because the higher currents place  additional thermal and mechanical stress on the cell, contributing to faster wear and a decline in  long-term capacity retention [33].  Since the voltage change is directly proportional to the applied current—higher currents lead to  more substantial voltage drops, ultimately affecting the battery's capacity and efficiency. This  relationship highlights the importance of selecting the appropriate C-rate for battery applications,  particularly in scenarios where optimal capacity and efficiency are crucial. Proper management of  C-rate and temperature conditions is essential for ensuring that the battery performs within its  intended parameters.    
--- FILE: 2024_12_MulèCascio.pdf | PAGE: 20 ---
  Antonino Mulè Cascio    20    Figure 11 and 12: Discharges at different C-rate (A) and Temperature (B)  The effect of temperature on battery capacity is more pronounced than that of the C-rate, primarily  because temperature influences ion mobility and diffusion within the solid-state structure of the  battery. As shown in Figure 12, a decrease or increase in the operating temperature leads to a change  in the battery's capacity, this is due to the fact that increasing temperature increase the degradation  rates of all components in the LiB which include maximum charge storage capacity [34].At low  temperatures instead there is a significant cell resistance polarization leading to a lower state of  charge and causing a significant decrease of the capacity and faster degradation upon continuous  cycling. The increased resistance at low temperatures is believed to be mainly associated with the  changed migration behavior of Li+ at each battery component, including electrolyte, electrodes, and  electrode-electrolyte interphases [35].  3.2.1.1  Impact of Compression on battery performance   After conducting preliminary tests on the cells the impact of compression on the batteries was  studied to better take into account the external stresses on the battery and the changes in  performance that would be shown.  3.2.1.2  Compression at different Temperatures  In the second part of the study, it was observed that applying compression affected the cell's  available capacity. Differences in the discharge curves were observed when comparing discharges  conducted with and without compression, which influenced both the shape and slope of the curves.  Additionally, tests were performed at varying temperatures—10°C, 25°C, and 40°C—which also  resulted in noticeable changes in the discharge profiles, further highlighting the impact of  temperature on the cell's performance.     Figure 13: Comparison between Compressed discharge and Not Compressed   In Figure 13, the difference between a compressed battery and an uncompressed one is evident, with  compression decreasing the cell’s capacity by approximately 300 mAh. It is in fact reported in  literature that the extracted energy decreases with the increase in the external pressure. It is also  
--- FILE: 2024_12_MulèCascio.pdf | PAGE: 21 ---
  Antonino Mulè Cascio    21  reported that compression affects capacity and that a lack of compression correlates with accelerated  aging. This occurs because an uncompressed battery, free to expand, is more vulnerable to  mechanical stresses that can cause damage. For this reason, automotive battery packs are often  designed with cells stacked and compressed to prevent swelling [36].  External mechanical pressure significantly affects the electrical performance of lithium-ion batteries  (LIBs) by altering the separator's porosity and the electrodes' wettability, which in turn impacts  capacity fade during the battery's lifecycle. In the literature [36], it has been shown that the  interaction between temperature, pressure, and discharge rate contributes to the nonlinear behavior  observed in LIB performance. This nonlinearity arises from a combination of interconnected  phenomena: mechanical pressure can reduce electrode delamination, compress the separator, and  enhance electrode wettability. While reduced delamination and improved wettability generally  have positive effects on performance, excessive compression of the separator can lead to pore  blockage and increased tortuosity, ultimately degrading battery functionality. The extent of these  effects depends on the material properties and technology used in the separator, defining the  pressure threshold beyond which performance deterioration occurs. Understanding these  interactions is essential for optimizing battery design and ensuring reliable operation over time.  3.2.2  Discharges at different conditions BOL vs AGED    Figure 14: Difference between BOL vs AGED conditions  In Figure 14, it is possible to observe the differences in performance between the battery at the  beginning of life (BOL) and after it has undergone calendar aging. The NMC was subjected to  calendar aging at a SOC of 80% and 50%, at a temperature of 60°C for 120 days. The aging process  had a noticeable impact on the battery's capacity, reducing it by approximately 150 mAh. This  capacity reduction is a direct consequence of the chemical and physical degradation that occurs over  time, which compromises the battery's ability to hold charge and maintain its performance,  especially at high C-rates. The comparison between BOL and aged conditions highlights the  significant effect of long-term storage and elevated temperature on battery degradation. [37]

Over extended use, batteries exhibit changes in their  voltage response, which can be observed through shifts or alterations in the peak positions. Specifically, the heights and shapes of the peaks in the IC curve offer insights into the  changes in the electrochemical reactions occurring within the battery, as well as the increase in  internal resistance. This reduction in active material and capacity can be attributed to the degradation of  the electrode materials, which occur over time due to thermal stress, cycling, and other aging  mechanisms. The IC curve, therefore, serves as a diagnostic tool for identifying the onset of aging  and understanding the underlying degradation processes, particularly in terms of the battery's  ability to store and deliver energy efficiently.  3.2.4  Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS)  Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS) was used to characterize the cells, focusing primarily  on evaluating the high-frequency resistance (HFR) parameters. Since electrochemical impedance  varies as a function of frequency, adjusting the frequency allows for the distinction between fast and  slow phenomena within the cell.  
--- FILE: 2024_12_MulèCascio.pdf | PAGE: 23 ---

Hybrid Pulse Power Characterization (HPPC) Model  4.1 HPPC profile and results  In the second part of this thesis, various tests were conducted to collect data to set up an equivalent  circuit model. The protocol used consisted of laboratory tests, identification of cell parameters based  on the test results, and creation of a simulation model in the MATLAB/Simulink environment,  utilizing the Simscape Electrical library. To develop the model, the laboratory tests performed have  been discharged tests to estimate the actual cell capacity and HPPC tests to determine the equivalent  circuit parameters. SOC–OCV testing involved a complete charge/discharge cycle at a C-rate of  1/25C so that the OCV-SOC curve was derived, then HPPC tests were conducted according to the  test profile shown in Figure 22 and 23:    Figure 22 and 23: HPPC profile, (A) current steps and (B) a singular corresponding voltage response  
--- FILE: 2024_12_MulèCascio.pdf | PAGE: 25 ---
  Antonino Mulè Cascio    25  The tests conducted followed a structured protocol: a current impulse was applied, and the resulting  voltage response was measured. The current profile used for testing alternate between +1C and -1C  pulses, with each pulse followed by a relaxation period. Tests begins after charging the battery and  allowing a 1-hour relaxation. Each test included a preliminary 5-second measurement to capture the  initial open-circuit voltage (OCV), followed by an impulse, a relaxation phase, another impulse, and  a final relaxation before discharging the battery by 10% to repeat the test till the battery reaches SOC  0. Ideally, relaxation times should exceed the cell’s time constants, allowing voltage stabilization  before the next pulse, however, given the large time constants for LFP cells, a 10-minute relaxation  period between pulses was used. In the case of NMC cells, a pulse duration of 30 seconds was  sufficient, while LFP cells required a longer duration of 60 seconds due to their extended time  constants. This is to both better describe the time constants and to increase the accuracy. It is in fact  reported [39] that if the pulse width and rest time are both small, increasing either of them can  improve the identification accuracy significantly. For high states of charge (SOC), a discharge pulse  was applied first to avoid overvoltage and prevent the system from switching to constant voltage  (CV) mode. For low SOC values (near 0), the sequence was reversed, with a charging pulse applied  first to avoid excessive voltage drop. Using a fitting model, parameters that describe the system were  derived, these parameters formed the basis for an equivalent circuit model (ECM) to represent  battery behavior. As detailed in the following chapters, the model components characterize the  battery's voltage response and enable performance simulation.
